Do you see the slightly weird looking <radical>rake</radical>? It's lying on the floor, waiting to be used.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>substitute</radical>.

Your leader (ｲ) has become a bent spoon (匕). Well, that's quite a <radical>change</radical>. Why would your leader transform like this? Maybe they're leading a movement of people transforming into spoons, like in protest or something. And why not? If you want to change the world, start by changing yourself. Into a spoon.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>peoples</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>surplus</radical>.
If you were to look at a <radical>giant</radical> from above, this is what you would see. Do you see the head and two arms? The giant is facing towards the right.
This is the <radical>barracks</radical> radical. Do you see that soldier doing push-ups in front of the barracks? That's gonna be you if sarge finds out you skipped review duty.

The life thread is cut with a sword by the Moirai. They are, in Greek mythology, the ones who decide when to let you die, by cutting your life thread. This is probably most well known in the story of <radical>Hercules</radical>, so we'll go with that with this radical.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>specialty</radical>.
I don't know what this thing is, but it's <radical>lovely</radical>. It has two eyes, a funny mouth, and a scraggly beard. It's lovely, and nothing else, okay? So remember it that way.

Do you see the big guy on top, holding spatulas and looming over a grill and open flames? That's why this is the <radical>charcoal</radical> radical. Without charcoal, this guy ain't grillin' nothin'.
This is the <radical>clothes</radical> radical, it looks a little like clothes hanging on a clothes hanger, right? Now that these clothes are hung up, you've gotta get to the rest of that pile…

We can see your rib cage, and bad shellfish are the ones to <radical>blame</radical>. These shellfish gave you terrible food poisoning, and now you're so emaciated that your rib cage is visible. Don't blame yourself for what you ate — blame the shellfish for doing this to you.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>district</radical>.
Hey, it's that giant you learned before. But... but its arms are chained. They're chained because you caught the giant and now it's your <radical>servant</radical>!
If you look at this radical right, you'll see a <radical>NOSE</radical> (with a squinty eye on the left).
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>above</radical>.

Do you see the big guy standing on top of that giant lip ring? A little odd. Wait, is he using it as a diving board? Very odd. Does he want to jump into that odd-looking mouth beneath him? How supremely odd!

You only have some ice and a stick for your spoon, because you're way up north. At the top of the world, there's only ice to eat, and — if you're lucky — a bit of stick for flavor. That's the <radical>north</radical> for you.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>oversee</radical>.

Under the ground there's a thread. It traces your <radical>lineage</radical>. Follow it down through generations of buried relatives to find out your lineage probably involves Genghis Khan or Charlemagne. Feel the thread and the dirt in your hand as you literally trace your lineage.

Poor turtles. We don't like them here. This is a <radical>turtle shell</radical>. See the shell with just a tail remaining? It's the only thing we didn't remove off the turtle. It's just a shell with a tail, so basically it's just a turtle shell.
This is the <radical>call</radical> radical. Do you see how it looks like an old-timey phone with the handset on top? "Nothing better than a phone for making a call," as my dad used to say.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>exit</radical>.

Imagine this in your mouth. It's one tooth that sticks out more than any other. It's your <radical>fang</radical>. Can you see this sticking out of a wolf mouth instead? Try that if you can't picture yourself with a fang this cool.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>line up</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>showy</radical>.

He's a creeper and he's Four-T (forty). If someone like this creeps on you, they're just a <radical>bully</radical>. When you get to forty you aren't supposed to creep on people anymore. You bully. You jerk.

See how there’s a lid on top of the treasure chest? That’s because the whole thing is a <radical>rocket</radical> which contains all the necessary items (treasures) to live in outer space. The bottom part of the radical shows you that this is a top secret project, though, so keep this private in your own head.
There's a door over the bookcase. That makes this a <radical>library</radical>!

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>beforehand</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: What does your mama tell you to do in the street? Look before you cross! You gotta do it beforehand, or it could be too late.
See the CP in this radical? It stands for <radical>Cat Pirate</radical>. Meoaarrrr.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>same</radical>.

See that lid on top? It's actually a flying saucer. "Take me to your leader," say the aliens inside, arriving from a strange-looking moon. When do you think you'd see something like this? At <radical>night</radical>. When people see UFOs or the moon, it's usually night. That's why this is the night radical.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>certain</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>interval</radical>.

Put a lid on the mouth of a child and what will you <radical>receive</radical>? At best, a very unimpressed look from that poor child. If you want to receive nice things, putting lids on children’s mouths isn’t the way to go about it.

This is the inside radical, since it looks like a person (人) inside a… head (冂)? I guess if you think about it, every person is sort of trapped inside their own head. Imagine a second, tinier version of you sitting up inside that head of yours, like a mecha pilot. Yep, that's real you. The you inside.

Your flowers become your servants. You plant them, you water them, you bring them up, then you cut them down and put them in your <radical>storehouse</radical>. They do what you want because they become YOUR servants, not the other way around. That's why you can tell them to sit in the storehouse where they wait until you come to eat them.
See the rock in the <radical>catapult</radical>? It even has little legs to hold it steady so it can catapult better.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>member</radical>.
This looks like a <radical>claw</radical> of some kind already, making it quite easy!
See the guy? See how he was CUT IN HALF??? That must have been one heckuva <radical>slice</radical> to do that to a person.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>belt</radical>.

This is the <radical>turtle</radical> radical. You can tell because there's a big shell in the middle, a whole head on top, and a tail at the bottom. You probably could have guessed this was a turtle without me even telling you, it's so turtle-like.

See the <radical>shuriken</radical> stuck in the ground? In case you don't know, a shuriken is just a
throwing star — that thing ninjas use. This looks just like one, right? That's why it's the shuriken radical.

This radical looks like a big, weird caterpillar bug thing. But, for the sake of everyone's sanity, we'll just call it <radical>sake</radical>, okay? Keep in mind, we mean sake as in "for the sake of X," not as in the alcoholic beverage!

This radical is a <radical>greenhouse</radical>. There are windows in the middle, flowers protruding along the top, and plants bursting up through the trellis below. The plants have officially taken over!

Alternatively, you can remember this one using the radical components:
Flowers need the sun to get big. To help them grow as big as possible, we put them in the greenhouse.
The sun AND the moon are out? With both their light-powers combined, it's incredibly <radical>bright</radical> outside.

There's a shellfish, but it's got some kind of fancy headgear. Is that… a crown, perhaps? It looks really <radical>valuable</radical> — and the shellfish wearing it must be even more valuable to be worthy of such a status symbol!

Alternatively, you can remember this radical with its components: in the middle of the ground, there's a shellfish. Why? 'Cause it's super valuable. The safest place to keep a valuable shellfish is buried in the middle of the ground.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>departure</radical>.

This radical is the sun with its hair sticking out. Why is the sun's hair sticking out like this? It ate wayyy too many <radical>sweet</radical> things causing it to have too much energy, making its hair stand on end. It also kind of looks like a sweet, sweet candy with the wrapper sticking out. Remember it how you'd like.

This is the radical for <radical>south</radical>. See how it's pointing south? You can think of the cross on top as a compass rose, and the arrow below (that ¥-looking part) as pointing down south. It's a compass pointing nowhere but south!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>right</radical>.

There's an explosion around your legs. It was just as the fortune teller warned. This is the <radical>omen</radical> she was talking about. Think about what happens after the omen hits. What horrible fortune teller magic will happen???
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>prize</radical>.
There's a stick going through some juicy meat. This is a <radical>skewer</radical>.

You see something with a little flag next to it and put it in your mouth. It was spicy! You look at the little flag and it says...hot. You just ate a <radical>hot pepper</radical>.

This is a post with signs on it. And on top is a winter marker, showing that if you go north it's winter up there. The signs say things like "Narnia ↑" and "Meridell ←" and "Bananaland →" so you know it's a <radical>signpost</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>wide</radical>.

The horns on the king give him an ego. Which in turn gives him a sense of <reading>righteousness</reading>. He shouldn't act all righteous like that, but I suppose it's what kings do. If you had horns and a big ego, you'd probably think you were the epitome of righteousness too.

This is a <radical>melon</radical>. Imagine a melon cut in half, and you're looking at its insides from the side. See those precious private melon parts? You're gonna keep those for yourself, because melons are delicious and not for sharing.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>bone</radical>.
This is the shell of a <radical>grenade</radical> that has blown up. BOOM! It exploded, splitting it down the middle.
We already have a roof radical, so we're going to use the secondary kanji meaning for this radical. It's <radical>shop</radical>, remember?
You're sliding some dirt around with a tree you cut down. This contraption you've made is called a <radical>plow</radical>. Use it to push dirt around!
Stand up on the moon so you can look down on your countries. The thing with all the lines and borders are the borders of all the countries you rule, for you are an <radical>imperial</radical>.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>business</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: You have spikes growing out of a sheep with fins. Turn this thing into a business! You could totally charge people money to look at it. Sure, you could also donate it to science, but a business-minded person like you knows a business opportunity when you see one. Step right up! Just five dollars for a glance at the rare spiky mer-sheep!

This kind of looks like big (大), which I think you'll remember you learned by pretending this was a big guy. This big guy, however, has a funny leg... a peg leg. That makes him a <radical>pirate</radical>. Also, his arms are in the "YARRRR" position.

It's kind of hard to see, but if you look at this the right way it looks like a food <radical>can</radical>. See the lid being pulled off in the top-left corner? And that horizontal line in the middle? That’s the can's label.

If you pick up your sword (刀) and see a drop (丶) of blood, it might mean you accidentally grabbed it by the <radical>blade</radical>. Blades are sharp, so be careful when you handle them — you don't want to get drops of blood everywhere.
A turtle that stands up isn't a turtle anymore. It's evolved into a monster. What kind of monster? A <radical>dragon</radical>! Rawwwr.
Yourself (oneself) is in prison. Look at the prison as it wraps around you. It wraps you up and holds you tight. That's why this is the <radical>wrap</radical> radical!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>protect</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>renew</radical>.

Under this roof is a pig with her little ones. Your pig, because it's your <radical>house</radical>! You keep your piggies inside where it's nice and warm. They're all members of your family, so they deserve to live in your house too.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>request</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: Look at the ground! You spilled some water drops, so I request that you wipe them up. I'd do it myself, but you're the one who spilled them, so I'm requesting that you do it. Pretty reasonable request, right?

This radical looks like a small animal (匹) has a crab (其) sticking out of it. Often when a crab is eating a small animal, that small animal was put inside a crab trap to catch the crab, luring it in with the small animal. That's why this radical is <radical>crab trap</radical>.

You see a narwhal struggling with a measuring tape, trying to measure his <radical>height</radical>! His fins can't reach the end of the tape, but of course he wants to include his glorious tusk. Measuring height is not an easy tusk… er, task for a narwhal, but he'll figure it out. Probably.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>name</radical>.

Although a little bit modified, there is a turtle shell that's on a mustache with this radical. The only thing with a mustache that hangs around turtles is Splinter, the giant rat from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. So this radical is <radical>Splinter</radical> (the giant rat).

This looks like the guy from the big radical, but he's got something extra on his belly. That's his exposed belly button, because he's a sumo wrestler now: big and <radical>fat</radical>. In sumo, more fat means more power, so imagine he's been training to get as strong and fat as possible.

You know the animal radical. This is just like that with a little extra. It's an animal already... which means all you have to do is remember what kind of animal. In this case, it's a <radical>badger</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>reality</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>scroll</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>noon</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: You have a <radical>private</radical> <radical>mouth</radical> that's a <kanji>machine</kanji>. But you have to keep your machine mouth private because it would scare all the non-machine people around you.

Who's in the coffin next to that child? It's his <radical>teacher</radical>. Teachers are pretty much dead around 3 p.m. every day, and it's the kids in their class who wear them down. It ain't easy being a teacher, you know.
This radical looks just like a top hat. That's why it's <radical>top hat</radical>!

See all the arms sticking out of this radical? Those are for hanging lots of coats and things on, because this is a <radical>coat rack</radical>. Kind of a weird coat rack, but definitely a coat rack.

See the samurai on top of the giant bean? He's standing over it and using it as a <radical>drum</radical>. Back in the day, samurai used drums to communicate and amp themselves up in battle, and when things were desperate, any ol' giant bean would do. Can you imagine a samurai drumming out a war beat on a giant bean drum?

This radical is made up of horns and older brother. Why horns? They're part of your older brother's new <radical>guard</radical> uniform. He's a guard now, of a bank or a museum. And the horns are actually part of his guard hat, which of course makes him a more intimidating guard.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>feeling</radical>.

This radical looks like a <radical>helicopter</radical> coming straight at you, doesn't it? You can't see the tail part because it's behind the bigger front cab of the helicopter. But you can see the front windows and the big spinning blade on top.

This radical is a <radical>mantis</radical>—you know, the praying kind! See those big buggy eyes, the antennae sticking out on top, and those long, pointed legs underneath? Don't worry though, these guys don't bite.

This radical is made of dirt, legs, and winter. If you have to bury your legs in the dirt in winter, it's probably because you got <radical>frostbite</radical>. You had to leave your dead legs behind. :(

If you look closely and carefully, sometimes you can see some private legs in winter. Whose legs? <radical>Spider</radical> legs! It's too cold for them in winter, so they hide in cracks and crevices, but sometimes you can see their little leggies sticking out anyway.
There's something made of leather with some dirt on the bottom of it. It's a <radical>boot</radical>!

You see a cow in the evening. You get closer and realize it's doing a <radical>dance</radical>. All cows dance in the evening. Can you picture it? The cow is dancing, so majestic, in the setting sunlight.

This radical is made up of blackjack and clothes with the six kanji on top. If you see six people playing blackjack and wearing the same clothes you should know that they're all <radical>nurse</radical>s. Nurses play blackjack together to cool down between shifts and they usually don't have time to change out of their uniforms. That's why this radical is nurse.
There are fins wrapped in a towel in winter. Who is drying these fish fins to eat them? A <radical>penguin</radical>.

This radical means <radical>stomach</radical>, since it kind of looks like one. See the big stomach sitting on top of some intestines that snake downwards? Just keep in mind this radical is specifically for the stomach, and the stomach only — not all the other stuff attached to it.

You could also remember it with a mnemonic: To eat a rice paddy the size of the moon, you'd need a pretty impressive stomach. Every doctor and scientist in the world would probably be jostling to get a look at your incredible stomach and see how you managed to fit a moon-sized rice paddy into it.

If you're wearing a hat and have dirt on your mouth, chances are you're staying in a <radical>cottage</radical>. That's because cottages are usually in the countryside, which means you're likely spending time out in the garden, with a hat on and dirt all over your mouth. You know, your average cottage experience. And hey, this radical even kind of looks like a cottage.
This looks like a box with something sticking out of it. When something is sticking out of something else it's <radical>convex</radical>.
It looks like there is a dent in this box. When there is a hole or a dent in something it's called <radical>concave</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>below</radical>.
When a mama watches over a man, it gives him the <radical>courage</radical> he needs to take on any foe.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>tall</radical>.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>sell</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: A samurai has come bearing foreheads and legs that he's trying to <kanji>sell</kanji>. He thought it was a waste to leave all his slain enemies on the battlefield, so he gathered up their foreheads and legs to sell on the black market for some extra cash. Hey, no judging! A samurai's gotta sell what a samurai's gotta sell, okay?

Lying on the <radical>ground</radical> is something that looks just like the ground, the number <kanji>One</kanji>. Why is this One lying down? It's been shot by the number two. It's lying there, bleeding out and dying. The number One doesn't have long to live.
data.meaning_hint: To remember the meaning of <kanji>One</kanji>, imagine yourself there at the scene of the crime. You grab <kanji>One</kanji> in your arms, trying to prop it up, trying to hear its last words. Instead, it just splatters some blood on your face. "Who did this to you?" you ask. The number One points weakly, and you see number Two running off into an alleyway. He's always been jealous of number One and knows he can be number one now that he's taken the real number one out.
data.reading_mnemonic: As you're sitting there next to <kanji>One</kanji>, holding him up, you start feeling a weird sensation all over your skin. From the wound comes a fine powder (obviously coming from the special bullet used to kill One) that causes the person it touches to get extremely <reading>itchy</reading> (いち).
data.reading_hint: Make sure you feel the ridiculously <reading>itchy</reading> sensation covering your body. It climbs from your hands, where you're holding the number <kanji>One</kanji> up, and then goes through your arms, crawls up your neck, goes down your body, and then covers everything. It becomes uncontrollable, and you're scratching everywhere, writhing on the ground. It's so itchy that it's the most painful thing you've ever experienced (you should imagine this vividly, so you remember the reading of this kanji).

data.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji <kanji>two</kanji> and the radical <radical>two</radical> are the exact same things. Therefore, you know the kanji for two already!
data.meaning_hint: More simply put, you can just know that this kanji is the double of one. It's two lines, that's not all that hard to remember!
data.reading_mnemonic: How do you count to <vocabulary>two</vocabulary>? Just use someone's <reading>knee</reading> (に), and then their other knee. There — two knees!
data.reading_hint: Imagine asking to borrow the two knees of a stranger in the street, just so you can count to two. They're confused at first, but then they present each knee to you in a loving sort of way. Yep, that's two knees alright.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Nice! This kanji is the same as the radical that looks just like it (down to the meaning, even!). The radical is <radical>nine</radical> and the kanji is <kanji>nine</kanji>, making the meaning of this kanji really easy to remember as long as you know the radical first.
data.meaning_hint: If you know your radicals well, this kanji will be a breeze!
data.reading_mnemonic:
Although this kanji has two on'yomi to learn, the pronunciations of those two on'yomi are very similar, so that should make them easier to remember.

When you were <kanji>nine</kanji> your favorite foods were <reading>coo</reading>kies (く) and <reading>cu</reading>cumbers (きゅう). Yum yum!
data.reading_hint: Picture nine-year-old you, lining up nine cookies and nine cucumbers. You dip a cookie in milk and bite into it, then dip a cucumber in and take a bite. Nine bites each until they're all gone. Ah, you miss being nine.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Lucky for you (as is the case with many of the lower-stroke kanji), this kanji is the same as the radical you've already learned. The radical that makes up this kanji is <radical>seven</radical> and the kanji (which is exactly the same) is also <kanji>seven</kanji>. So, if you know the radical, you know the meaning of the kanji as well.
data.meaning_hint: Make sure you know your radicals well and you'll be A-Okay on this one!
data.reading_mnemonic:
You know this kanji means <kanji>seven</kanji>, so let's use that to remember the reading too. <kanji>Seven</kanji> is a lucky number, usually, but this time it isn't so good: 

<kanji>Seven</kanji> percent is all she got on her test after <reading>she chea</reading>ted (しち) on it.
data.reading_hint: How unbelievable is it that someone got <kanji>seven</kanji> percent on a test, especially if you try to cheat? Imagine the girl you loathe the most from school, and imagine her cheating on the test (it's important it's a girl, because of the "she" part in <reading>she chea</reading>ted (しち). Then, imagine your happiness when she's super upset about getting seven percent on it. Serves her right, obviously.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how the radical version of this kanji meant <radical>person</radical> because it looks like a person with their arms down and their legs spread out? Well this is a <kanji>person</kanji> too!
data.meaning_hint: Know the radicals, and you shall know the kanji.
data.reading_mnemonic: Only one <kanji>person</kanji> at <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (にん) complained about the new <reading>jean</reading>s (じん) policy, and that person was you.
data.reading_hint: Imagine how angry you were about the policy. You'll have to come up with something to be angry about yourself (pick something that would actually make you angry, like maybe you're only allowed to wear cut off short-shorts jeans at Nintendo now), but if you pick something good, you'll definitely remember the two readings for this. Just remember you're working at Nintendo, and the policy has to be something about jeans. Then, imagine yourself as the only person complaining and everyone else in their dumb jeans (or lack-thereof) shaking their head at you because you're being a fool.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>enter</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>enter</kanji> as well.
data.meaning_hint: Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
data.reading_mnemonic: Turns out, after you <kanji>enter</kanji> the tent (remember how the person in the radical is entering one?), you're given a <reading>new</reading> (にゅう) one! Why? No idea, but hey — it's new!
data.reading_hint: Imagine lights turning on and flashing, and an entire audience inside. You're at a game show, and the announcer announces the neeeeew tent in his announcey voice. Feel the surprise. Feel the happiness. Feel the excitement. A beautiful new tent all for you!

data.meaning_mnemonic: This isn't exactly the same as the <radical>fins</radical> radical, but it's close. Sometimes this will happen (where we have to use a slightly "modified radical" version of the original), so it's good to understand that now, early on. In this case, we have fins. How many fins? <kanji>Eight</kanji> fins. How do you know that? Because you caught four fish with two fins each.
data.meaning_hint: Count the fins out in front of you, all the way from one to eight. It'll help if you actually do this. Now smell each fin, and think "Wow, I have to smell all eight of these?" Yes, you do.
data.reading_mnemonic: After you count and smell all <kanji>eight</kanji> of your fins, it's time to put them away. You open a large <reading>hatch</reading> (はち) and put them in. This is where you keep your fins, always putting in eight at a time because that's what the boss wants.
data.reading_hint: You've asked him why you can only put eight fins at a time in the hatch, but he never wants to answer. What could be down in the hole that the hatch covers? Why is there a hatch at all? What's with numbers and hatches being mysterious?

data.meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the meaning of this kanji are the same. Both are <kanji>power</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: If you know the radical, you should be feeling fine… No, you should feel powerful!
data.reading_mnemonic: Who has the most power of anyone? It's the <kanji>Power</kanji> Rangers. They are battling their arch enemy <reading>Ricky</reading> (りき). They defeat him and <reading>lock</reading> (りょく) him up, so that he can't hurt anyone ever again.
data.reading_hint: Know anyone named <reading>Ricky</reading> (りき), even a famous person like Ricky Ricardo or Ricky Gervais? Imagine that person's face on the monster the <kanji>Power</kanji> Rangers are fighting. Now, imagine the Power Rangers <reading>lock</reading>ing (りょく) him up. He looks much less scary once he's locked up. Phew.

data.meaning_mnemonic: This <radical>cross</radical> is the symbol for the number <kanji>ten</kanji>. A good way to remember this is to think about all the religions that have crosses and also important sets of tens.
data.meaning_hint: If you're familiar with Christianity, they have a cross and ten commandments. Cross = ten, you see?
data.reading_mnemonic: This cross in particular has <kanji>ten</kanji> <reading>jew</reading>els (じゅう) on it. Two on each arm and two in the middle. That's ten jewels!
data.reading_hint: Picture the jewels on this cross. Maybe draw it out on a piece of paper so the visual really sticks. Each cross is really a symbol for different sets of ten things, and in this case, it's ten jewels.

data.meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is made up of the ground radical (which also happens to be the kanji for "one") and the radical for two. Combine <radical>one</radical> and <radical>two</radical> together and what do you get? <kanji>Three</kanji>!
data.meaning_hint: This one should be pretty self explanatory! Even easier, you can look at this kanji and see it has three straight lines. You know what one looks like. You know what two looks like. So... this is three!
data.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Three</kanji> is the number of chances you get with <reading>San</reading>ta-san (さん). He has a list, and when you get to three "naughty things" lines, that's it. You're on Santa-san's three strikes and you're out list.
data.reading_hint: Picture Santa-san sitting at his desk at the North Pole, eating cookies, and marking one, two, then finally three lines next to names. Once the third line appears, the kid doesn't get presents anymore.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You find a <radical>toe</radical> on the <radical>ground</radical>. It's weird, because it's <kanji>above</kanji> the ground, not where toes belong.
data.meaning_hint: Focus your imagination on how body parts should be buried, not above ground like this. Sure, finding a toe is a little strange, but finding a toe above the ground? Downright silly.
data.reading_mnemonic: Of course when you find a toe <kanji>above</kanji> the ground, you want to know where the toe came from. When you examine it, you see a name written on there. This toe belongs to the local clumsy farmhand, <reading>Joe</reading> (じょう).
data.reading_hint:
Try to remember Joe, the local farmhand. He is a recurring character that will come up anytime the reading for a kanji is じょう.

He is a very big man, and he wears farmer's clothes. It's important to imagine your version of Joe as very big, because it will help us to differentiate him from Jo-Anne, who is the character associated with the similar, but shorter reading (and character) じょ. Although Joe will develop as you go through all the じょう reading kanji, for now, just imagine him as a big, kinda slow dude, who works for a local farmer. Also, he only has nine or fewer toes, apparently.

data.meaning_mnemonic: There's the <radical>ground</radical>, and there's a <radical>toe</radical> just <kanji>below</kanji> it. Yep, you know this means "below" because the ground has a toe below it in this kanji.
data.meaning_hint: Where's that toe again? Below the ground. Maybe it's your toe. Imagine digging it out and thinking, Ugh, why does it have to be under the ground like this? So irritating. Will I be able to sew it back on in time to save it?
data.reading_mnemonic: You keep digging in the ground for the toe <kanji>below</kanji>, but instead you hit something hard and metallic. You try to dig around it, but it's huge. Turns out it's a <reading>car</reading> (か). Keep digging until you unearth the car below. (Inside, you find the toe you were looking for.)
data.reading_hint: There's another useful on'yomi reading that just isn't useful enough for you to learn now. That reading is げ, but we're only going to worry about that much, much later when you have to learn one or two vocab words that read 下 as げ. That's the problem with really common kanji — too many readings.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mouth</radical> radical and the <kanji>mouth</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!
data.meaning_hint: If you learned your radicals — which the WaniKani system forces you to do (unless you're cheating) — you'll already know the meaning of the kanji.
data.reading_mnemonic:
Do you remember seeing the construction worker こういち earlier in the 工 mnemonic? If you haven't yet, not to worry!

For kanji with こう readings (there are a lot of them!) we will use the character こういち every time. He's one of the people who started this website, so we'll do our best in the mnemonics to embarrass him as much as possible. Anyways, remember that whenever you see こう, think こういち.

Everyone agrees, the <kanji>mouth</kanji> is <reading>こう</reading>いち's best feature. You stare at it lovingly as he whispers sweet kanji readings to you.
data.reading_hint: You just can't forget all the cool things about kanji learning he said from that mouth. What a great mouth こういち has. How are the lips of his mouth both so skinny and fat at the same time?

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>big</radical> radical and the <kanji>big</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!
data.meaning_hint: So, if you know the radical, you know the meaning of this kanji as well.
data.reading_mnemonic: There's this big guy (that's how you remember the radical, remember?), and he's wearing a huge <reading>Tie Dye</reading> (たい, だい) shirt. Because he's so huge, the tie dye shirt is also super huge. Everything about him is pretty big, but the tie dye stands out more than anything.
data.reading_hint: When you look at the big guy in your head, imagine him covered in tie dye head to toe. Think about how ridiculous it looks on him, especially since he's such a big guy. Shirt. Sweatpants. Hat. Shoes... it goes on and on.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The radical for <radical>woman</radical> and the kanji for <kanji>woman</kanji> are exactly the same.
data.meaning_hint: That means if you know your radicals well, you know the meaning of this kanji as well! How swell.
data.reading_mnemonic: When you think of a <kanji>woman</kanji>, think of <reading>Jo</reading>-Anne (じょ), though she usually goes by just "Jo."
data.reading_hint: Whenever the reading じょ comes up, we will use the character Jo-Anne. She's quite a short woman, which is to help us differentiate じょ from じょう (who is the giant, oafish farmhand Joe). じょ is a smaller lady, じょう is a giant man.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mountain</radical> radical and the <kanji>mountain</kanji> kanji are the same.
data.meaning_hint: Make sure you're studying your radicals. If you are, then you're studying your kanji as well!
data.reading_mnemonic: Think about <kanji>mountains</kanji> talking to each other, calling each other by their names and adding the Japanese name-ender <reading>san</reading> (さん) to each of their names. "Hello, Everest-<reading>san</reading>." "Oh hi, Fuji-<reading>san</reading>."
data.reading_hint: Be sure to imagine this vividly. The more absurdly you can imagine it, the more likely you are to remember the reading, <reading>san</reading>.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>river</radical> radical and the <kanji>river</kanji> kanji are the same as each other!
data.meaning_hint: So, if you know the radical you know the kanji as well.
data.reading_mnemonic: You're standing next to a <kanji>river</kanji> that's actually used as a <reading>ca</reading>r <reading>wa</reading>sh (かわ).
data.reading_hint: Imagine standing by the river, watching all those cars floating by. They start off really dirty, but the river washes them all clean.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>construction</radical> radical and the <kanji>construction</kanji> kanji are the same!

This kanji also means <kanji>industry</kanji>, which is what construction is, if you think about it. It's all part of the construction industry.
data.meaning_hint: Know your radicals and you'll know this kanji's meaning.
data.reading_mnemonic:
Every time a kanji uses the こう reading (there are a lot!), we'll use the character こういち. He's one of the people who started this website, so we'll do our best in the mnemonics to embarrass him as much as possible. Like this:

You see some <kanji>construction</kanji> in front of you. There, standing shirtless (only suspenders and a hard hat) is <reading>こう</reading>いち, looking back at you.
data.reading_hint:
If こういち as a construction worker somehow doesn't make your legs tremble, that's okay. Just make sure you take this story to a ridiculous enough level to construct a memory in that brain of yours. Be mad at him for not following construction site regulations — where's his shirt, shoes, and pants, and why is he using the bulldozer like that?!

Alternatively, say you really like what you see (you're going to have to imagine a much better-looking version of こういち's face, though). You and こういち make eye contact a little too long. He nods, puts his cigarette out, and takes off his hard hat, letting his long Fabio-esque locks flow. You beckon him over and he comes. What happens next is up to you and your own imagination. My guess is you have a very deep conversation about kanji and the best ways to learn it.

Anyway, when you see 工 in a kanji, it will often take the こう reading. Make sure to remember that, because it comes up quite a bit!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the meaning of this kanji are almost the same! The radical is <radical>sword</radical>, but we're learning Japanese, so can you name a Japanese <kanji>sword</kanji>? That's right, the most common is a <kanji>katana</kanji>, which happens to be the meaning of this kanji as well.
data.meaning_hint: This kanji also looks a lot like the kanji 力. To avoid getting them confused, remember that this one is missing the little nubbin at the top, because 90% of the power comes from the sword to cut your enemies down (which is why the sword kanji is 90% of the power kanji).
data.reading_mnemonic: So now you have this sweet <kanji>katana</kanji> in your hands and you're swinging it around like an idiot. Feel free to make whooshing noises as you swing it around. To become a master katana wielder, you decide to travel to <reading>とう</reading>きょう (Tokyo). とうきょう has the best sword and katana schools in the world, so it makes sense to travel to とうきょう.
data.reading_hint: Imagine trying to travel to とうきょう with your katana. Airport security is not happy with you trying to take a katana on the plane, so you get a full cavity search. I hope you don't have any other swords hidden anywhere.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>dirt</radical> radical and the <kanji>dirt</kanji> kanji are the same!
data.meaning_hint: As long as you know the radical dirt, you know the kanji dirt.
data.reading_mnemonic: Who spends a lot of time in <kanji>dirt</kanji>? <reading>Do</reading>gs (ど) do! Dogs dig in dirt, they roll in dirt, sometimes they try to eat dirt (which isn't so great).
data.reading_hint: Dogs and dirt just go together!

data.meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical you learned, so it means <kanji>thousand</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: As long as you know the "thousand" radical, you'll know this kanji as well!
data.reading_mnemonic: Remember the thousand people going down the slide on a cross in the radical 千? Turns out each one of them was carrying a <kanji>thousand</kanji> <reading>cen</reading>ts (せん). Go ahead and try to calculate what a thousand times a thousand cents would come out to. It's quite a lot, actually.
data.reading_hint: Problem is, as they all tumble down the slide the change falls out of their pockets, so there's a thousand times a thousand cents scattered all over on the floor under the slide.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>evening</radical> radical and the <kanji>evening</kanji> kanji are the same. If you know the radical you know the meaning of the kanji.
data.meaning_hint: Do what you're meant to do. Study those radicals!
data.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>evening</kanji> is when all the <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう) come outside to play.
data.reading_hint:
Young people love staying up the entire evening doing youth-people things, and it's really obnoxious for us curmudgeonly folk.

Note: All the ゆう readings will use the word "youths" as a keyword for the mnemonic, so bear that in mind for any future ゆう reading you'll encounter.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>child</radical> radical and the <kanji>child</kanji> kanji are exactly the same.
data.meaning_hint: So, if you know your radicals, you know your kanji as well! This won't last forever (where radicals are exactly the same as the kanji) so enjoy it while the kanji are still small and simple!
data.reading_mnemonic:
The main reading here is し, so to remember it we'll use this mnemonic:

There is a <kanji>child</kanji> standing in front of you. You look closely at the child but something seems wrong. You rub your eyes and when you open them again, there is a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) in front of you. A sheep?! You yelp, blink again, and it's back to being a child. Are… are all children really just sheep?
data.reading_hint: The child (sheep) runs away and you chase after it. Every time it's about to turn a corner it looks like a sheep again, but whenever you yell and point, it changes back into a child. You're the only one who can see this sheep child!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>small</radical> radical and the <kanji>small</kanji> kanji are exactly the same.
data.meaning_hint: Knowing radicals sure is nice, huh?
data.reading_mnemonic: This <kanji>small</kanji> kanji would be the perfect gift to give to the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). The Shougun loves little things, and the <kanji>little</kanji> kanji represents all of that.
data.reading_hint: You read that right, shougun is written with a long う sound. Make sure you spell it right from now on!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical that look like this are exactly the same. They are both <kanji>street</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: As long as you know the radical street, you know the kanji street.
data.reading_mnemonic: So you're walking down this <kanji>street</kanji>, and off in the distance you see the silhouette of somebody. A lady. Big, black curly hair and red eyes. It is the street-woman, Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう).
data.reading_hint: Mrs. Chou is a character you'll see a lot throughout WaniKani, anytime the reading is ちょう like this one. A lore will develop around her, so the more vividly you can imagine your Mrs. Chou right now, the easier things will get later. In general, she's a mean, evil woman, so as long as you imagine her within those parameters, you're good. And, when I say she is a "street-woman" in the mnemonic, I don't mean she is homeless. She has a nice, middle-class home that's not outside of her financial means. What I'm saying is she wanders the streets looking for evil things to do. These are HER streets. So whenever you see the street radical, know that Mrs. Chou is probably going to show up!

data.meaning_mnemonic: Think about it this way. There is a famous fishing lure inventor, working on his best work ever. He’s old, and he’s been trying to make the best fishing lure for the last 50 years, and knows this will be his last invention. Then he figures it out. He takes one <radical>barb</radical>, and connects the end of it to the top of another <radical>barb</radical>. When he does this, he knows his work is finally <kanji>finish</kanji>ed.
data.meaning_hint: Make sure you look at this amazing fishing lure too - hold it in your hand, see the two barbs fused together. Think about how strange this lure is. Is this really the best in the world? Will this really finish all other fishing lures?
data.reading_mnemonic: How does the fish lure maker test his newly <kanji>finish</kanji>ed lure out? The one he just finished? He gets in a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat and rows out into the sea.
data.reading_hint: Make him think that he can’t just use his new lure on the side of the lake / ocean / whatever. He has to get out there, but unfortunately all he has is a crappy row boat. Imagine the row boat being terrible, leaky, and dangerous, which is why you’re surprised when he goes for it. That’s a terrible row boat to use! If you do this, you'll focus your mind on the rowboat part of things, which will help you to remember the reading of this kanji.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You're sitting on your <radical>stool</radical> <kanji>again</kanji>!!?
data.meaning_hint: Imagine your super comfy, state-of-the-art stool. You take it everywhere with you, and you're always sitting on it. Again, and again, and <kanji>again</kanji>. You love that stool.
data.reading_mnemonic: Your friends are starting to worry about you, because you're always sitting on that stool. "What is the <reading>matter</reading> (また) with you?" they scream! You might want to imagine that all your friends have Jamaican or British accents to make this one fit a bit better!
data.reading_hint: Imagine your friends getting more and more annoyed with your constant stool-sitting habits! They really don't get it. What is the matter with you?! Why can't you just stand like everyone else? Don't you know sitting is the "new smoking"!?

data.meaning_mnemonic: What's something with <radical>nine</radical> sides? Just add a <radical>drop</radical> and you'll have something that's almost a <kanji>circle</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: It's not quite a <kanji>circle</kanji> though. You just need to add a <radical>drop</radical> of liquid to the edges to smooth it out to become a full circle.
data.reading_mnemonic: Do you know about the adorable cat Maru? If not, you should check it out. May seem like a distraction, but if you come back knowing the reading for this kanji, then it's totally worthwhile. When you think about a circle, think about Maru all rolled up in a little circle, being super adorable. Don't tell me it doesn't melt your heart just thinking about it. Alternatively, you could also look at this kanji and think of Maru inside of a box, with his little tail sticking out of it. Whatever works best for you, just get yourself to "Maru."
data.reading_hint: Obviously if you "don't know this reading" well enough, you should watch some more Maru videos. I'll understand... just make sure you come back someday, okay?

data.meaning_mnemonic: On the <radical>ground</radical> you put <radical>barb</radical>s at the bottom of a <radical>slide</radical>. This is your special <kanji>talent</kanji>. When you go down the slide, you fly right past the barbs like some kind of daredevil. Any normal kid would land on the barbs and get hurt, but you have this talent.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine yourself placing the barbs in front of the slide, thinking about how talented you are. It took years of training to perfect this talent. But it was worth it. Everyone on the playground respects you now.
data.reading_mnemonic: But then people start to say that no human could have so much <kanji>talent</kanji>, that you must be a <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい). Are you really a talented cyborg?
data.reading_hint: Cyborgs have brain implants and cool bionic limbs, so they're basically the most talented people around.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The radical <reading>middle</reading> and the kanji <kanji>middle</kanji> are both the same. So if you know one, you know the other.
data.meaning_hint: Make sure you're studying your radicals, otherwise you might find yourself in the middle of a kanji-learning problem.
data.reading_mnemonic:
To remember the reading for this kanji, we use the word Chewbacca to pull up ちゅう in our memory.

If you remember back to the radical 中, a stick was stuck in the middle of the mouth of something. Let's say it was your mouth, and when you look up to see who did it, there stands <reading>Chew</reading>bacca. He's even doing his Chewbacca yell. And it isn't a stick in your mouth, it's an arrow from his bowcaster. It just so happens Chewbacca's bowcaster looks just like this kanji too. Go figure.
data.reading_hint: Imagine the fear and shock you'd feel after finding out it was Chewbacca who shot the middle of your mouth (and head). Touch his fur. Look really close at his weapon. Give him a sniff, too. Just so that memory never fades away.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>five</radical> radical and the <kanji>five</kanji> kanji are the same.
data.meaning_hint: Know your radicals, friend-o.
data.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Five</kanji> is the number of buildings <reading>Go</reading>dzilla (ご) will knock down. Oh, look! There he goes now.
data.reading_hint: One, two, three, four, five—GODZILLA IS HERE GO GO, RUN!

data.meaning_mnemonic: Just imagine a beast with a <radical>lid</radical> for a head and <radical>fins</radical> for feet, running around looking as insane as possible (really imagine it!). When it runs up to you, it shows you the top of its lid-head. On it is written the numbers 666. Why? Because it's a spawn of the devil, and the number <kanji>six</kanji> is the devil's number.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine this beast doing various crazy things, the crazier the better (to help you remember). Make sure all these things are associated with the devil and the devil's number (<kanji>six</kanji>), so you can remember the meaning of this kanji.
data.reading_mnemonic:
Whenever we need to remember the reading ろく we just use the word <reading>rock</reading>. 

So, think about the devil and the devil's number. What is often associated with those things? Why, <reading>rock</reading> (ろく) and roll is. Imagine the lid-head fin-legged beast suddenly blasting out rock music in the middle of his destructive mayhem.
data.reading_hint: Sing along with the monster, if it helps you to remember the reading of this kanji.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Here we have a <radical>head</radical> with a <radical>lid</radical> in it, near the top. Imagine the top of someone's head being closed by a lid. Open that lid up and peer inside... it's full of <kanji>yen</kanji> coins, the currency of Japan. Jackpot! And all those yen coins have a nice <kanji>round</kanji> shape, naturally.
data.meaning_hint: This kanji can mean both "yen" and "round"! It's OK if you can't remember both meanings. But it might help to think about how round the yen coins are inside this person's head, which can also be pretty round…
data.reading_mnemonic: What does the word <kanji>yen</kanji> sound like? It sounds like <reading>えん</reading>. Why? because back in the day, Japanese used to have a "ye" sound, but now it doesn't. Instead, it's an "e" sound, which is why yen = えん!
data.reading_hint: Picture these round えん in your mind. Maybe look some up online too, just to be safe. See how round those yen (えん) are?

data.meaning_mnemonic: The radical <radical>heaven</radical> is the same as the kanji <kanji>heaven</kanji>, making this an easy kanji to memorize.
data.meaning_hint: If you know your radicals well (and you should!) you know the meaning of this kanji well, as well!
data.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Heaven</kanji>... nowadays, people aren't all that good. Things have gotten bad. That's why the acceptance rate to get into heaven is only <reading>ten</reading> (てん) percent!
data.reading_hint: Imagine yourself in line to get into heaven. You're super worried, because you're not sure if you'll get in. You heard there was a one in <reading>ten</reading> chance... those aren't good odds. Feel nervous in your imagination. Feel worried. Feel the pressure as you get closer and closer to the gate... will you make it?? Ten percent!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>hand</radical> radical and the <kanji>hand</kanji> kanji are identical in looks and meaning! That should make things easy!
data.meaning_hint: Make sure you're studying your radicals. It won't be forever that radicals and kanji overlap so nicely like this!
data.reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading て we will use the word "television." You have great hands. Go ahead and look at them. OH MY GOD. You have little <reading>te</reading>levisions (て) on your hands. They are playing the dumbest show you can think of, too, both hands at the same time.
data.reading_hint: You try to shake your hands off, but it's no good. The televisions are stuck, and the volume won't go down. You have no idea how you got these televisions on your hands. All you know is that you want them off right this instant.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>writing</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>writing</kanji> as well.
data.meaning_hint: If you can't remember the radical for writing, maybe you could try… writing it down?
data.reading_mnemonic:
This kanji has more than one important reading you need to learn! But don't worry, here's a mnemonic to help you:

You always put <kanji>writing</kanji> on your <reading>bun</reading>s (ぶん) to keep them from getting eaten by the bun <reading>mon</reading>ster (もん). What kind of writing? Usually it's just an X to show the monster these buns are off-limits. (In fact, it kind of looks like the X part in 文. Hmm…)
data.reading_hint: Imagine writing a big X (or even a big 文) on all your buns, then showing them to the bun monster. Watch as he turns and goes at the sight of the writing, all disappointed. Not today, bun monster.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> radical and <kanji>sun</kanji> kanji are the same, huzzah! Also, if you want to remember <kanji>day</kanji> as well, you can just think about how a day is the time it takes for the sun to cross the sky.
data.meaning_hint: The radical for this one is easy too, making the meaning for this kanji super easy as well!
data.reading_mnemonic:
There are so many on'yomi for this kanji, but since this kanji is so important and common, you'll end up learning them all eventually whether you want to or not. For now, you're only going to have to learn one of the readings, and that one is にち. 

The <kanji>sun</kanji> is so hot. It focused its rays to take out one man... and that man is Friedrich <reading>Nietzsche</reading> (にち), famous philosopher. He philosophized one too many things about the sun, so the sun decided it was time he paid.
data.reading_hint:
This reading will be easier to remember if you know of Friedrich Nietzsche... so do your research and learn about him if you don't. He's a pretty historical dude. Imagine the sun totally pissed off, too. It makes a grunting noise as it builds up a sun beam to blast him off the face of the earth.

Also note that there's another reading worth learning as well: じつ. The reading can be remembered by thinking "<reading>Gee! Two</reading> readings?" Because, seriously, two readings? Too many...

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>moon</kanji> kanji is made up of the <radical>moon</radical> radical. This kanji is also used to mean <kanji>month</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: This should be EZPZ as long as you know the radicals already!
data.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>moon</kanji> really <reading>gets</reading> (げつ) to your <reading>guts</reading> (がつ). Staring at the moon for too long will give you terrible indigestion, so be careful!
data.reading_hint:
Use the げつ reading when this kanji means "moon", in words like "moonlight". Use げつ for counting months, and saying things like "last month and "next month", too. Go for がつ in the names of months, like "January".

Don't worry too much about memorizing this pattern, though. You'll be getting lots of practice soon!

data.meaning_mnemonic: This is another kanji that is the same as the radical. Both <radical>tree</radical> and <kanji>tree</kanji> are the same in looks and meaning.
data.meaning_hint: So, how are those radicals doing? Do you know them well?
data.reading_mnemonic: You’re walking through the trees, looking at them. They look ominous. Suddenly, you trip and fall. The trees start to <reading>mock</reading> (もく) you. Even the mocking birds mock you. It’s terrible. It’s painful. You’re being mocked as you pull yourself up off the ground.
data.reading_hint: Feel the shame, feel the irritation. Make yourself want to run away from those dumb trees that are mocking you.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>water</radical> radical and the <kanji>water</kanji> kanji are the same.
data.meaning_hint: So it should already be clear what the kanji means. As clear as… water.
data.reading_mnemonic: When you go swimming, you launch yourself into the <kanji>water</kanji> from a tire <reading>swi</reading>ng (すい). It's one of those quintessential summer memories, right? Kids swimming in a lake or pond, flying off a swing and splashing down in the water. In your mind, try to associate water with that swing to remember this reading.
data.reading_hint: Maybe it's a hot rubber tire swing burning your arms (that swing's been hanging in the sun all day), or maybe it's a rope swing grazing your palms. Either way, imagine how that feels as you fly off it, then sense the cold water of the lake or pond suddenly enveloping you. Some of the water even gets into your mouth. Imagine it tastes sweet for some reason. Why? All this sensory stuff tied to the water and swing will help you remember the すい reading later. The more vividly you imagine it the better.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>fire</radical> radical and the <kanji>fire</kanji> kanji are the same as each other.
data.meaning_hint: If you know the radicals then this one is EZPZ.
data.reading_mnemonic:
Whenever we need to remember か, we use the word <reading>car</reading>.

For this kanji, when we think <kanji>fire</kanji>, we ought to think of something on fire. What's on fire? It's obviously your very own <reading>car</reading> (か)! Oh Goddd NOOO!
data.reading_hint: Oh no... Oh no!! If you don't have a <reading>car</reading>, imagine what it'd feel like if your car just exploded and burned down. If you do have a car, imagine your own car in this situation. It should be a terrible feeling, if you imagine it well enough. So, when you think <kanji>fire</kanji>, remember the fear you had when your car was given to the flames. Now you have to walk everywhere, sad :(

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>dog</radical> radical and <kanji>dog</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!
data.meaning_hint: Soon there will be very few kanji/radical-same combos ... so enjoy it while you can.
data.reading_mnemonic: Every <kanji>dog</kanji> likes to <reading>ea</reading>t <reading>noo</reading>dles (いぬ). Like that movie where the dogs share a noodle and end up kissing, right? So when you see 犬, just imagine how those two eat noodles.
data.reading_hint: P.S. Don't actually let your dog eat noodles, at least not with marinara sauce. Disney didn't show you how that Lady and Tramp date probably ended — unromantically, with indigestion.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> radical and the <kanji>king</kanji> kanji are the same!
data.meaning_hint: Hopefully you're a king of radicals... because if you are, this kanji was super easy for you!
data.reading_mnemonic: When you see the <kanji>king</kanji> you need to say, "<reading>Oh</reading> (おう) King! Oh King, oh no, oh why are you looking at me like that? Oh King... you aren't going to chop off my head are you? OH NO!"
data.reading_hint:
You need to be polite when you talk to the king and add "Oh" to the beginning, otherwise the king will be pretty angry and bad things might happen.

We're going to use the 王 kanji for all おう mnemonics from now on. So make sure you always remember to say おう King!

data.meaning_mnemonic: There are two <radical>mountains</radical> in front of you... and probably a bunch more around you too. You are in a pass, and don't know how to get out. You are frantically looking for the <kanji>exit</kanji> before you freeze to death. The most important thing is to find the exit from this mountain range - your life depends on it.
data.meaning_hint: In your imagination, really feel like your life depends on getting out. The important part is the feeling of "needing to get out of the mountain pass." If you have this feeling, you'll be more likely to remember that this kanji means exit, because that's what you want to do when you see this kanji.
data.reading_mnemonic: As you're trying to <kanji>exit</kanji> this mountain range, you suddenly realize that someone is actually hunting you. What? Make sure to feel that sudden realization. It's crazy. Then, you find the exit and run towards it. Sadly, the hunter is waiting there, and he <reading>shoots you</reading> (しゅつ) through the leg, knocking you down.
data.reading_hint: Focus on the surprise of realizing you're being hunted while trying to find the exit to the mountain range, then focus on the next part, where you get shot. View it in your head as the hunter shooting you. Powww!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<radical>Narwhal</radical> <radical>mouth</radical>s are on the <kanji>right</kanji> side of their head. In fact, some people didn't think they had mouths at all because they weren't looking from the narwhal's right. Rookie mistake.

See how the "mouth" radical is to the right of the "narwhal" radical? That should help you remember that this means <kanji>right</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine looking at a narwhal from the front. No mouth. Now look at it from its right side. Mouth!
data.reading_mnemonic: How did we know to look from its <kanji>right</kanji>, though? Because the <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう) figured it out. Youths think in ways that older people usually don't. That's why they can see the swirls on cereal, hear the music behind noise, and of course, look at things from the right side.
data.reading_hint:
Imagine a bunch of youths walking in a group and looking at everything from the right. You remember when you were a youth and you used to look at everything from one side too.

Note: All the ゆう readings will use the word "youths" for the reading mnemonic. You can think of these "youths" as a group of younger people who cause a lot of the problems in this world.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Imagine contorting yourself in such a way that your <radical>mouth</radical> now has your <radical>legs</radical> inside it. You've bent your body in all the wrong ways to achieve this. In fact, if you look at yourself, you look like a square now... You're just a person with <kanji>four</kanji> sides.
data.meaning_hint: If you can see this kanji as a kind of square, you should be able to remember it means "four" as well, since squares always have four sides.
data.reading_mnemonic: Now that you have <kanji>four</kanji> sides, you look like a four-sided animal: the <reading>shee</reading>p (し). Look at yourself in the mirror and see an adorable four-sided sheep looking back at you. Imagine yourself with perfectly square wool. (You can only see four sides because mirrors aren't 3D. So you're a flat, cartoonish sheep.)
data.reading_hint: What's better than a four-sided sheep?

data.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Narwhal</radical>s do <radical>construction</radical> with their <kanji>left</kanji> hands (or flippers, I guess). That's because all narwhals are left-handed!
data.meaning_hint: Picture a bunch of narwhals constructing an underwater ice village. They're all working away with their left hands.
data.reading_mnemonic: In their <kanji>left</kanji> hands, the narwhals all hold <reading>saw</reading>s (さ). That's because the ice for their homes is already there, so they just need to saw away at them to make the shapes they want. Narwhal construction is actually very simple.
data.reading_hint: If you're right-handed, imagine trying to use these left-handed saws. It flips and flops all over until you drop it. But if you're left-handed it feels just right!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>book</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>book</kanji> as well.

Take note that the second, third, and fourth meanings of this kanji are <kanji>origin</kanji>, <kanji>real</kanji>, and <kanji>main</kanji>. You can figure this out by thinking about how books mainly have their origins in real life.
data.meaning_hint: Make sure you know those radicals, yo! And good luck with all the meanings (sorry sorry sorry).
data.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Book</kanji>s are one of the best ways to <reading>hone</reading> (ほん) your intellect, you know?
data.reading_hint: Just think about books and how you use them to hone your skills. Or read a book about honing things. Like swords.

data.meaning_mnemonic: There is a line on the <radical>ground</radical> so you <radical>stop</radical>, making a giant sign pop up that says <kanji>CORRECT</kanji>! You obeyed the rules of the road and did the correct thing. Good on you.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine walking, staring at the ground until you come across a line that you're supposed to stop at. If you stop, the big "correct" sign appears, chiming a happy tune.
data.reading_mnemonic: You did the <kanji>correct</kanji> thing, so here's your reward: a <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい) from the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう) himself!
data.reading_hint: Perhaps a slightly unorthodox weapon for a ruler of medieval Japan, but you won't complain about a saber from the Shogun himself!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> has a big <radical>drop</radical> of liquid in his hand... but then he bounces it! The drop was really a <kanji>ball</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: This kanji looks just like a king bouncing a <kanji>ball</kanji>, no? If not, imagine the kanji itself bouncing the drop (the <kanji>ball</kanji>) over and over again. Kanji are surprisingly playful like that.
data.reading_mnemonic: When he's done playing with it, the king gives his <kanji>ball</kanji> to <reading>Tama</reading>ra (たま), the resident ball girl, for safekeeping.
data.reading_hint: Try to remember Tamara the ball girl. She'll come up anytime the reading for a kanji is たま, and usually she'll be involved with some kind of ball or round object. That's her job, after all.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>rice paddy</radical> radical and the <kanji>rice paddy</kanji> kanji are the same, making this one super easy to remember, at least meaning-wise.
data.meaning_hint: Just know your radicals, and you will know your kanji as well.
data.reading_mnemonic:
To remember the reading た, we use the word "taco."

You're in the rice field... but when you lean down to examine the rice more closely, you see that it's not rice that's growing, it's a bunch of little <reading>ta</reading>cos (た), blossoming out of the ground.
data.reading_hint: Smell the tacos. Touch the tacos. Taste the tacos. This is definitely a very strange rice field.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The radical <radical>white</radical> and the kanji <kanji>white</kanji> are the same.
data.meaning_hint: Study your radicals hard! Most important thing!
data.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>white</kanji> team was the first to be able to <reading>hack</reading> (はく) the <kanji>white</kanji> iPhone.
data.reading_hint: Imagine two teams (black and <kanji>white</kanji>), wearing their team colors, working really hard on hacking the iPhone. It is a huge contest, and people are watching with a lot of tension, to see who will hack the <kanji>white</kanji> iPhone first. Feel that tension, and see the colors separating them so vividly. The colors are important, and the excitement of the winner holding up the <reading>hack</reading>ed iPhone is too.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>eye</radical> radical and <kanji>eye</kanji> kanji are the same as each other, so now you know them both.
data.meaning_hint: Well... you'll know them both as long as you studied your radicals, young grasshopper. If you didn't, then you're just a young grasshopper who needs to study their radicals.
data.reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>eyes</kanji> are important to you, right? Sadly, one of your eyes is missing right now, because a sheep grabbed it and pulled it out, and is now running away from you, yelling his sheep call.... "<reading>Mehhhhhh</reading> (め)!"
data.reading_hint: Of course, feel the pain of your eye being gone... and struggle to get it back. You eventually give up because the sheep is too fast, but then you come up with an idea. What if I call out back to the sheep in its own language? Go ahead and cover one eye and start making "MEHHH" noises to see if you can get the sheep to come back to you and give you your eye. It's up to you whether it works or not, but be sure to feel frustrated by its reaction, or happy by it. Either one works.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>stone</radical> radical and <kanji>stone</kanji> kanji are the same thing!
data.meaning_hint: Know your radicals and therefore know your kanji. It's just that simple.
data.reading_mnemonic: You throw a <kanji>stone</kanji> through a window... and now, you can see something very <reading>sexy</reading> (せき).
data.reading_hint: Whoops, maybe you shouldn't throw stones through windows, or you'll see people's sexy times.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The radical <radical>stand</radical> and the kanji <kanji>stand</kanji> are the same thing, so now you know them both.
data.meaning_hint: If you're keeping up with your radical studies, you're also keeping up with your kanji studies!
data.reading_mnemonic: Think of someone who has to <kanji>stand</kanji> up straight for you. These people are pros in hospitality. These are the doormen at the <reading>Ritz</reading> (りつ).
data.reading_hint: Imagine the doormen being extra straight… too straight in their standing. On their uniform is “The Ritz” written in fine lettering, and as you walk past them, they stand up straight and say “Welcome to the Ritz!” Whatever you do, while you’re thinking about it, make sure you think about how they stand up so straight, and associate it with these doormen, who work, specifically, at the Ritz. If you effectively imagine all this, you should be able to remember this on’yomi. Go through it like it’s a movie in your head!

data.meaning_mnemonic: Under the <radical>ground</radical>, there's a <radical>prison</radical> with <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> inmates.
data.meaning_hint: Picture ten thousand inmates crammed into this underground prison. Then, imagine yourself as the warden doing a head count to make sure all ten thousand of them are present.
data.reading_mnemonic: To entertain the inmates, the prison is stocked with <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> volumes of <reading>man</reading>ga (まん).
data.reading_hint: As the warden, you need to select all ten thousand of these manga volumes yourself. Which manga will you choose? Better start drafting your top 10,000 manga list now.

data.meaning_mnemonic: If you use a <radical>slide</radical> to <radical>enter</radical> a building, you'll be sliding for a <kanji>long time</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine a never-ending slide that goes deep down inside a building. You can't see anything in the dark around you, you just plunge down and slide forever. And forever is a long time, my friend.
data.reading_mnemonic: You slide for such a <kanji>long time</kanji> that you get hungry. Luckily, once in a while a <reading>cu</reading>cumber (きゅう) comes tumbling down the slide next to you.
data.reading_hint: Cucumbers are tasty, but not when you've been eating them for a long time.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>now</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>now</kanji> as well.
data.meaning_hint: Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
data.reading_mnemonic: Right <kanji>now</kanji> the <reading>con</reading>dors (こん) are in danger! Not next week, not next year, right now! Haven't you heard that deforestation and pollution are killing all of the condors?!
data.reading_hint: Go outside right now and do something to save the condors. If you don't do something right now there won't be enough time left!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>origin</radical> radical and the <kanji>origin</kanji> kanji are the same!
data.meaning_hint: Know your radicals!
data.reading_mnemonic:
The <kanji>origin</kanji> of everything can be found in <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん). Genji is the name of the main character in the world's first ever novel, "The Tale of Genji." 

Picture him as a rich, pretty boy who cares a ton about his looks and gets along really well with all the ladies. He's also really great at poetry, which helps the lady situation.
data.reading_hint: Genji's origin story is pretty important when it comes to mnemonics and Japanese literature. He's going to keep popping up on your kanji journey, so make sure you remember him!

data.meaning_mnemonic: You have <radical>fins</radical> in <radical>private</radical>. But, you want the world to see them, so you take them <kanji>public</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: Picture yourself in private, with fins. You wish others could see them. "That's it," you decide. "It's time to show the world. I'm going to make my fins public!"
data.reading_mnemonic: You head out into the <kanji>public</kanji> where everyone can see your fins, but... things have changed. All people are the same. There are thousands of <reading>こう</reading>いちs walking around, and they all stare at you (though they pretend like they aren't).
data.reading_hint: How long have you been hiding in private with your fins? The public areas have changed, and all the people have become こういちs. One mother こういち--pushing a baby こういち--looks up and stares at your fins. Now you remember why you never go out in public.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>inside</radical> radical and the <kanji>inside</kanji> kanji are exactly the same, yay. But is the radical inside the kanji here, or is the kanji inside the radical? I don't know, it's inside-ception.
data.meaning_hint: Hold that radical knowledge inside your head! It'll lure new kanji knowledge inside, like bait or something.
data.reading_mnemonic: If you need to get <kanji>inside</kanji> something, the quickest way is to use a <reading>kni</reading>fe (ない). With a knife, you can cut something open and see what's inside it and <kanji>within</kanji> it.
data.reading_hint: Don't get any weird ideas — we're talking about using a knife to get inside bags and packages and stuff. If you imagined something else, that's on you. We can't take responsibility for whatever dark knife-related imagery you may have inside your head.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>fins</radical> that fell onto my <radical>sword</radical> were sliced into many <kanji>part</kanji>s. Following this logic, this also means <kanji>minute</kanji>, which is part of an hour, and <kanji>divide</kanji>, which is the action of splitting something into many parts.
data.meaning_hint: Picture the fins falling onto the sword, and being divided into many parts. And if those fins represented hours, they’d be divided into minutes. Makes sense, right?
data.reading_mnemonic: Now that the fins have been cut into neat <kanji>part</kanji>s, it's time to cut something else: <reading>bun</reading>s (ぶん).
data.reading_hint: This is how you feed your people: neatly divided, delicious buns. Picture these delicious buns divided into perfectly shaped parts. Yummy.

data.meaning_mnemonic: If you have <radical>seven</radical> <radical>swords</radical>, there's only so much you can do with them. The main thing? Probably using them to <kanji>cut</kanji> something.
data.meaning_hint: Take these seven swords and swing them around. <kanji>Cut</kanji> everything in your path, including yourself. Then, think about how dumb it was to try to use seven swords at once, and then feel the pain of the cut you gave yourself. Ouch, ouch ouch.
data.reading_mnemonic: Because having seven swords for yourself is too much, you decide to take the swords and divide them up amongst pairs of people. You <kanji>cut</kanji> them into pairs, and give <reading>sets</reading> (せつ) to everyone who needs them in the village.
data.reading_hint: Just make sure you think about how you need to give them away in <reading>sets</reading>, and not anything else. This is the most important thing to think about in your head as you're trying to establish the mnemonic for your kanji reading memory. It's gotta be sets.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>slide</radical> is <radical>dry</radical> at <kanji>noon</kanji>. The sun is brightest at noon, so it dries the morning dew off the slide, making noon the perfect time to slide.
data.meaning_hint: Picture all the kids out sliding on the slide at noon during their lunch break. It's hot and dry and they're very happy.
data.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Noon</kanji> also happens to be the time <reading>Go</reading>dzilla (ご) decided to attack for the same reasons: it's dry and kids are using the slide.
data.reading_hint: Watch in horror as Godzilla's giant foot crushes all the kids and their slide at exactly noon. You'd better go...

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>narwhal</radical> sitting on a <radical>stool</radical> is your <kanji>friend</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine that narwhal sitting there. It waves its flipper and says "hi friend" to you.
data.reading_mnemonic: "Hi <kanji>friend</kanji>," says the narwhal. "I must warn you about all the <reading>you</reading>ths." (ゆう)
data.reading_hint: Your narwhal friend goes on to warn you about all those youths, and how they will try to take away your friendship with their good looks and young ages.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical, so this means <kanji>fat</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: We've fattened you up with lots of juicy radical knowledge, so this one should be pretty easy.
data.reading_mnemonic: Imagine a <kanji>fat</kanji> person who loves to sleep on <reading>futo</reading>n (ふと).
data.reading_hint: Picture this fat person curled up all cozy-like on their Japanese futon. They look so content! Have you ever slept on a proper Japanese futon, by the way? We're talking premium, cloud-grade comfort — luxurious enough to make you feel like a real fat cat.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <radical>small</radical> <radical>slide</radical>. The thing about small slides is that <kanji>few</kanji> people can use them. Not everyone can fit their bum in a small slide — only a few small ones can make it down.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine a small slide (how could you not, after you see the radicals?). So few people can use this thing, really, but there are a few little ones who can fit on it at least.
