data.meaning_mnemonic: You need your <radical>net</radical> to be <radical>straight</radical> before you <kanji>put</kanji> it on the ground and try to lure something into it. You put your net there to catch something, but if it's twisted or tangled, it won't be very effective.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine that some wild animal wanders into your net. Yes! You knew putting the net there was a good idea. But wait… Oh no, it escaped! It turns out your net wasn't straight when you put it there.
data.reading_mnemonic: Then you decide to <kanji>put</kanji> <reading>chee</reading>se (ち) in your net. With a perfectly straight net and the cheese you put down as bait, there’s no way this fails. Success is all about how you put the net down and the cheese you put in it.
data.reading_hint: Imagine the smell of the cheese as you put it in the net. Maybe a sharp cheddar? The aroma really carries. All the better to attract more animals! Soon you’ll be putting your cheese-eating prey on the dinner table.

data.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Dollar</radical>s and <radical>shellfish</radical> are used to pay <kanji>expense</kanji>s and <kanji>cost</kanji>s. Shellfish used to be used as currency, so they're like the coins that go with dollars.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine opening your bank account and looking at all of your monthly expenses. Now drag the little dollar and shellfish icons over to cover all of those costs.
data.reading_mnemonic: What is the biggest <kanji>expense</kanji> and <kanji>cost</kanji>? It's the <reading>hea</reading>t (ひ) bill.
data.reading_hint: When you see how expensive your heat is, you feel a heat going through your body too.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> only uses the <radical>helicopter</radical> with the highest <kanji>value</kanji>. They choose to fly in only the very best, most valuable helicopter. That's why it's worth way more than the others. Actually, any helicopter they use goes up in value. That's the amazing effect of a good leader.
data.meaning_hint: Can you understand the value of this helicopter? The leader flew it to war and back! So of course it's worth a lot!
data.reading_mnemonic: To further increase the helicopter's <kanji>value</kanji>, the leader tied it to a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). Wow, now it has the value of a helicopter and a car combined! For a total value of… Well, imagine for yourself what value the car adds.
data.reading_hint: Imagine driving a valuable car with the leader's helicopter on top. Yeah!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>womb</radical> is a <radical>circle</radical> of <radical>power</radical> where a <kanji>force</kanji> of nature is formed. The womb has the power to create life. Life is a force of nature, and the circle of life starts in the womb.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine yourself in the womb, the circle of power. You’re being born into the world. Feel the force of your mother all around you.
data.reading_mnemonic: Now pretend you're the mother. You'll need all the <kanji>force</kanji> you can muster to bring that baby into the world, so you grab hold of your special <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい) and slice it about in the air to give you the extra force you need.
data.reading_hint: All that force works wonders, and when the baby's born you slice through the umbilical cord with your saber.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>Viking</radical> who knows how to use a <radical>bathtub</radical> will have to <kanji>manage</kanji> all the baths for the other Vikings. Vikings aren't so great with bathing... if you can get one Viking to figure it out he has to manage the rest of them.
data.meaning_hint: Picture a Viking trying to manage his Viking friends so they'll use the bathtub properly. He has to manage which people go in when, how hot or cold the water is, and provide all the soap. It's a very important job.
data.reading_mnemonic: The poor Viking trying to <kanji>manage</kanji> all the others keeps having to confiscate <reading>a</reading>corns (えい). "You can't take baths in acorns and wood, it has to be water!" he shouts.
data.reading_hint: Some of the Vikings managed to fill their bathtubs with acorns and are trying to rub themselves clean with them instead of water...

data.meaning_mnemonic: You can use a <radical>jackhammer</radical> to <kanji>indicate</kanji> and <kanji>show</kanji> someone where the prize is buried. You buried the prize to keep it safe, but the jackhammer is great at unearthing it. Jackhammers do a great job and show where the treasure lies. They indicate quite clearly where one needs to go.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine using this jackhammer to show someone where the prize is buried. Feel the vibrations through your hands and the rest of your body.
data.reading_mnemonic: Actually, you're unearthing <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ). He’s the treasure. For your soul. He’s here to show you that Jesus is still a hip and cool guy and he wants to <kanji>indicate</kanji> to you that having faith in Jesus and God and stuff is super rad. Jesus is all like, “Who has two thumbs and wants to <kanji>show</kanji> you the way of the Lord? This guy.”
data.reading_hint: Picture Jesus getting all over the top and super preachy about his religious beliefs. He’s doing everything he can to indicate to the crowd that he’s the best, and show them how cool he is. Listen to Jesus preach to the crowd, desperate for their attention.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You take all of your <radical>thread</radical> and <radical>allocate</radical> them into one place to <kanji>unite</kanji> them. With all your thread united and wrapped together, you're ready to <kanji>rule</kanji> and <kanji>govern</kanji> the world!
data.meaning_hint: Allocate all of your thread like you would your cash: by uniting it! Not at a bank, but in a big, intertwined lump. Now nobody can stop you and your big lump of thread!
data.reading_mnemonic: You're busy trying to <kanji>unite</kanji> all of your thread, twisting and tying and wrapping, and suddenly you look at the ball in your hands and see <reading>とう</reading>きょう. You've united this thread into the shape of とうきょう. There are even little pins for all the famous neighborhoods and tourist spots. This is strange, because you don't remember putting them there.
data.reading_hint: Try to do this yourself at home. Unite all of your thread and poof! There's とうきょう!

data.meaning_mnemonic: Taking <radical>orders</radical> from a <radical>geoduck</radical> will place you into enemy <kanji>territory</kanji>. Geoducks make terrible commanders, so if you take orders from one, expect to end up in unknown territory, potentially even enemy territory. Be prepared.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine this geoduck shouting orders at you to march into enemy territory. See its gross body as a mouth forms and starts shouting out orders.
data.reading_mnemonic: Not wanting to end up dead in enemy <kanji>territory</kanji>, you decide to escape this geoduck leader by getting on a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat and rowing your way outta there. The geoduck commander orders you to halt your escape, but you still get in your row boat and row away.
data.reading_hint: Feel yourself in the row boat as you imagine rowing away to safe territory. Hear the geoduck in the background shouting at you from shore, ordering you to return to land.

data.meaning_mnemonic: With a <radical>bamboo</radical> <radical>tree</radical> resting atop your <radical>head</radical>, you devise a <kanji>plan</kanji>. The plan is actually for getting the bamboo tree off of your head. You’re trapped under it.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine being trapped under this bamboo tree that is resting on your head. You’re stuck. Feel the weight of the bamboo tree pressing on your head as you try and devise a plan to get out from under it.
data.reading_mnemonic: But why is this bamboo tree so heavy? You look to each end of the bamboo and realize that there is a <reading>sack</reading> (さく) tied on each end. Each sack seems to be filled with heavy rocks. Looks like someone made a <kanji>plan</kanji> to trap you here. Now you have to devise a plan to escape!
data.reading_hint: Bamboo is usually kind of light, but this bamboo has a sack of rocks tied to each end making it heavy. Imagine yourself trying to remove this bamboo tree by pushing it up and away from you. It’s like doing a bench-press, bamboo style.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The only <radical>flowers</radical> that the <radical>moon</radical> <radical>gladiator</radical>s will <radical>water</radical> are <kanji>wisteria</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: The moon gladiators have a thing for wisterias.
data.reading_mnemonic: Since they're on the moon, where did they get the <kanji>wisteria</kanji> from? Actually, from one of the points on earth that is nearest to the moon, Mt. <reading>Fuji</reading> (ふじ).
data.reading_hint: Imagine them reaching down from the moon and plucking some wisteria up from Mt. Fuji then taking them back up to the moon. Now they water them.

data.meaning_mnemonic: That <radical>scarecrow</radical> with the <radical>knife</radical> is the <kanji>vice</kanji> president. Yeah, I know how he looks, and I'm pretty sure he does some murdering on the <kanji>side</kanji>, but you didn't hear that from me.
data.meaning_hint: I don't know how we managed to get a knife-wielding scarecrow as a vice president, there's a side of politics I don't get, I guess. I mean, just look at him up there. If something happens to our president we're stuck with that thing.
data.reading_mnemonic: It's the <kanji>vice</kanji> president's turn to speak at the podium and he just clears his throat and yells, "<reading>F**k</reading> (ふく) you!" to the crowd, holding up his knife. They cheer.
data.reading_hint: What's going on? Normally if a vice president yells f**k you there would be... I dunno... consequences? What's happening?!

data.meaning_mnemonic: There's an <radical>arrow</radical> in a <radical>turkey</radical> that you can <radical>see</radical> in your <kanji>view</kanji>. The turkey seems to be viewing you too, from afar.
data.meaning_hint: View the turkey as the turkey views you. View the arrow stuck in it too.
data.reading_mnemonic: As you <kanji>view</kanji> the turkey, Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) suddenly comes into your view too. He towers over the injured turkey, leans down, and... pulls the arrow out!?
data.reading_hint: As you view this strange scene, Genghis Khan turns and views you viewing him. He points two fingers to his eyes and then to you, and marches off into the woods. You also view the turkey running off in the other direction.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A great <radical>leader</radical> can look <radical>straight</radical> at something and know its <kanji>value</kanji>. That social media site? 44 billion dollars. That job position? 50k a year. A four-day work week? Um… sorry, no, there's no value there. See? Leaders can see straight to the heart of matters to grasp something's true value.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine how terrifying it is when your leader looks straight at YOU. Don't worry, though — you've got more value than you give yourself credit for, and your leader can surely see that.
data.reading_mnemonic: One thing your leader knows has great <kanji>value</kanji> is <reading>chee</reading>se (ち). Say goodbye to your days of casually snacking on cheesy treats from the conbini, because your leader's decided the value of cheese is going up 1000%!
data.reading_hint: Imagine the despair you feel walking down the cheese aisle at the store and seeing how one little pack of string cheese now costs the same as your monthly rent. Why did your leader have to spike the value of cheese like this?

data.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>mouth</radical> is like an <radical>escalator</radical> you use to <kanji>suck</kanji> and <kanji>inhale</kanji> things into your body.
data.meaning_hint: If you're ever having trouble remembering how to suck or inhale, just picture an actual escalator that leads into your mouth. That'll definitely help.
data.reading_mnemonic: Use this mouth ability to <kanji>suck</kanji> <reading>cu</reading>cumbers (きゅう) into your mouth. Cucumbers are shaped like cylinders so you can suck them into your mouth like this. Just as nature intended.
data.reading_hint: You can inhale a cucumber too, I suppose, but don't tell anyone I told you to.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Lying in the <radical>dirt</radical>, a <radical>drunkard</radical> puts her <radical>mouth</radical> to the <radical>ground</radical> to understand the <kanji>region</kanji>. She loves to know all the regional differences among wines and other alcohols, and to her there's no better way to do this than putting her mouth on the ground and literally tasting each region.
data.meaning_hint: Picture this drunkard in the dirt, her mouth pressed to the ground. "Ahh," she says, "so this is the taste of the Bordeaux region." Then she has a glass of Bordeaux, and starts noting all its particular regional qualities.
data.reading_mnemonic: Turns out she thinks everything from this <kanji>region</kanji> is <reading>icky</reading> (いき). In fact, to the drunkard, every region tastes icky and gross. You don't have the heart to tell her it's the dirt and ground, not the region itself, that tastes icky…
data.reading_hint: Imagine her crying out, "Why are there such icky, earthy notes in all these regional wines?!" Feel the second-hand embarrassment for her. In her drunkenness she can't understand that putting her mouth on the ground makes everything taste icky, no matter what region it's from.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You're always comparing yourself to the <radical>next</radical> <radical>woman</radical> because you're obsessed with your <kanji>figure</kanji> and <kanji>appearance</kanji>. It's not healthy, but when physical <kanji>form</kanji> is the only thing that matters to you, comparing yourself to the next woman over becomes a matter of habit.
data.meaning_hint: Try to picture this proverbial "next woman." Ugh, her figure is just perfect. And her appearance? So put-together.
data.reading_mnemonic: Plot twist: when you're comparing yourself to the next woman, the <kanji>figure</kanji> and <kanji>appearance</kanji> you're picturing is actually that of a <reading>shee</reading>p (し). No wonder you're always dissatisfied with your appearance. You're not a sheep, you're a human!
data.reading_hint: Imagine standing in front of the mirror, wishing desperately that you could see the figure of a sheep reflected back at you. What do you have to do to attain that round, fluffy appearance???

data.meaning_mnemonic: If someone gets under the <radical>canopy</radical> over your <radical>heart</radical> you should <kanji>respond</kanji> to them.
data.meaning_hint: You usually ignore everyone, but this one person... they really got under there and touched your heart. You finally feel like they're the right person to respond to.
data.reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>respond</kanji> and it turns out it was to the <reading>王</reading> (おう).
data.reading_hint: The 王 touched your heart, you responded, and now you're together. It's like a fairy tale!

data.meaning_mnemonic: You extend your <radical>fingers</radical> toward the <radical>sun</radical> from atop a <radical>coat rack</radical> because you are about to <kanji>present</kanji> your ideas to a crowd. You need to be striking an authoritative pose from an elevated position in order to <kanji>submit</kanji> your thoughts persuasively.
data.meaning_hint: Extending your fingers upward makes you look like some sort of prophet, and sitting up on the coat rack puts you head and shoulders above all your listeners. Well, go ahead: present your ideas. (You do have something to present, right?)
data.reading_mnemonic: So, what are you going to <kanji>present</kanji> to everyone? A slideshow about <reading>ta</reading>ter tots (てい). You made a little PowerPoint to present your personal ranking of the best tater tots you've ever eaten — with photos, of course.
data.reading_hint: At the end of your presentation, you ask everyone to submit a feedback questionnaire, and you present free tater tot samples to everyone who does. What a fun presentation.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You use your <radical>fingers</radical> in the game of <radical>football</radical> to <kanji>aid</kanji> and <kanji>assist</kanji> the other players. And when you smash your fingers in football, you need to get some aid yourself.

If you're from the UK, just imagine someone kicking or stomping on your fingers instead.
data.meaning_hint: Picture yourself playing football. You catch the ball with your fingers and then assist your team by running and smashing your body into the enemy team. But in the process you smash your fingers... so you need to go to the aid tent.
data.reading_mnemonic: When you need <kanji>aid</kanji> for your football wrecked fingers you can't help but feel like it's the <reading>en</reading>d (えん) for you. Your fingers hurt so much, you don't even want the nice nurses to aid you.
data.reading_hint: You can't assist your team anymore because you got hurt. This isn't fair! It's the end. The end of your life and your career. Boo hoo hoo!

data.meaning_mnemonic: See all those <radical>icicle</radical>s to the <radical>dog</radical>'s left? Good thing they all fell on his left, or he would've been in a terrible <kanji>condition</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: Picture a bunch of big, sharp icicles all falling down directly next to this dog. Now imagine the condition he would've been in, had they all fallen directly on top of him. Poor little thing.
data.reading_mnemonic: What saved the dog's <kanji>condition</kanji> was none other than <reading>Joe</reading> (じょう), the local farmhand. He constantly keeps an eye on the dog's condition, including any dangerously sharp icicles that could descend on him.
data.reading_hint: Good guy Joe, always worrying about his dog's condition. Everyone needs a farmhand like Joe.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You have a great <radical>ability</radical> because your <radical>heart</radical> gives you the <kanji>appearance</kanji> of a superhuman. Your heart is really strong and powerful, fuelling your body to the best of its ability. All this together gives you the appearance of someone in top condition.
data.meaning_hint: See yourself in this ideal appearance. Everyone loves to look at you because you look so awesome. Your heart has given you many great abilities. Feel strong and powerful in this body of yours.
data.reading_mnemonic: While you may have the <kanji>appearance</kanji> of someone who is super strong, powerful, and awesome, you do have one shortcoming. You don’t know how to <reading>tie</reading> (たい) a tie. Actually, you don’t even know how to tie your shoes, let alone your tie. How embarrassing.
data.reading_hint: Since you don’t know how to tie a tie or tie your shoes, you wear slip ons and clip ons. Hear the noise of Velcro being undone as you kick off your shoes and unclip your tie after a hard day’s work at the office.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You use the <radical>power</radical> of your <radical>mouth</radical> to spit <radical>shellfish</radical> at people as a form of <kanji>congratulations</kanji>! In fact, you yell "CONGRATULATIONS!" as the shellfish come pouring out of your powerful mouth.
data.meaning_hint: Shellfish were once used as currency, so this totally makes sense. Just think of the shellfish as money coming out of your mouth as you say your congratulations.
data.reading_mnemonic: When you say <kanji>congratulations</kanji> like this, you look just like a <reading>ga</reading>rgoyle (が). You're crouching down, your mouth wide open, just like a stone gargoyle.
data.reading_hint: The next time you're congratulating someone, assume the gargoyle stance and dump all of their congratulatory shellfish on them from your mouth.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Wrap <radical>vines</radical> around a <radical>stool</radical> to <kanji>obtain</kanji> it. Don't worry about paying for it, sneak into the stool store and tie some vines around the legs. Then when you leave, pull the vines and the stool will come out after. That's how you obtain a stool!
data.meaning_hint: You can obtain a lot of goods this way without needing any cash. Just don't tell anyone I told you.
data.reading_mnemonic: Today you want to <kanji>obtain</kanji> a new pair of <reading>shoe</reading>s (しゅう). You tie your vines around the stool they're on, and slowly inch them toward the door.
data.reading_hint: You have to pull very slowly, or the shoes will fall off the stool. But you really, really want to obtain these particular shoes (they're really sweet), so you keep scooting them toward you.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of the <radical>restaurant</radical> says, "<kanji>Halt</kanji>!" to everyone who wants to come in. The leader looks them up and down. Stares into their eyes. And then, maybe, they may go into the restaurant to eat.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine being told to halt in front of your favorite restaurant, then being turned away. Noooo! Better start sucking up to the restaurant leader.
data.reading_mnemonic: People only <kanji>halt</kanji> because they want this restaurant's world famous <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots. Which is probably why there is a leader out front making sure only people who can really appreciate the tater tots can get in to eat them.
data.reading_hint: HALT! NO TATERS FOR YOU!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leather</radical> radical and the <kanji>leather</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Cool!
data.reading_mnemonic: One way to get <kanji>leather</kanji> is to skin a male chicken, a <reading>cock</reading> (かく). Not a very efficient way to get leather, but one way nonetheless.
data.reading_hint: You won’t get much leather from a cock, but you could skin one in a pinch, should you really need a little extra leather.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Reaching your <radical>ear</radical> is the <radical>sound</radical> of a <radical>drunkard</radical> who can’t find <kanji>employment</kanji>. You hear him before you see him because he’s behind some trash cans. Being a drunkard, he’s like, super wasted and just kind of rambling to himself, making strange sounds. No wonder he can’t find employment.
data.meaning_hint: Hear the strange sounds this drunkard is making. Let his ramblings enter your ears and imagine what he could be trying to say.
data.reading_mnemonic: Since this guy is such a pathetic drunkard, it comes as no <reading>shock</reading> (しょく) that he can’t find <kanji>employment</kanji>. If he did find employment, I would be filled with both shock and awe.
data.reading_hint: Actually you find out that he does have employment. He’s a garbage man. Feel the shock of making this shocking discovery. How can this drunkard possibly hold down his job like this?

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>demon</radical> radical and the <kanji>demon</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Wicked!
data.reading_mnemonic: How do you keep a <kanji>demon</kanji> locked up? Use a <reading>key</reading> (き). Use a lock and key and keep that demon locked up safely behind bars so he can’t get out and do bad demon stuff.
data.reading_hint: Picture yourself locking up a demon with a special demon containing key. Hear the key click into the lock as the demon screams to be set free.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Every <radical>husband</radical> you <radical>see</radical> sets a new <kanji>standard</kanji>. It seems like husbands are just getting better and better these days, and whenever you see one the standard has gone up again.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine what you see these standard-setting husbands doing. Maybe you see one listening intently to his partner's tedious story. Another lays his coat over a puddle for some lady to walk across. Wow, you see the husband standard going up everywhere.
data.reading_mnemonic: A good husband knows that a high <kanji>standard</kanji> is the <reading>key</reading> (き)… to his beloved's heart and to a happy marriage. The second he lets his standards slip, he knows the marriage is in trouble. Maintaining a high standard is definitely the key.
data.reading_hint: You can even imagine the sound of a key in a lock every time you see a husband setting a high standard. Like as soon as that one guy put his coat down over that puddle, you heard a key click and a heart open up. *click* And when some random husband politely opened a door for you? *click*

data.meaning_mnemonic: They <radical>say</radical> that <radical>flowers</radical> held by a <radical>turkey</radical> on a <radical>stool</radical> are good to <kanji>defend</kanji> yourself with. Even better than a guard dog they say. People are so confused by the turkey sitting on a stool holding flowers that they just lose their will to fight. This turkey is great to defend yourself and your home.
data.meaning_hint: Picture this turkey holding its flowers while sitting on its stool. Hear it gobbling as it defends everything around it with its mere presence.
data.reading_mnemonic: The only thing this flower-bearing turkey can't <kanji>defend</kanji> against is <reading>Go</reading>dzilla (ご). Godzilla is pretty much undefeatable, especially for a turkey. The turkey is totally unable to defend anything from the mighty Godzilla.
data.reading_hint: Imagine Godzilla approaching the flower turkey. Hear Godzilla roar as the turkey gobbles in fear before being crushed beneath the massive and scaly foot of Godzilla.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>roof</radical> falls on you right between your <radical>rib cage</radical> and your <radical>mouth</radical>, slicing through you like a <radical>knife</radical> and managing to completely <kanji>divide</kanji> your body in two.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine the shock you feel as you look down and see this massive fallen roof dividing your body in two between the mouth and rib cage. Of all the places to get divided in two, the rib cage-to-mouth region is by far one of the worst.
data.reading_mnemonic: Who caused this roof to fall on you and <kanji>divide</kanji> your body in two? <reading>Wari</reading>o (わり) and his <reading>wa</reading>lrus (わ) sidekick. Wario's always been a bad guy, but since teaming up with his walrus buddy, he's gotten into some really twisted stuff… like using roofs to divide people in half, guillotine-style.
data.reading_hint: Why did Wario and his walrus choose you, of all people, to divide in two? They were after your fortune. Now that you're out of the way, they're planning to divide it up amongst themselves, fifty-fifty.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You place a <radical>cross</radical> on this <radical>drunkard</radical>'s <radical>clothes</radical> to show him you <kanji>judge</kanji> him. In fact, you yell, "I JUDGE YOU FOR BEING DRUNK AND WEARING THESE CLOTHES, TAKE THIS!"
data.meaning_hint: He yells back, "YOU CAN'T JUDGE ME, I CAN DO WHAT I WANT. GET THAT JUDGEY CROSS OFF ME!"
data.reading_mnemonic: As you <kanji>judge</kanji> each other, your <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい) comes stomping over and slams the drunkard against the wall. With your trusty cyborg coming to your rescue, you can continue to judge this guy all you want.
data.reading_hint: The cyborg joins in, "A judge would convict you if the fashion police brought you in. I have a bunch of meat and robot parts and even I'm better looking than you."

data.meaning_mnemonic: From the top of a <radical>mountain</radical> you see something that looks like a <radical>big</radical> <radical>lip ring</radical> jutting out into the ocean: it's a <kanji>cape</kanji>! You know, the geological formation where a big piece of land sticks out into the ocean? That kind of cape.
data.meaning_hint: Cape Cod, for example. Picture it now (or look it up if you need to). Really does look like a big lip ring stuck in the side of Massachusetts, doesn't it? Imagine seeing that cape from the top of your mountain, wind blustering around you.
data.reading_mnemonic: Looking down at the <kanji>cape</kanji>, you realize capes always make the coastline look jagged, like a <reading>saw</reading> or <reading>key</reading> (さき). Thanks for keeping the coastline interesting, you saw-key capes!
data.reading_hint: Try to draw that bit of coastline where the cape is. Nice, easy, smooth lines, until BAM! — the cape. Now the coastline is all jagged like the edge of a saw or key.

data.meaning_mnemonic: There's going to be a <radical>tsunami</radical>. So you get up on your <radical>roof</radical>. You see people across the <radical>street</radical>, in a <radical>rice paddy</radical>. They watch as you put on a pair of <radical>fins</radical>. And you begin <kanji>acting</kanji>. This is your last chance to <kanji>perform</kanji>!
data.meaning_hint: But why? Because this acting will distract everyone from the impending tsunami. You dance around in your fins, pretending to swim. It's a wonderful performance.
data.reading_mnemonic: As the <kanji>acting</kanji> <reading>en</reading>ds (えん), so do you all.
data.reading_hint: The performance and the tsunami end together. How poetic.

data.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Loiter</radical>ing around with a <radical>brush</radical>? Sorry, but you're breaking the <kanji>law</kanji>. If you have a brush, that's okay. If you're loitering, that's okay. If you combine the two? Well... watch your back.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine a police officer coming for you. He's yelling at you because you have a brush and you're loitering. He grabs you, throws you to the ground, telling you what you're doing wrong.
data.reading_mnemonic: Where were you loitering with your brush, breaking the <kanji>law</kanji>? Right outside the <reading>Ritz</reading> (りつ) Hotel. You'd think that it would be okay since you were staying there, but the law is the law.
data.reading_hint: Imagine the hotel staff watching as you get thrown to the ground. You yell "won't the Ritz do anything to help me??" They won't.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>drop</radical> of water falls from a <radical>bear</radical> onto the <radical>ground</radical> and needs to be wiped up with a <radical>towel</radical>. Only a <kanji>teacher</kanji> or an <kanji>expert</kanji> could get away with getting close to this wet bear to wipe up after it.
data.meaning_hint: The expert is also your teacher, and she's showing you how to clean up after this bear.
data.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>teacher</kanji> tells you to start with something smaller, after all, you're not an <kanji>expert</kanji> yet. You have to practice on a wet <reading>shee</reading>p (し). "I became a wet, dangerous animal expert by starting with sheep, you will too!" your teacher says.
data.reading_hint: Your teacher assures you this wet sheep is far less dangerous to clean up after than a wet bear. They're the expert, so you should listen and wipe up after that sheep.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Put your <radical>hand</radical> over your <radical>eye</radical> to <kanji>watch over</kanji> others.
data.meaning_hint: You know that way cartoon characters and pirates watch out below them, with their hand shading their eye? That! Now imagine doing that right now.
data.reading_mnemonic: As you <kanji>watch over</kanji> your friends and neighbors you see movement in the distance. Oh no, it's Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) and his army!
data.reading_hint: Welp, nothing much watching over them will do now. Genghis Khan is probably going to take over your town, so I guess you can watch if you want but... I wouldn't.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Riding a <radical>tsunami</radical> you see a <radical>turkey</radical> carrying a <radical>cross</radical>, but that’s pretty <kanji>standard</kanji> here. This is your dreamland. You always dream about tsunamis and the turkeys carrying crosses that ride them. This might be strange for other people, but for you it’s pretty normal.
data.meaning_hint: See this tsunami riding turkey in your mind. Hear it gobble loudly as it waves its cross around. Remember, this is standard fare for you. Nothing unusual here.
data.reading_mnemonic: These wacky dreams are only <kanji>standard</kanji> fare in <reading>June</reading> (じゅん) though. You don’t have them any other time of the year, just in June. You don’t know why June is the only time you have dreams about tsunami riding turkeys, but that’s just the way it is.
data.reading_hint: It’s usually pretty toasty in the month of June (in the Northern Hemisphere, at least) so imagine going to bed in this heat. Feel the spray of the refreshing tsunami water in your dream as the turkey continues to ride those tsunami waves with his cross.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>shellfish</radical> with a <radical>knife</radical> makes all the <kanji>rule</kanji>s. It isn't supposed to be making rules, but it has a knife, so who's going to argue?
data.meaning_hint: Picture a shellfish wielding a knife and shouting out new rules to all of the nervous people standing around it.
data.reading_mnemonic: The first <kanji>rule</kanji> the shellfish enacts is that all humans take off their <reading>sock</reading>s (そく) and give them to him. Hmm... is this some kind of nasty shellfish? Who would want socks?
data.reading_hint: Once everyone follows the rule, and the shellfish is on top of a pile of socks, he cackles, "It's easier to stab your toes with my knife now! Let's get to more rules!"

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> put <radical>flowers</radical> on a <radical>cliff</radical>. That is their <radical>task</radical>. It is to <kanji>provide</kanji> and <kanji>equip</kanji> the cliff with flowers.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine a leader carrying flowers up to the top of a cliff. They are saying "I must provide more flowers to the cliff" as they climb up.
data.reading_mnemonic: Why do they <kanji>provide</kanji> and <kanji>equip</kanji> the cliff with flowers? It's all for the <reading>bee</reading>s (び).
data.reading_hint: "The bees must be equipped with more flowers. I will provide these flowers for the bees!"

data.meaning_mnemonic: Take this <radical>road</radical>'s <radical>measurement</radical>. Hmm. It seems a bit too long. As you measure it, you continue down this road, wondering where it will <kanji>lead</kanji> you.
data.meaning_hint: Roads are really long, so I imagine it would take a long time to measure it (if you want to go from end to end). Imagine yourself pulling a tape measure along with you, all the while thinking, "Where will this lead me?”
data.reading_mnemonic: Where does the road that you're measuring <kanji>lead</kanji> to? To a <reading>dou</reading>ghnut (どう) shop!
data.reading_hint: What a perfect way to end this road measuring. You're hungry. Nom nom nom. Imagine eating your fill, and taste the doughnuts in your mouth. You just walked a long way!

data.meaning_mnemonic: In the <radical>morning</radical>, if you want your <radical>hat</radical> to <radical>dry</radical>, you need to hang it on a <kanji>tree trunk</kanji>. In the morning, everything is covered in dew. The grass is wet, the leaves are wet, but the tree trunk isn't wet! It was protected by the rest of the tree, so you can hang your hat there to dry.
data.meaning_hint: Picture everything early in the morning covered in damp dew. Even your hat is uncomfortably wet. Now walk up to a large tree trunk and touch it—it's dry!
data.reading_mnemonic: You lean against the <kanji>tree trunk</kanji>, waiting for your hat to dry, and suddenly you realize Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) is on the other side of it. You look around and see that all of the tree trunks around you have Mongols drying their hats under them.
data.reading_hint: Now that you think about it, Genghis Khan was the one who taught people that tree trunks stay dry in the morning!

data.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <radical>bow</radical> and you want to make it <radical>long</radical>. To do that, you'd naturally just <kanji>stretch</kanji> it.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine holding this bow in your hands, and then stretching it into a longer bow. Feel the strain on your arms as you try to stretch wood. You can feel it stretching, but it's strenuous.
data.reading_mnemonic: As you <kanji>stretch</kanji> the bow, you hear someone running at you. "That's my bow you're stretching!" yells Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう). She is not happy that you're stretching her things. You should probably try to un-stretch it, put it down, and run before she beats you.
data.reading_hint: Now Mrs. Chou is hitting you with the stretched out bow. You cry and apologize, but she won't listen. "I'm going to stretch you, like you stretched my bow," she says. Then she does it.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of a <radical>hundred</radical> <radical>forehead</radical>s in the <radical>heart</radical> of <radical>winter</radical> is <kanji>superior</kanji> at being <kanji>gentle</kanji>. These hundred foreheads are sensitive, especially in the heart of winter, so the leader must be very gentle. Not just any kind of gentle though—the superior kind of gentle that will keep a hundred foreheads following.
data.meaning_hint: As a leader, you are superior. You’re so gentle to these foreheads. See yourself caring for them in the winter. Feel the chill in the air as you wrap the foreheads in blankets and prepare heating pads for them.
data.reading_mnemonic: You need to be <kanji>superior</kanji> because all of these foreheads belong to <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう). They don't know how to take care of themselves, though they try to convince you they can. They're too young to know any better.
data.reading_hint: Picture the youths trying to show you that they are the superior ones, then they sneeze, their eyes fill with tears, and you have to gently tuck them back into bed. Silly youths.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You need to go up on the <radical>roof</radical> and use it like a <radical>slide</radical> <radical>seven</radical> times to make this your <kanji>house</kanji>. A house isn't a <kanji>home</kanji> until you've slid down its roof exactly seven times, you know.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine staring down at the ground as you prepare to use the roof of your house like a slide. I hope you aren't afraid of heights, because you have to do this seven times in a row.
data.reading_mnemonic: When you slide down the roof of your <kanji>house</kanji>, you end up with a <reading>tack</reading> (たく) in your butt cheek. All the roof shingles on your new <kanji>home</kanji> are attached with tacks, so it's honestly a miracle that you only got one tack stuck in you.
data.reading_hint: Feel the tack stab into your butt as you slide down your house's roof. Ow! Weirdly, though, it kinda makes you feel more at one with the house — like it's really your home now.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> of <radical>shrimp</radical> crashes into a <kanji>swamp</kanji>. Now the swamp is filled with shrimp. They used to live in the ocean, but the tsunami has carried them to their new home in the swamp.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine yourself in the swamp when the tsunami hits. Feel the water crash into you along with the shrimp. You’re all wet and shrimpy now.
data.reading_mnemonic: Your house was right next to the <kanji>swamp</kanji> and on this side of your house you had many a <reading>tack</reading> (たく) there to hang things on. Now, on every tack there is skewered a shrimp. The force of the tsunami drove them into the tacks on the side of your house.
data.reading_hint: Look at the side of your house. It’s covered with shrimp that have been impaled on the tacks. Perfect for dinner.

data.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Dirt</radical> shifts <radical>direction</radical> in <radical>winter</radical>, and instead of the usual stuff it starts to grow <radical>shellfish</radical> that are very <kanji>extravagant</kanji>. These shellfish are so extravagant because they can only be grown in the dirt in winter (after the dirt has shifted "direction" and started sustaining shellfish instead of plants, that is).
data.meaning_hint: Imagine tasting this incredible extravagance. Shellfish normally have a briny flavor, but these ones have earthy notes. Earthy shellfish?! I've never heard of something so extravagant. Try to imagine that extravagant, expensive flavor on your tongue.
data.reading_mnemonic: To make this experience even more <kanji>extravagant</kanji>, you eat them with a <reading>zei</reading>ber (ぜい), a German saber. A fork is just too plain for these extravagant shellfish — you gotta use a zeiber for maximum extravagance.
data.reading_hint: Imagine trying to use a zeiber to skewer an extravagant shellfish, then raise it to your mouth. You probably cut your lips a little bit, to be honest. It's all very impractical, but that's what it means to be extravagant.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Moving in the <radical>direction</radical> of a <radical>gun</radical>, an <radical>alligator</radical> can <kanji>carry out</kanji> a murder once it reaches it. This alligator wants to kill someone. The alligator wants to carry out their execution.
data.meaning_hint: See the alligator swim really slowly in the direction of a gun. See the alligator as it prepares to carry out the murder. It’s scary.
data.reading_mnemonic: In order to <kanji>carry out</kanji> this murder, the alligator has to sneak up on its prey, so it can shoot it. You look across the water and see a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) grazing by the shore. The alligator is going to carry out a murder on that sheep!
data.reading_hint: Watch as the alligator slinks under the water, holding the gun above the water. When it gets close enough, it carries out the murder on the sheep. Shooting it right in the chest. Now it can eat the sheep without worrying about needing to chomp on it.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> can <radical>see</radical> the <kanji>present time</kanji> for what it really is. The future isn't important. The past isn't important. The present is when everything <kanji>appear</kanji>s.
data.meaning_hint: People are constantly asking the king to do things for them and solve their problems. But the king can see exactly what needs to be done at the present time, and what can wait until tomorrow.
data.reading_mnemonic: At the <kanji>present time</kanji> the king is <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん). The time has finally come for him to get serious, and as they say, there's no time like the present.
data.reading_hint: Picture pretty Genji, carefully instructing his followers what to do at the present time and what can wait.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Giving <radical>cleat</radical>s to a <radical>child</radical> carrying an <radical>umbrella</radical> is the best way to gather <kanji>milk</kanji>. You don't have any containers, so the child has to hold milk in the upside-down umbrella. The cleats are so the child can run back and forth to transport the milk around.
data.meaning_hint: See this child running in his cleats. Picture him holding the umbrella upside-down, milk sloshing all about as he runs.
data.reading_mnemonic: But where is this child exactly? He’s in <reading>New</reading> (にゅう) York City. What’s he doing in New York City you ask? Well, he's milking a cow. Why is there a cow to be milked in New York City? Good question. It’s the end of the world and New York City is the last remaining civilization. This is how people live now. <kanji>Milk</kanji> is important.
data.reading_hint: Imagine post-apocalyptic New York City. Milk is a hot commodity here so it’s important not to spill any of the milk. Imagine yourself carrying the milk in the umbrella and being careful not to spill any of it.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> that wants <radical>peace</radical> can <kanji>call</kanji> for it. If you don’t have a mouth, you can’t call for peace. So use your mouth and call for peace when you can. Peace is great.
data.meaning_hint: Call for peace. Say it aloud. I’m using my mouth to call for peace!
data.reading_mnemonic: But before you <kanji>call</kanji> for peace, you must first placate the masses. To do so, you astound them with your <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ) skills. Once they are so entranced by how talented you are with a yo-yo, you easily convince them to make peace.
data.reading_hint: Imagine yourself whirling this yo-yo about while you call for peace. Imagine yourself doing a variety of tricks with it as you slowly convince the people to agree to peace.

data.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Dirt</radical> can <radical>become</radical> a <kanji>castle</kanji> at any time. You just have to have the right conditions. The right time, the right people, and any patch of dirt can grow into a huge castle.
data.meaning_hint: Every great building, especially castles, started off as just a plot of dirt, you know? It's kind of inspiring what we can become.
data.reading_mnemonic: Once you turn dirt into a <kanji>castle</kanji>, that's all <reading>she wro</reading>te (しろ). That's it. It's done. The story is over.
data.reading_hint: Once a castle is there, there's really no turning back. So just remember that when dirt becomes a castle, that's all she wrote.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>leader</radical> wishing to stop <radical>criminal</radical>s will write a moving <kanji>haiku</kanji>. The leader pleads with the criminals to stop their crimes, to look within, and to realize there's more to life (like poetry!).
data.meaning_hint: Unfortunately, the leader of the criminals also writes haiku, and they want all the criminals to keep doing crimes. Look inside and see how much you want what others have, write a haiku, and then steal!
data.reading_mnemonic: A <kanji>haiku</kanji> is still a <reading>hai</reading>ku (はい). Whether it's written by a law abiding leader or a criminal leader.
data.reading_hint: Just remember: a haiku is always a haiku.

data.meaning_mnemonic: If you can eat <radical>grain</radical>s while running up <radical>stairs</radical>, you'll <kanji>excel</kanji> at everything.
data.meaning_hint: This special workout routine is so hard that, if you can do it, you'll be able to excel at every other thing you try.
data.reading_mnemonic: In order to <kanji>excel</kanji> at this, though, you need a good pair of <reading>shoe</reading>s (しゅう).
data.reading_hint: You have to eat the grains AND run up the stairs, or you aren't actually excelling. Good shoes will help you get there faster and protect your toes.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You use your <radical>fingers</radical> at <radical>dawn</radical> to <kanji>carry</kanji> many things. You have to carry yourself out of bed. You have to carry your backpack or purse or laptop bag to school or work. Your fingers have to carry a lot of weight around at dawn.
data.meaning_hint: Think about your morning routine. You carry yourself into the bathroom and carry a toothbrush into your mouth. You carry your coat and bag out the door.
data.reading_mnemonic: Once you're <kanji>carry</kanji>ing everything, and the dawn sun is shining bright, you start getting <reading>tan</reading> (たん). Especially those fingers you're using to carry things.
data.reading_hint: Picture yourself carrying a coat and a bag, walking through the rice fields to work, with the hot, dawn sun shining down, making your fingers get tanner and tanner.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
When you have a <radical>guest</radical> over, you give them a <radical>geoduck</radical> because it's worth a huge <kanji>amount</kanji>. You're nothing if not a hospitable host.

This kanji, weirdly, can also mean <kanji>picture frame</kanji> or <kanji>forehead</kanji>. Why? Who knows. Just imagine going to a museum and seeing a geoduck in a picture frame, and scratching your forehead in confusion because it's supposedly worth a vast amount of money. Modern art, am I right?
data.meaning_hint: Picture a geoduck with a huge amount listed on a price tag attached to it. What amount did you imagine? That's the amount you're basically giving away to your guests.
data.reading_mnemonic: The geoduck you gift to your guest is worth such a lavish <kanji>amount</kanji> that it makes them <reading>gawk</reading> (がく). Everyone gawks when they see a geoduck, really — first at how weird it looks, and then at the amount it's worth.
data.reading_hint: Imagine one of your guests gawking in disbelief as you hand them a huge, freshly-caught geoduck worth an ungodly amount of money. Revel in their gawking stare. Feels good, doesn't it?

data.meaning_mnemonic: If you want <radical>control</radical> over the <radical>clothes</radical> you wear, you'll have to <kanji>manufacture</kanji> them yourself. You'll never truly control your own wardrobe as long as you're letting big apparel companies manufacture it.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine setting up a little assembly line in your backyard and hiring all the neighborhood kids to manufacture clothing you've designed. You pay them in candy and lord over them like a Victorian-era factory boss.
data.reading_mnemonic: Encouraged by your success in clothing manufacturing, you also start to <kanji>manufacture</kanji> <reading>sa</reading>bers (せい). Sabers are another thing you're very picky about — handle shape, blade curvature, etc. — so you want to control how they're manufactured too.
data.reading_hint: Imagine one of your child laborers handing you a freshly-manufactured saber. Feel the weight of the saber in your hand. Give it a little swing. Does it meet your manufacturing standards?

data.meaning_mnemonic: You take your <radical>scooter</radical> to <radical>Korea</radical> and everything is <kanji>different</kanji>!
data.meaning_hint: Imagine scooting down a street in Korea and seeing how different literally every single thing is compared to what you're used to in Japan.
data.reading_mnemonic: What's also <kanji>different</kanji> is that there's a weird tiger bouncing on its tail alongside you yelling that its name is <reading>Tigger</reading> (ちが). You didn't know Tigger was living in Korea these days. That's definitely different.
data.reading_hint: Tigger is different in Korea too. For one, he's a white tiger now, and he's, like, really aggressive. Wait, was he always like that?

data.meaning_mnemonic: What does a <radical>car</radical> and the <radical>Death Star</radical> have in common? They're both used to <kanji>transport</kanji> people and things.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine stuffing a bunch of Stormtroopers in your car so you can transport them across the country. Well the Death Star can transport even more Stormtroopers, faster, and through space!
data.reading_mnemonic: Right now you and the Death Star are <kanji>transport</kanji>ing <reading>yu</reading>rts (ゆ). They're the universe's #1 best transportable homes!
data.reading_hint: It's easy to transport a yurt even without a car or the Death Star.

data.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Fire</radical> in <radical>nature</radical> will <kanji>burn</kanji> down everything in its path. In nature, there are no firefighters to contain the flames, so the <kanji>blaze</kanji> will burn until nothing's left.
data.meaning_hint: Feel the fire all around you as it burns. You're out in nature — the middle of a forest fire. Hear the woods crackle as they burn up around you.
data.reading_mnemonic: What is the worst thing that could <kanji>burn</kanji> in this fire? Your <reading>nen</reading>doroid (ねん) collection. You've spent a lot of time and money collecting all these cool and rare and unique nendoroids and now they've all burned in the fire.
data.reading_hint: Cry your eyes out as you smell the burning plastic of your nendoroids. Worst. Day. Ever.

data.meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>spirit</radical> blesses your <radical>older brother</radical> it's time to <kanji>celebrate</kanji>! This isn't something that happens every day to everyone's older brother. Yours is very good and very lucky. So celebrate with him!
data.meaning_hint: Imagine what celebrating would be like. Imagine an older brother too, if you don't actually have one.
data.reading_mnemonic: Unfortunately, the two of you <kanji>celebrate</kanji>d too much, and you went a little crazy. The spirit grabbed your brother and <reading>shook</reading> (しゅく) him. Shook him so hard his head popped off.
data.reading_hint: Never celebrate too hard. Otherwise you'll always have to think about the time a celebration spirit shook your brother till his head fell off.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The American <radical>flag</radical> is the <radical>reason</radical> you need to <kanji>deliver</kanji> this package. The flag is inside the package, and you need to deliver it to the president. He lost his old flag, so now it’s up to you to deliver this new one to him. What more of a reason do you need?
data.meaning_hint: You need to deliver this flag to the president. Imagine yourself running as fast as you can while carrying the parcel in order to get it to him. Your lungs are tired and your legs burn, but you must deliver the flag as soon as possible!
data.reading_mnemonic: To <kanji>deliver</kanji> this flag is something you just have <reading>to do</reading> (とど). Need to do. Want to do. There is no one else to do it. This is something only you are equipped to do.
data.reading_hint: The world depends on you to do this delivery. If you fail, the United States will be ruined. You have to do it! Deliver that flag now! Run! Run!

data.meaning_mnemonic: You have an <radical>animal</radical> for a <radical>husband</radical> with <radical>horns</radical> that are <kanji>narrow</kanji>. This animal husband of yours is a goat. A goat with narrow horns. Why is this animal your husband? You’re weird, that’s why.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine yourself married to this animal husband with horns that are narrow. It’s a strange marriage. Listen to the goat making its goat noises as it clomps around your home. Now hug your goat husband and feel its soft fluffy coat against your skin.
data.reading_mnemonic: I’m not even going to get into the <reading>sema</reading>ntics (せま) of how this weird relationship of yours works. Nope, this reading explanation is on the straight and <kanji>narrow</kanji>. Need to know basis. Classified. All that junk. There will be no discussion of the semantics between you and your goat lover.
data.reading_hint: But that doesn’t mean you can’t imagine the semantics. The finer points of the relationship. Go ahead, imagine all the weird stuff that comes with the territory for having a goat as a husband. Use all that weird stuff to remember this kanji and its reading. Want an example? Just imagine the goat doing dishes! Goats don’t have hands! Hahahahaha!!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>door</radical> leading to the <radical>moon</radical> can be broken down with one’s <kanji>shoulder</kanji>. It’s not a very sturdy door to the moon, so it’s quite easy to drop your shoulder and ram it open.
data.meaning_hint: Picture yourself smashing through this door using your shoulder and seeing the moon on the other side. Hear the splintering of wood as your shoulder crashes through the door and feel the impact with your body.
data.reading_mnemonic: "Wow, your <kanji>shoulder</kanji> is just like my <reading>cata</reading>pult (かた)!" you hear someone shout. As you turn you're just in time to see a man catapulting through his own moon door!
data.reading_hint: Now the weird man is inspecting your shoulder really closely and he keeps muttering "catapult powers" under his breath. It's very unsettling, but he's kind of right. A shoulder works just like the mechanism that winds up a catapult.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>moon</radical> shines on your <radical>roof</radical> in the <radical>evening</radical> and a <radical>snake</radical> suddenly appears! Wait, that's not a snake, it's your <kanji>arm</kanji>, sticking out from under the roof.
data.meaning_hint: Arms really look like snakes in the moonlight. Picture it. Your arm is long and shiny, just like a snake.
data.reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>arm</kanji> is exposed to the moon and the outside and you feel a chill. Where are your clothes? Ah, you're n<reading>ude, eh</reading> (うで)?! I guess it is pretty common to sleep in the nude, eh?
data.reading_hint: Your arms are nude, eh? That's why they look like snakes, you know. You should be more careful.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You approach the <radical>Moon</radical> in a <radical>helicopter</radical> and see a <radical>woman</radical> there on the surface, touching her <kanji>waist</kanji>. She's posing with one hand on her waist, like she's Sailor Moon or something. I guess that would explain what she's doing here on the Moon!
data.meaning_hint: Imagine flying your helicopter closer to the woman. Even as you touch down she never takes her hand off her waist. You get closer and try to see why she's touching her waist like that.
data.reading_mnemonic: Once you get close, you see that her <kanji>waist</kanji> looks weird and… puffy? You realize she's stuffed some <reading>子 shee</reading>p (こし) under her skirt's waistband to line her waist with them. Guess it's cold up here on the moon, so the 子 sheep keep her waist warm. And they had to be 子 sheep, otherwise they wouldn't be small enough to fit under her clothes.
data.reading_hint: Imagine how warm your waist would be if you stuffed a bunch of 子 sheep into your waistband. Just don't let anyone see you do it. Pretty sure that's animal cruelty…

data.meaning_mnemonic: If, at a certain <radical>angle</radical>, you approach an <radical>insect</radical>, you’ll be able to <kanji>touch</kanji> it without it noticing. Most of the time, insects will run away from you when you try and touch them, but if you do so from the right angle, the insect will have no idea.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine yourself approaching this insect from a sneaky and stealthy angle. Now touch it. What does it feel like? Smooth? Hard? Fuzzy? Feel the insect in your mind as you touch it.
data.reading_mnemonic: Uh oh, looks like this particular insect is a lightning bug so when you <kanji>touch</kanji> it you get a <reading>shock</reading> (しょく). Did you know that lightning bugs contain bazillions of volts inside them? Well they do, and if you touch one, you get a shock. A very big shock.
data.reading_hint: Feel this electrical shock to your system as you touch the lightning bug. This discourages you from ever touching another insect again. You don’t enjoy the shock.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <radical>cross</radical> for a <radical>drunkard</radical>'s <radical>car</radical>, to <kanji>place on</kanji> its dashboard. Drunkards should not drive, and when you <kanji>put on</kanji> a cross, it prevents the car from starting!
data.meaning_hint: Imagine the power that starts emanating from the cross once it’s placed on the car, it can’t move even an inch. Nope, it's not going anywhere until its owner sobers up.
data.reading_mnemonic: You have a lot of crosses to <kanji>place on</kanji> drunkard cars, so you get your <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい) to do it for you. The cyborg doesn't need sleep, so it can patrol the streets 24/7 for the sake of public safety. What a saintly cyborg.
data.reading_hint: Picture your cyborg, approaching a drunkard's car to place a cross on it. You see it open a big compartment on its chest, and it's filled with crosses.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the <radical>flag</radical> lies a <radical>mask</radical>—yet another <kanji>layer</kanji> of secrecy. You’re standing in front of a crowd, giving a rousing speech. Hiding your face is the flag of your country, and behind that flag you’re also wearing a mask, just in case the flag falls down. The extra layer of secrecy is just to be safe.
data.meaning_hint: These layers are meant to protect you. We all have layers we hide behind sometimes, you know? You can't be totally transparent with everyone.
data.reading_mnemonic: Someone jumps up on stage and starts peeling off your <kanji>layer</kanji>s! You stand there, first goes the flag, then the mask, then ... your <reading>sou</reading>l (そう) is laid bare. No, literally. You don't have a body, your soul was under that mask. And now it's floating there for all to see.
data.reading_hint: Everyone in the crowd is completely silent, staring at your soul, with all of its layers peeled off.

data.meaning_mnemonic: There is a <radical>lantern</radical> on top of a <radical>knife</radical> in the <radical>dirt</radical>. You walk up to take the knife and lantern when you realize it's just a <kanji>model</kanji>. It all looked real from far away, but now that you're up close you can see none of it is real.
data.meaning_hint: Why would anyone make a model that looks like a lantern and a knife sticking into the ground?
data.reading_mnemonic: You touch the <kanji>model</kanji> and see that it's made of <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい)! Someone really into lanterns and knives must have been given this model cake as a birthday present! Though they left it out here so they probably didn't like it.
data.reading_hint: Haven't you seen any of those crazy cakes modeled after things like movies, towns, giants hams, and purses? They're all the rage. Next time you make a cake try to make it look like a model lantern and knife with fake cake dirt and everything.

data.meaning_mnemonic: There are people under a <radical>canopy</radical> on the <radical>street</radical> forming their own <kanji>agency</kanji>. They're banding together right here in the street, making a new <kanji>government office</kanji>!
data.meaning_hint: Imagine them putting together papers, talking to politicians, and standing in the street outside the capitol. They demand for this agency to be formed. They are doing all the correct, legal things to do it too.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This new <kanji>agency</kanji> is just starting to make progress when you hear a low rumble... then a screech.

"THIS IS MY STREET. NO NEW AGENCIES ON MY STREET!" Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう) cries as she barrels into everyone.
data.reading_hint: "Whenever you're in a 丁, you're in my territory," she yells, taking out a few agency members with her fists. "You won't be starting any kind of agency here, not on my watch." And she lights it all on fire.

data.meaning_mnemonic: If you use your <radical>spirit</radical> to <radical>see</radical> something, it means you really <kanji>look at</kanji> it. You're not just seeing something passively with your eyes, you're actually looking at it with your whole spirit.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine using your whole spirit to look at something. Like, you feel your spirit flowing out from your eyes and enveloping whatever you're looking at. It's kind of trippy. When's the last time you really looked at something like that? Try it now.
data.reading_mnemonic: The first thing you want to <kanji>look at</kanji> like this is a <reading>shee</reading>p (し). You've seen a lot of sheep, but you've never really looked at them closely, so your image of them is kind of… woolly.
data.reading_hint: Look at a picture of a sheep now. Really look at it with all your spirit. Bet you start noticing some things you'd never seen before, right?

data.meaning_mnemonic: When a <radical>sheep</radical> tries its hoof at <radical>construction</radical>, it gains <kanji>distinction</kanji>. Now that is something that really sets a sheep apart! After all, have you ever seen a sheep working in construction?
data.meaning_hint: Note that the sheep has to sweep its tail to one side so that it doesn't get in the way of all the construction tools. That's why it looks a little different here. Imagine a sheep in a hard hat, with its tail on one side, getting down to some construction. How very distinctive.
data.reading_mnemonic: The extra <kanji>distinction</kanji> of this sheep is that its really skilled with a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). That's why it's so good at construction.
data.reading_hint: Imagine the sheep holding the saw in its hooves. It isn't easy to grip a saw with hooves, but this is no ordinary sheep.

data.meaning_mnemonic: On your <radical>bamboo</radical> <radical>roof</radical> is a <radical>bear</radical>. It is pulling the bamboo off, because it wants to use it to make a long <kanji>pipe</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: Bamboo is great for pipes, and the only place for the bear to get it is your roof. So, that's why it's there.
data.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>pipe</kanji> will be for Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん), who would like some pipes for his house.
data.reading_hint: Watch the bear take away your bamboo. Follow it to Genghis Khan's house. There, the bear installs the pipe in Genghis Khan's bathroom.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>elephant</radical> radical and the <kanji>elephant</kanji> kanji are the same. But! This kanji has another meaning: <kanji>phenomenon</kanji>. If you were the first person to see an elephant, you'd call it that too.
data.meaning_hint: Picture the first Japanese person to see an elephant. He stops dead in his tracks, points and screams out, "What a phenomenon!"
data.reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Elephant</kanji>s are great and all, except that when they die they turn into elephant <reading>zo</reading>mbies (ぞう). But you never see these zombies because the <reading>shou</reading>gun (しょう) has a special project in place that destroys all elephant bodies when they die.

Hint: The readings and meanings for this kanji match up really nicely. ぞう is always for elephant and しょう is always for phenomenon. Remember it like this, the elephant is the zombie and the shougun keeps everyone from finding out about this phenomenon.
data.reading_hint: Picture the shougun standing over a pit of zombie elephants. None of these are getting out on his watch, letting people believe in such crazy phenomenons.

data.meaning_mnemonic: When <radical>dawn</radical> reaches this <radical>village</radical> it increases in <kanji>quantity</kanji>. That's right. Every morning the <kanji>amount</kanji> of people or animals living here goes up by at least one.
data.meaning_hint: Picture dawn, the sun rising, the birds chirping, and the screams of a new born baby rise in the village. Or Maybe it's a new sheep! Or a new hat that someone just finished making.
data.reading_mnemonic: Today's dawn has brought with it an increase in the <kanji>quantity</kanji> of <reading>row</reading>(りょう) boats! Aww, aren't they cute? Look at all of the new row boats lined up together. They all have their own sets of oars too.
data.reading_hint: When every dawn brings a new amount of people, those new people are going to need that same amount of row boats.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>dirt</radical> where you just <radical>stand</radical> and <radical>see</radical> is a <kanji>boundary</kanji>. You don't want to cross the boundary, you just stand there and see over it. As a general rule, you can stand in the dirt and see beyond boundaries, but you don't usually cross them.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine a big line in the dirt where you stand and see over into the other side: that's a boundary. The boundary between your home and your neighbor's, the boundary between cities or countries… Some you can cross, and some you can't.
data.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>boundary</kanji> you're looking at now is the <reading>Kyo</reading>to (きょう) boundary. Kyoto is one of the most famous places in Japan, so you can imagine its boundary is really clear and marked by all kinds of boundary signs that say KYOTO.
data.reading_hint: Picture yourself outside of Kyoto. Picture the boundary between you and Kyoto. Now hop over it!

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> is showing his people how to put a <radical>net</radical> around a weird <radical>zombie</radical> by walking around it in a <kanji>loop</kanji>. It's a weird zombie because it has the ground on top of its head instead of dirt.
data.meaning_hint: Watch as the king loops the net around and around and around the zombie, keeping it completely pinned down.
data.reading_mnemonic: The king also explains that this <kanji>loop</kanji> technique was used by Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) when he was conquering cities. He'd loop around the entire place with a net and trap them.
data.reading_hint: Picture Genghis Khan looping around and around just like the king is looping around and around this zombie.

data.meaning_mnemonic: On the <radical>ground</radical> there's a <radical>ceremony</radical> where everyone keeps <radical>stop</radical>ping. This stopping ceremony is being performed by the <kanji>military</kanji>. They'll march one direction, then stop and turn, then march another direction, then stop again.
data.meaning_hint: The military really seems to have a thing for stopping a lot during their ceremonies.
data.reading_mnemonic: You look closer at the people in the <kanji>military</kanji> and realize that every time they stop they take a drink of <reading>boo</reading>ze (ぶ)!
data.reading_hint: This is a ceremony for celebrating the military so I guess they can drink as much booze as they want, but this seems very strange to you.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You have to use two <radical>axe</radical>s to open these <radical>shellfish</radical>. That seems like overkill, but it is necessary. These particular shellfish are of very high <kanji>quality</kanji> meaning they won't open so easily.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine the highest quality shellfish you've ever seen. They're hard, smooth, and basically impenetrable.
data.reading_mnemonic: You finally get all of the shellfish open and you're admiring their <kanji>quality</kanji>, when your <reading>shih tzu</reading> (しつ) jumps up on the table and gobbles them down. NO! You try to chase after the little dog, but it's too late. They're gone.
data.reading_hint: I guess your shih tzu knows good quality shellfish too. :(

data.meaning_mnemonic: On this <radical>scooter</radical>, there's an <radical>angel</radical> with a <radical>drop</radical> of sweat coming off of it, because it forgot to <kanji>mention</kanji> something to you! It seems like it's something important too, since they're sweating so much.
data.meaning_hint: The angel just visited you, but it forgot to mention something important (probably life-threatening, it's an angel after all), and now you see it scooting at top speeds toward you.
data.reading_mnemonic: "I forgot to <kanji>mention</kanji>, you have to study nin<reading>jutsu</reading> (じゅつ)!" the angel yells. But it's too late, there are ninjas jumping out of the bushes around you and taking you hostage.
data.reading_hint: The angel really should have mentioned ninjutsu earlier. Then maybe you would have gone straight to a dojo to learn instead of falling into a ninjutsu trap yourself. The angel definitely failed its mission.

data.meaning_mnemonic: When a <radical>leader</radical> wants to work <radical>together</radical>, it means they want what you have to <kanji>offer</kanji>. Congrats! Now you can <kanji>accompany</kanji> them everywhere and offer them hot towels and bottled water, or whatever it is you do…
data.meaning_hint: Picture handing things to your leader as you accompany them somewhere. You're happy to do this, but you know you have so much more to offer than a hot towel and a pretty face. When will they see what you really have to offer?!
data.reading_mnemonic: Once a year, the leader will <kanji>offer</kanji> you a vacation in <reading>きょう</reading>と. It's an all-expenses-paid trip! The catch is that you have to <kanji>accompany</kanji> your leader to きょうと…
data.reading_hint: Picture you and the leader enjoying some matcha together under the cherry blossoms in きょうと. Yeah, this was definitely worth it. So glad you took them up on their offer and accompanied them.

data.meaning_mnemonic: There’s a <radical>flag</radical> under the <radical>blackjack</radical> table that you can <radical>kick</radical> in order to <kanji>expand</kanji> the table. Sometimes you only have a few people playing blackjack so you don’t need to kick the flag at all, and sometimes  there are many people playing blackjack so you need to kick the flag many times in order to expand it to a proper size.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine yourself kicking this flag to see the blackjack table expand. Feel your foot kicking the flag. You’ve kicked it so many times that your leg is sore, but you need to expand the table some more so you keep kicking it. Imagine the blackjack table making that sound Mario makes whenever he gets a mushroom and expands in size.
data.reading_mnemonic: The blackjack table does have a limit though of how many times it will <kanji>expand</kanji>, and that limit is <reading>ten</reading> (てん). You can only kick the flag to get the table to expand ten times.
data.reading_hint: Imagine yourself kicking the flag ten times. Count it off in your head and imagine each instance up to ten. Any more kicks after ten don’t cause the table to do anything, but it does cause your leg to get sore.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A sudden aversion to <radical>shellfish</radical> makes you <radical>anti</radical>-shellfish, so you <kanji>sell</kanji> off every shellfish in sight.
data.meaning_hint: If you're serious about being anti-shellfish then you should sell all the ones you have.
data.reading_mnemonic: You're going to <kanji>sell</kanji> all of our shellfish to <reading>Han</reading> (はん) Solo. He isn't anti-shellfish like you, and he knows how to turn a profit too!
data.reading_hint: Picture yourself selling all of your shellfish to Han Solo. You stand there with your arms crossed, and Han just shakes his head at you and continues to toss them onto his spaceship.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You're stuck in a <radical>tree</radical> after using the evacuation <radical>slide</radical> to jump out of your <radical>jet</radical> — a stunt you pulled after hearing your <kanji>stock</kanji>s and <kanji>share</kanji>s had taken a dive in the market.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine lying battered and bruised in the upper boughs of this tree and thinking about all your worthless stocks and shares. Hopefully you had fun jumping out of your private jet, 'cause you can't afford to ride in it anymore.
data.reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>stock</kanji>s and <kanji>share</kanji>s fell so hard that they probably went "<reading>KABOO</reading>M (かぶ)!" when they hit rock bottom.
data.reading_hint: Imagine watching a real-time graph of your stock portfolio as its value plummets. The line dives toward the x-axis, and then… KABOOM! Not a cent of value left. Oh well… At least you had fun shouting "KABOOM" as your stocks crashed.

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>building</radical>'s <radical>root</radical>s will <kanji>limit</kanji> the things under and around it.
data.meaning_hint: Picture the roots of a building: metal beams going into the ground. Now imagine trying to build something like a subway under there. It's not good! The building limits what can go under it.
data.reading_mnemonic: The person who hates these <kanji>limit</kanji>s more than anyone else is <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん). He wants to be able to tunnel under buildings, sneak in, smooch ladies, and sneak back out. But all the building root limits make that impossible!
data.reading_hint: Picture Genji tunneling under a building where a cute lady lives. He's trying to get in, but the building roots limit how far he can dig. No! Now how will he steal a secret kiss?!

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>beggar</radical> lies sprawled on the <radical>ground</radical> so you <kanji>give</kanji> him some money. You feel bad for the beggar on the ground, so that’s why you decided to give him something.
data.meaning_hint: See the beggar on the ground. He’s writhing in agony and moaning for help. Imagine how sad and pitiful he looks.
data.reading_mnemonic: When you set the money down next to the beggar he shouts, “No! I want a <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ)!” so you go to the corner store and buy him a yo-yo with the money instead. You <kanji>give</kanji> the yo-yo to the beggar and he looks very happy.
data.reading_hint: Now watch as the beggar plays with the yo-yo you just gave him. He’s actually pretty good with it. See the beggar doing insane tricks with his new yo-yo as passersby give him change for his impressive yo-yo performance.

data.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Now</radical> your <radical>mouth</radical> can <kanji>include</kanji> more words than ever before! With our new and improved “Mouth Now!” program, your mouth will include more words than you ever thought possible!
data.meaning_hint: Imagine how your repertoire of new words will impress all your friends and family. Don’t include them on your secret that you used the Mouth Now! program, just feel super smart with all the words you now know.
data.reading_mnemonic: If you buy now, we’ll also <kanji>include</kanji> a handful of books by <reading>Gan</reading>dhi (がん) himself. Gandhi didn’t use our program, but we’re sure if he’d had the opportunity to, he would have used it. So buy now, and get the words of Gandhi in your hands as well as your mouth!
data.reading_hint: Since you bought the program, you also got the Gandhi books included with your order. Imagine yourself reading them and learning all about non-violent resistance. Fascinating.

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> rises over the <radical>capital</radical>, shines down on your <radical>hair</radical>, and casts a long <kanji>shadow</kanji> on the ground in front of you.
data.meaning_hint: Feel the heat of the sun on your back as you look down over your capital, your long hair blowing over your shoulder. Your shadow stretches in front of you and it's honestly pretty impressive.
data.reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>shadow</kanji> is being cast over a small <reading>a</reading>corn (えい) lying on the ground. Looking at it, you realize your shadow will keep the acorn from growing up big and strong, unless you move…
data.reading_hint: Imagine seeing this tiny acorn darkened by your shadow. Do you keep standing there, admiring the view and casting your shadow over the acorn? Or do you move and let the acorn grow into a tree, to someday cast its own shadow?

data.meaning_mnemonic: There’s a <radical>tsunami</radical> coming and your <radical>older brother</radical> is in no <kanji>condition</kanji> to escape. Your older brother has brittle bone syndrome so there’s no way he’ll be able to escape the tsunami in time in his condition.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine your poor brother and the condition he is in. His glass bones and paper skin make it impossible for him to move very fast. Imagine the sad face he makes when he realizes his fate.
data.reading_mnemonic: His <kanji>condition</kanji> gets worse and you have to travel all the way to his home in <reading>きょう</reading>と to get him out.
data.reading_hint: This is also, incidentally, where the tsunami's condition is the worst, so you better get to きょうと quick!

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> carries your <radical>yurt</radical> and you on a <radical>stool</radical> under it away. You are now in <kanji>transit</kanji>.
data.meaning_hint: Imagine being carried away on your stool by the tsunami, with your entire yurt floating around you too. You're both in transit... to somewhere. You don't know where though.
data.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>transit</kanji> of yourself and your yurt home is due to the <reading>water</reading> (わた). This is water transit.
data.reading_hint: You hope the tsunami's water will drop you off somewhere nice. Somewhere it's easy to jump on a different kind of mass transit, to get back home again.
