data.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen 一番 (number one), but what is this <kanji>eye</kanji> on the end? Like in the word 〜丁目, the 目 here marks a position in a sequence. So, add this to "number one" and you have <vocabulary>the first thing</vocabulary> or simply <vocabulary>the first</vocabulary>.

Just imagine your collection of eyeballs you have at home. (You have a collection of eyeballs, right?) You have them lined up in a display case and you're explaining the first one to your friend. It's not first because it's the best or anything — you love all your eyeballs equally, after all — but it does happen to come first in sequence in your display right now.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is just the vocab word 一番 plus the word 目. If you know both of those readings you'll be able to read this one as well.

data.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>return</kanji> the <kanji>doing</kanji>s of another person, you're doing it to <vocabulary>get even</vocabulary> (whether it's a nice thing or a mean thing).
data.reading_mnemonic: The readings are a bit weird, here. 仕 gets its on'yomi reading... you should be okay with that. 返し gets the kun'yomi reading, though, which is the reading you saw with the word 返す in level 9. You can tell this part uses the kun'yomi vocab reading because it has that hiragana attached to it. Just remember to distinguish between the two parts of the word to remember the readings.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen the word 高い from a couple levels ago. This word is related to that. It's like 大きい versus 大きさ, where one describes the other. In this case, the 高さ is the <vocabulary>height</vocabulary> of something (while 高い is tall). This word isn't "price" though. For that you'd ask いくらですか？ (how much is it?).
data.reading_mnemonic: Use the reading of 高い (たかい) to help you to learn and remember the reading for this one. They're the same except for the hiragana at the end.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen the word 楽しい, which means "fun." This is obviously very similar looking, though this one means <vocabulary>looking forward to</vocabulary>. Why? Because it has a み on the end, saying "who is going to have fun? It's <reading>me</reading>! That's why I'm looking forward to it!"
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just like 楽しい, so make sure you know that and you'll be able to read this one as well.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 向く and 向ける by now. They mean "to face" and "to turn toward." This has a similar idea. When you add 向け to something imagine you're turning it, aiming it at someone. It's aimed at them, meaning it's <vocabulary>made for</vocabulary> them. Turn a book toward someone, now it's <vocabulary>aimed at</vocabulary> them, it's made for them. See the connection?
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 向く so work off of that word to be able to read this one.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen that 研究 is "research" from previous vocab, and you might remember 所 can mean "facility." So this word means <vocabulary>research institute</vocabulary> or, of course, <vocabulary>research facility</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will also help if you know the reading of 研究 already.

Also note that 所 is normal in first reading, but gets rendaku'd in the second reading, meaning しょ becomes じょ. Both readings are valid and they don't affect the meaning, so it just comes down to personal preference!

context_sentences.en: This research institute is famous throughout the country.
context_sentences.ja: ここは、全国でも有名な研究所です。

context_sentences.en: This shampoo was created at a research institute in the United States.

data.meaning_mnemonic: Taking the <kanji>nearby</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> will get you to your destination more quickly (because it's more close by!). This is a <vocabulary>shortcut</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>short way</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a bit weird in this one. It uses the kun'yomi reading for both kanji, even though it looks just like it should be all on'yomi reading. It's like you're taking a <vocabulary>shortcut</vocabulary> with your kanji readings and doing the native Japanese readings (kun'yomi) instead of the more intellectual Chinese ones (on'yomi). Luckily, you've hopefully seen both of these kanji as vocab already. You have ちか for 近 (short for 近い) and you have 道 (みち), just like the word "street" you learned before. Combine these together and you have the reading for this word. Perhaps it's like this because you're combining a couple concepts together into one word, at least when it comes to "short + way."

context_sentences.en: There's a shortcut if you turn down this road to the right.
context_sentences.ja: この道を右に曲がった方が、近道ですよ。

context_sentences.en: Not all shortcuts are safe roads.
context_sentences.ja: 全ての近道が、安全な道という事じゃない。

context_sentences.en: If you take a shortcut, you can go to the cherry blossom viewing venue quickly.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 助ける means "to help." This word, 助かる, is related, but it's a bit different. It means to be helped or to be saved. It's intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. Imagine shouting "I'm saved!" No direct object, right? Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 助ける, so hopefully you know that word and can apply that knowledge over here.

context_sentences.en: I'm sure they'll be fine. It's okay.
context_sentences.ja: きっと助かるよ。平気。

context_sentences.en: When I left the house, there was a taxi right in front of my eyes and I was saved.
context_sentences.ja: 家を出たら、目の前にタクシーがいて、助かった。

context_sentences.en: The teacher told us in advance what kind of answers we will be asked for on this test, which was very helpful.

data.meaning_mnemonic: There is an <kanji>interval</kanji> (of time) that you need "to suit" (合う). To suit that interval, you need to be there before the time in question. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to be in time for</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to make it on time</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be on time for</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading for 間 when you learned 間もなく. And the reading for 合う is just that of the word 合う. If you remember them both, you'll remember this word!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You hopefully know the word 返す, which means "to return" (as in, you're doing the direct action of returning something). This word, on the other hand, is the version where something just returns (and you're not doing the action of returning it). Use the る to help you to remember this. る the Kangaroo is returned to you. You don't do any of the returning, it just happens or someone else does it. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to be returned</vocabulary>.

Note this word is often combined with くる (to come), which reinforces the aspect that something is coming back to you.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 返す, so as long as you know that you'll be able to apply it here to learn the reading of this word as well.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen the word 楽しい, which means "fun." This is basically the verb version (ends in an う sound, right?) of that. That means this is <vocabulary>to enjoy something</vocabulary>, or just <vocabulary>to have fun</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 楽しい, so be sure to know that word and you'll be able to apply it over here.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen the word 決める before. This is similar, except instead of deciding something, something gets decided. Rules are decided, a schedule gets decided — that kind of thing. It's intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. So 決まる means to be decided. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 決める, so make sure you know that word so you can apply that knowledge over here.

context_sentences.en: Hey mom, when will it be decided what we will eat today?
context_sentences.ja: ねえママ、今日は何を食べるか決まるのはいつ？

context_sentences.en: Has the day of enrollment been decided?
context_sentences.ja: いつが入学の日か決まりました？

data.reading_mnemonic: The readings just come from two vocab words you've hopefully seen already: 投げる and 付ける. So long as you know the readings for those words, the reading for this word should be no problem for you.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen the word 化ける (to transform) before, and here's a related word: 化かす. This means <vocabulary>to bewitch</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to trick</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to deceive</vocabulary>.

Why? In Japanese folklore, foxes, spirits and other yokai often transform in order to bewitch, trick, or deceive humans. To 化かす them, in other words.

This verb is transitive, so it needs a direct object — you bewitch, trick, or deceive someone. You know this because when a fox wants to bewitch someone, they have to <reading>cuss</reading> (かす). They say a magic cuss word that lets them change forms and fool people. Those tricksy foxes…
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 化ける, so make sure you know that word and you'll be able to learn this word's reading as well.

context_sentences.en: This fox is a genius at enchanting people.
context_sentences.ja: このキツネは人を化かす天才だ。

context_sentences.en: "I’m sorry I couldn't make it the other day. I was bewitched by a fox." "No worries. Things like that can’t be helped."
context_sentences.ja: 「先日は来れなくて、すみませんでした。キツネに化かされちまってねえ。」「心配しないでください。それはどうしようもない事ですから。」

data.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji version of 話 means <kanji>talk</kanji>. This word also means <vocabulary>talk</vocabulary>, but it means a few other things as well. This can refer to a <vocabulary>speech</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>story</vocabulary> as well. Basically anything that involves a talking session. So, before you go, I hope you stay awhile and listen to my 話.
data.reading_mnemonic: Hey, tell that <vocabulary>story</vocabulary> about the time you met the <reading>花-shee</reading>p (はなし). You know — the sheep that had 花s growing out of it instead of wool. No one else here has ever met a 花-sheep, so I bet they'd all love to hear your story.

context_sentences.en: No matter how many times you tell me the same story, I still don't understand.
context_sentences.ja: 同じ話を何回されても、よく分かりません。

context_sentences.en: A talk about Japanese toilets again?
context_sentences.ja: また日本のトイレの話ですか？

context_sentences.en: Could you listen to me for just a little bit?
context_sentences.ja: 少しだけでいいので、話を聞いてもらえないですか？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji means <kanji>yonder</kanji>, which is like "over there." This is the verb version of "yonder." That being said, "to yonder" isn't really a thing, so you have to think of what happens when you "look yonder." This word means <vocabulary>to turn toward</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary>. You're looking yonder, but you have to turn towards said yonder to look that way.

This word can also mean <vocabulary>to be suitable</vocabulary>, as in a good fit for a job, role, or situation. After all, you turn toward the things you're most suitable for, right?
data.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You turn <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary> a new direction and look out into the distance. There is a single cow out there. It turns to face you too, and says <reading>moo</reading> (む).

context_sentences.ja: こっちを向いてください。

context_sentences.ja: 家は西に向いていて、午後は日当たりがいいです。

data.reading_mnemonic: The readings are that of 知る and 合う. So long as you know those words, you should be able to read this one too.

context_sentences.ja: お知り合いですか？

context_sentences.ja: アイツと知り合いだとはゼッタイにバレたくない。

data.meaning_mnemonic: What's a <kanji>ride</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji>? It's a <vocabulary>boarding area</vocabulary>! This word is used widely to refer to any place where you board transportation, such as a <vocabulary>bus stop</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>taxi stand</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>train platform</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings. You didn't learn the kun'yomi reading for 場 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

You're in a country inhabited only by sheep, but luckily you've practiced your Sheepanese well enough to be able to baa for directions at <vocabulary>bus stop</vocabulary>s, <vocabulary>taxi stand</vocabulary>s, and <vocabulary>train platform</vocabulary>s.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
使う means "to use," right? Well, the <kanji>way</kanji> to use something is also known as <vocabulary>how to use</vocabulary> it. 

You'll see this on directions that explain how to use something, for example, or you can use it to talk about someone's <vocabulary>way of using</vocabulary> time, money, and other resources.
data.reading_mnemonic: This word uses kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You learned the つか reading with 使う, while the かた reading for 方 is the one you learned with other "how-to" words like 作り方 and 読み方.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You know 事 means "occurrence," but it can also mean "thing." So when you're <kanji>doing</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji>s all day, what are you probably doing? A <vocabulary>job</vocabulary>! All jobs really just amount to doing things.

Just like "job" in English, 仕事 can refer to a person's specific <vocabulary>occupation</vocabulary>, to <vocabulary>work</vocabulary> in general, or to a particular task depending on the context.
data.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi reading for 仕 and the kun'yomi reading for 事. Please note that 事 uses the reading こと, which you didn't learn with the kanji, but you have come across it once or twice by now, and because of the way rendaku works, it's changed to the voiced ごと.

data.reading_mnemonic: The readings are kun'yomi, but you should be familiar with 負ける and of course 犬 well enough to learn the reading here.

data.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 待ち comes right from 待つ. You know the drill by now.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>attach</kanji> your <kanji>energy</kanji> (imagine someone suddenly looking up at something, attaching their energy to it), you have noticed or realized something. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to realize</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to notice</vocabulary>. 

Don't confuse this with 気を付けて which is similar in that it has all the same kanji. It's just used a little different. Try to remember the difference before moving on.

data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the vocab word 時 twice, with the second one getting rendaku'd.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The place where they <kanji>accept</kanji> paperwork and <kanji>attach</kanji> stuff to it is <vocabulary>reception</vocabulary>. Hand them your forms, and they'll be covered with sticky notes and paperclips before you know it.

受付 is where things officially get received, checked in, or processed at a business, institution, or event. It can refer to the <vocabulary>reception desk</vocabulary> itself, the <vocabulary>receptionist</vocabulary> behind it, or even the procedures that get handled there, as in 受付番号 (application number, reception number) or 受付をすませる (finish check-in or registration).

Note that it can also be written as 受け付け, since it originally comes from combining 受ける (to receive something) and 付ける (to attach something).
data.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is a combination of the verbs 受ける and 付ける, the reading comes from them too: うけつけ.

data.meaning_mnemonic: You should know 開ける by now. This word is similar to that, except it has to do with when things are just open. It's the same thing, though. The meaning is also <vocabulary>to open</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic:
Do you remember the reading for 開ける, which you learned in level 10? That's right, it's あける! So if you know the reading of that word (I hope you do!) then you can apply that knowledge here.

Just a quick side note — 開く can also be read as ひらく, but we're going to focus on the あく reading here. Since ひらく has slightly different meanings, we won't accept it as a reading for this word, so be sure to enter あく!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You know 初 means <kanji>first</kanji>, and に can mark a point in time. So 初めに means <vocabulary>at first</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>in the beginning</vocabulary>. 

初めに has a lot of overlap with 始めに. But while 始めに is for the beginning of some larger process, 初めに refers more to doing something first or to the initial point of a certain time frame. You might say 初めにアクビをしたのは私です (I was the one who yawned first), for example, or 今年の初めに (at the start of this year).
data.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi, which you didn't learn with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you out. What are you beginning? You are beginning <reading>Haj</reading> (はじ). (Haj is the fifth pillar of Islam, and is a pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhu al-Hijja).

data.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means transmit, and this verb version is to be transmitted or to be conveyed. It's intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. A message is transmitted, or your feelings are conveyed — that kind of thing. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
data.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 伝える.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 放す is "to release"? Now you're learning the intransitive version. Instead of you doing the releasing, something gets released or freed. So this is <vocabulary>to get loose</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to escape</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be released</vocabulary>.

放れる describes something held in place coming loose and starting to move, like an animal breaking free from its tether or an arrow being released from a bowstring. You know this because it's pretty rare (れる) for something that's restrained to break free from its bonds. Escaping isn't easy, so it only happens on rare occasions.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same one you learned with 放す. If you can remember that word, you can apply the reading over here as well.

You might recall that this reading is the same as <reading>写</reading>る and might wonder if they're related. They are! It means <vocabulary>to heat something up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to warm something up</vocabulary>. It's all about you doing something to another object to make it hot, like putting it in the microwave.

The kanji reading is the same as 温かい. As long as you know that reading, you should be able to associate it with this word.

Just like you can say あったかい for 温かい, people often say あっためる in conversation. The "official" reading is still あたためる, so when typing out the kanji or taking a test, try to stick to あたためる.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen 起きる which is "to wake up." This is similar, except you are waking someone else up, which makes the meaning of this word <vocabulary>to wake someone up</vocabulary>. How do you differentiate between this and 起きる? Because of the す on the end. You wake someone up violently, wrenching their neck. They turn around and <reading>sue</reading> (す) you, making you wish you never woke them up.

This can also mean <vocabulary>to cause something</vocabulary>. I guess if you wake someone up and they're not a morning person, you could cause something... like trouble.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 起きる, so as long as you know that word you should be able to read this one. Of course, you can also imagine them yelling "OH!" when you shake them awake too, if that helps.

イギリス means "United Kingdom." So what is a "United Kingdom person?" You guessed it — a <vocabulary>British person</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>person from the UK</vocabulary>.

Fun fact: イギリス is thought to come from the Portuguese word for "English," which arrived in Japan way before the United Kingdom was a thing. Nowadays, イギリス usually means the whole UK, but it's sometimes used loosely to mean just England.
data.reading_mnemonic:
Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here.

And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: 

As with all words for nationalities, the 人 here is pronounced じん. All nationalities, including <vocabulary>Brit</vocabulary>s, love <reading>jean</reading>s (じん)!

This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>renew</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be renewed</vocabulary>. Like most verbs ending in まる, this is an intransitive verb, meaning it doesn't take a direct object. Something renews or gets renewed, or something changes. See? No direct object.

Although it's not often translated as "renew," 改まる implies a kind of renewal in the changes it's used to describe — whether it's the revision of regulations or the old year changing over to a new one. It can also be used for personal improvements, or describe a shift to a more formal demeanor in social situations.

More specifically, 一夫多妻 is a term for <vocabulary>polygyny</vocabulary>, or marriage between one man and multiple women. You'll mostly run into it in period dramas or discussions of history and anthropology, since it was common among the ruling elite of certain societies during premodern times.

果たして is a word used to express skepticism or uncertainty about an outcome. For example, you might hear a soccer announcer say 果たしてゴールできるのか？(will they indeed be able to score?) as a player runs down the field, or an anime character say 果たしてそうなのかな？(I wonder if that's really the case?) when they're doubting something they've been told. It sounds a bit dramatic and theatrical, so you'll run into it more in entertainment media than in casual conversation.

In some cases, it can also mean <vocabulary>as was expected</vocabulary>, as in 果たして失敗した (as expected, they failed), but this meaning is mostly limited to either older or quite literary writing.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 焼く is "to bake," "to burn something," or "to grill"? 焼ける is just the intransitive version. That means no direct object needed! So this verb means <vocabulary>to get baked</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to get burned</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to get grilled</vocabulary>. 

焼ける is used when something is heated and transformed by the heat. Depending on the context, it can refer to anything from a muffin getting baked, fish being grilled, or pottery being fired. You can even use it when your skin gets a tan or a house burns down. Well, that last one is kinda sad. I hope it never happens.

You can distinguish 焼ける from 焼く because when cooking, you always <reading>care</reading> (ける) to ensure the food gets baked or grilled really well. You want to make sure it's properly 焼ける'd (heated through) to be safe!

The kanji means <kanji>mix</kanji>, and you already learned its transitive and intransitive pair: 混ぜる (to mix) and 混ざる (to get mixed). 混じる is another intransitive verb, but it means <vocabulary>to be mixed in with</vocabulary>.

So how are 混ざる and 混じる different? 混ざる is used to talk about things that become mixed together as part of the same whole — like blended colors or intermingled groups. 混じる, on the other hand, is less about blending smoothly and more about something getting mixed in when it doesn't quite belong — static in your audio, scattered strands of gray in your dark hair, or even some random stranger sitting at your group's table.

You can remember this by thinking about how this out-of-place thing getting mixed in makes you want to <reading>jeer</reading> (じる): "Boo, get out of here! You don't fit in!"

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>come to an end</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is also about something ending: it means <vocabulary>to be finished</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be done</vocabulary>.

済む is used when something finishes or is resolved, often without further trouble, like 支払いが済む (the payment is completed). From this core idea of resolution, it also pops up in various other expressions about things coming to a close or being "enough."

For example, 気が済む means to feel satisfied with something such that you can get some issue out of your system, as in 気が済むまで泣く (cry till you feel better). Likewise, 〜で済む expresses that something on its own is sufficient, like 電話一本で済む (a single phone call is all it takes).

価 refers to the monetary value or the price of goods in a transaction. Although it's somewhat old-fashioned and less common these days, you may still see it used in advanced phrases like 価をつける (to set a price) or 一文の価もない (not even worth a penny).

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember 済む and how it means "to be finished"? Well this is the version where you're going <vocabulary>to finish something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to settle something</vocabulary> yourself. You can remember this because you like to finish things en <reading>masse</reading> (ます). It's always best get lots of things done all at once.

済ます describes actively bringing something to completion, as in 仕事を済ます (finish your work) or 食事を済ます (finish a meal). Unlike 終わらせる, which simply means "to bring something to an end," 済ます focuses more on dealing with something like it's a task on your to do list — you're getting it out of the way so you can move on.

Because of this, it's also often used in the pattern 〜で済ます to mean you're handling something in a way that goes no further than necessary, like 簡単な食事で済ます (just eat something quick and simple) or 電話で済ます (just deal with something by phone).
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with 済む, so if you know that you'll be able to finish this vocab.

You know that 経済 means "economy," and adding 的 to words turns them into adjectives. What's the adjective version of "economy"? <vocabulary>Economic</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>financial</vocabulary>.

経済的 describes things related to money and economics. It can refer to the actual economy, like 経済的問題 (economic problems), but can also be used on a personal level, like 経済的に難しい (financially difficult). Depending on the context, you'll also see it used to mean "<vocabulary>economical</vocabulary>" as in cost-efficient, where the focus is on saving money or using resources wisely.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>touch</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to touch something</vocabulary>.

触る is used when someone does the touching. It's not used to describe objects touching each other.

Note that 触る can be used with either the particle に or を, like 手に触る or 手を触る (to touch a hand). Using に simply marks the location you touch, while using を highlights your action of touching that specific area or object. So the former is intransitive and the latter is transitive, though there's some debate about that.

The kanji is <kanji>distinction</kanji>, and the verb version here means… a million things. Let's just focus on a few common meanings. Things with distinction tend to stick out from the others. They tend <vocabulary>to shine</vocabulary>, you know? And if you imagine shining a beam of light on something, that light tends <vocabulary>to project</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to extend outward</vocabulary>. It sticks out, shines on something, then makes that thing more distinct too. 

That's why you can say 光が差す (light shines), かげが差す (a shadow is cast), 指差す (to point at), or even カサを差す (to open and raise an umbrella). Basically, 差す usually has to do with causing something <vocabulary>to appear</vocabulary>, either by shining or projecting outward.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen how 捕まえる means "to catch," and this is its intransitive sibling: <vocabulary>to be caught</vocabulary>.

At its core, 捕まる means getting physically caught, whether you've lost a game of tag or been arrested by the police. Sometimes, it can be used in a more figurative sense too, like when you get held up by a really chatty person (you've been "caught" by them) or you finally manage to get a word with someone you've been trying to talk to (they've been "caught" by you).

You can tell this apart from 捕まえる by thinking about how it would really <reading>mar</reading> (まる) your reputation if you were <vocabulary>to be arrested</vocabulary> by the cops.

You're replacing the air as quickly as you can because if you don't you wouldn't be able to breathe in this small room.

替える means to replace something with another item of the same kind or equivalent, rather than changing its state. Wondering how it differs from 代える? While 代える stresses that you’re using someone or something “in place of another,” 替える simply indicates the act of swapping one thing for another similar thing.

Wondering about the difference between 代わる and 替わる? 代わる is used when someone or something takes the place of another, like filling in for a sick coworker. Whereas 替わる is used when things or situations switch places or are replaced with something new, like when talking about generations changing or a new governmental cabinet taking over.

This verb is intransitive, meaning it doesn't take a direct object. You'll sometimes see it with the particle を, though, because the を is showing a "path" rather than a direct object in this case. For example, 席を替わる (to switch seats) indicates your location is moving from one seat to another. Likewise, 電話を替わる indicates that a call is being handed off to another person.

総理府 was actually renamed 内閣府 in 2001, so you'd generally only use 総理府 to talk about the Cabinet Offices from back in the day.
data.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 総理 beforehand as well.

context_sentences.ja: 総理府次長がお前のことをさがしていたぞ。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
置く is <kanji>to put down</kanji> something. So a <kanji>location</kanji> where you put something down is a <vocabulary>place to put something</vocabulary>.

置き場 often follows another word, signifying it's the designated area where that specific item should be stored or parked. For example, 自転車置き場.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings. 置き comes from 置く, and you learned 場's reading with 場所, but here's a mnemonic to help you just in case:

You're looking for a <vocabulary>place to put something</vocabulary> that goes "<reading>baa</reading>" (ば). Your pet sheep won't stop baaing and it's getting annoying, so you want to put it somewhere. "Baa, baa," it bleats irritatingly as you search high and low for a good place to put it.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 載る is "to be placed on"? This one is <vocabulary>to place on something</vocabulary>, like a mug on a table. 載せる is transitive, and you know this because you do it your<reading>sel</reading>f (せる). Like 載る, 載せる also often refers to putting something in a written document or publication, so it can mean <vocabulary>to put on record</vocabulary>.

Note that 載せる is never used to refer to putting clothing or accessories on. That's 着る or 着ける respectively, which you've learned already.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is shared with 載る, so as long as you remember that you can remember this.

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stab</kanji> so the verb vocab version must also be <vocabulary>to stab</vocabulary>.

Wondering how it's different from 刺す? 突く refers to the act of pushing or pressing something with a tip of an object, often done forcefully and swiftly. So when you use 突く as in "to stab," your focus is on the forcefulness of the action. On the other hand, 刺す focuses more on the actual act of piercing into something or someone with a sharp thing. 

This is why 突く can be be translated many ways, like <vocabulary>to poke</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to jab</vocabulary>, and many more.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
触る means "to touch," and 触れる also means <vocabulary>to touch</vocabulary>. The word also means <vocabulary>to touch on</vocabulary>, as in touching on some subject. Just think of a subject that is <reading>rare</reading> (れる) for you to want to touch on.

触れる is often for when something happens <vocabulary>to come into contact with</vocabulary> something, possibly in a fleeting or momentary way. It's still used in phrases like "When I touched your hand," but has a lighter, more indirect and literary feel than 触る, which conveys a greater sense of purpose and intent behind the action.

触れる is often used in constructions like 手がカバンに触れる (one's hand touches a bag), where が indicates what's doing the touching and に marks what's being touched. If you see を instead of が, 触れる becomes transitive, changing the meaning to "to have your hand touch a bag."
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is totally different from 触る so don't let that fool you. In this case, you feel some <reading>fur</reading> (ふれ).

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 抜く means "to pull something out"? 抜ける describes something coming out of where it was, so it means <vocabulary>to come out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to fall out</vocabulary>. 

This can be used for air coming out of a balloon, hair falling out, or pages missing from a book. It also means passing through places or leaving a group you were a part of.

捕える and 捕まえる both mean "to catch," but 捕える tends to sound more weighty and literary — you're far more likely to see it in a book talking about the capture of a fleeing enemy general than to hear it from a kid who just caught a grasshopper.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 掛ける is "to hang something"? Well, 掛かる focuses on the fact that something is hanging, without specifying who did it. So it means <vocabulary>to be hung</vocabulary>. Use it to say a picture is hung on the wall, for example. 

掛かる can also mean <vocabulary>to be hooked</vocabulary>, whether it's the picture hooked to the wall or a fish that happens <vocabulary>to be caught</vocabulary> on a hook. 

These uses are all intransitive, so you don't need a direct object them. A hint for this is that 掛かる ends with okurigana that rhyme with ある, and those kinds of verbs tend to be intransitive.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 掛ける, so as long as you know that you know this too.

並列 is a relatively formal word for things being arranged side by side in alignment. You'll most commonly see it used in a technical sense, like with <vocabulary>parallel</vocabulary> circuits in electronic stuff. But it's also used to describe the orderly side-by-side arrangements of other things, such as vehicles parked next to each other in a row or soldiers standing in ranks.

並ぶ is intransitive, so it describes things being in a line, rather than things you're putting in a line yourself. You can remember this because you always say <reading>boo</reading> (ぶ) when you arrive at a store or a restaurant and see that there are already a bunch of people lined up outside.

But 街道 doesn't mean a modern highway that you drive on. It refers to the great <vocabulary>high road</vocabulary>s of the past that linked major cities and regions. In Japan, these were typically the Edo-period routes like 日光街道 (Nikkō Kaidō) and 中山道 (Nakasendō). It also works for other historically important routes, like ancient Rome's アッピア街道 (the Appian Way).

Remember this by imagining an olden-day <vocabulary>highway</vocabulary> full of people in <reading>kay</reading>aks (かい). data.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>deposit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to deposit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to entrust</vocabulary>. 

You use 預ける when you leave something in someone else's care for a while, expecting to get it back. For example, you can use 預ける when you deposit money in a bank, leave your coat in a cloakroom, or even when you park your bicycle in a parking area. You can also use it when you leave your child with grandparents or leave your dog at a pet hotel.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same, so this means <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>within</vocabulary>.

While 中 refers to the inside of something in a basic, positional sense, 内 tends to express a more abstract version of "inside," like 心の内を話す (express your inner feelings) or 温かい内に飲む (drink it while it's still warm). 

It also carries an implied contrast with 外 (outside), so it's often used to talk about yourself or your group, like うちの犬 (our dog) or うちの会社 (the company I work for). In this case, it's almost always written in hiragana as うち — which is why we used it like that in these examples (but hey, now you know where that うち is coming from!).
data.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word:

If someone were to peek <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary> your heart, they would say, "<reading>Ooh, chee</reading>se (うち)!" Most people's hearts are full of emotions and crippling insecurities and stuff, but yours has nothing but cheese <vocabulary>within</vocabulary> it. "Ooh, cheese… I love you so." That's all your heart's inner voice is ever saying.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 絶える means "to die out?" Well 絶やす is its transitive version, meaning <vocabulary>to let something die out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put an end to something</vocabulary>. 

絶やす is used when you stop something from continuing, like ending a family line, letting a tradition fade, or allowing a fire to go out. You know this because if you're putting an end to something, you probably don't like it, so you say "<reading>YAASS</reading>" (やす) with a big evil grin as you let it die out.

Note that 絶やす often appears in its negative form 絶やさない, because it's commonly used to describe the intent not to let something precious or important come to an end.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>acid</kanji> <kanji>element</kanji> is <vocabulary>oxygen</vocabulary>. In German it’s the same as in Japanese - it’s called “Sauerstoff”, including “sauer”, the word for “sour”. The noun version is “Säure” which means both “sourness” and “acid” (which again is the same in Japanese, the same kanji is used in both words). The word “oxygenium” in Greek/Latin literally means “acid maker”. Long ago chemists thought oxygen was a defining characteristic of acids, later they found out there are also acids without oxygen like hydrochloric/muriatic/salt acid and the defining characteristic actually is hydrogen. But the name stuck.

Or you could just imagine all the oxygen you breathe has turned into acid (oh no!), and it sucks to breathe. Whatever works for you.

In Japanese schools, 熟語 can sometimes refer to idioms or common word pairings in foreign languages. But when talking about Japanese itself, 熟語 simply means kanji compounds — kanji teaming up so their meanings can ripen into one neat little word!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned 迷う means "to go astray," and 迷わす is its transitive version, meaning it takes a direct object. So it means <vocabulary>to lead someone astray</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to perplex someone</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to mislead someone</vocabulary>.

While 迷わす can mean literally causing someone to get lost, it's more commonly used for the act of confusing someone — for example, overwhelming them with difficult choices or intentionally misleading them in a malicious way.

You know this verb is transitive because there's nothing <reading>worse</reading> (わす) than purposefully misleading someone. Intentionally leading someone astray is worse than anything!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 積もる (to accumulate) is used when something like snow or dust piles up over time. 積む is the transitive version, so it means <vocabulary>to pile something up</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to stack up</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to load</vocabulary>. You know this because you are the one <reading>mo</reading>ving (む) things to pile them up!

積む is often used for physical actions like stacking boxes or loading luggage, but it's also used in more abstract ways, such as building up experience or skills. Think of it like "stacking up" experience points to level up in your life!
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 積もる, so pile up your knowledge and remember it that way.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 離れる means "to separate," where something separates or moves away from something else? Well, 離す is the transitive version, so it takes a direct object and means <vocabulary>to separate something</vocabulary>. You can remember this because if you try to separate two people who don't want to be separated, they might sue (す) you in response!

離す is used when you detach or put space between people or objects. This could be literal, like when you 離す your bed from the wall, or more figurative, like when you carelessly 離す your eyes from something important. 

It can also mean <vocabulary>to let go</vocabulary> of something, because you're "separating" your hand from it. This use is very similar to 放す, but it doesn't have that nuance of setting something free — it's just the neutral act of letting go of something.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 離れる.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. This adjective describes things that are <kanji>valuable</kanji> in a way that transcends monetary worth, so it means <vocabulary>noble</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>invaluable</vocabulary>.

While 尊い is used for things you honor from the heart, 貴い leans toward a dignified, noble kind of value — the kind tied to high status or social rank. Because of that, you may encounter 貴い in stories about historical class systems or old social hierarchies. It doesn't appear as commonly as 尊い in modern Japanese, but you may still see it in descriptions of someone's noble presence or the sense of dignity they give off.
data.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. This has the same reading as 尊い (revered, noble), so if you remember that, you can read 貴い too! In case you forgot, here's a mnemonic to help you: 

How can you tell if someone comes from a <vocabulary>noble</vocabulary> background? Just check their <reading>toe toe</reading> (とうと). Most noble families are pretty inbred, so a lot of their members will have a big toe (the long とう) with another small toe growing out of it (short と). This is a common birth defect among inbred aristocrats. Of course, from their point of view, it's <vocabulary>invaluable</vocabulary> proof of how noble and superior they are.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Another verb version of the kanji 閉! This is a special one that can be either transitive or intransitive, so 閉じる means <vocabulary>to close something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to close</vocabulary>.

閉じる is for returning things that have expanded open back to their closed state. It's used for books, umbrellas, web browsers, and even eyes and mouths. There are some overlaps with 閉める (you can 閉じる or 閉める a gate, for example) but 閉める is mostly used for things like doors, windows, and curtains.
data.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is different from 閉める or 閉まる. Instead, 閉じる is read とじる.

Why? Because <vocabulary>to close something</vocabulary> that's expanded or spread open, you always use your <reading>toe</reading> (と)! It's easy enough with books, but umbrellas are a real challenge… But you, you can do it! You have the toe-tal control and can close anything expanded to the way it was before.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>descend</kanji>, but this verb vocab word is <vocabulary>to get off</vocabulary>, as in, to get off the train, or to get out of the car. If you think about trains back in the day, you had to descend down to the platform to get out of them, which is how this word became what it is. You know that this word is the "to get off" word because once you get off the train, you enter the <reading>real</reading> (りる) world, where hardships are real and not as comfy as the train.

Figuratively, this word also means <vocabulary>to step down</vocabulary>, as in "to give up" or "to resign” from something. For example, you can say ニュース番組を降りる (to step down from a news program) or ゲームを降りる (to drop out of a game).
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is unlike anything you've seen with this kanji. Just think about how you have <vocabulary>to get off</vocabulary> at <reading>O</reading>-station. None of the other letters are your stop. Just <reading>O</reading>-Station (お).

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>change</kanji>, and this verb is <vocabulary>to change something</vocabulary>. If you change one thing for another thing, you are going <vocabulary>to change</vocabulary> it, after all. This word refers to changing one thing for a similar thing.

変える and 代える sound the same and are sometimes used in similar contexts, but are different in nuance. 変える refers to the act of making something different, and involves altering the nature or state of something. For example, changing the layout of a room or changing one's perspective on an issue. 代える means to substitute or exchange one thing for another that is expected to fulfill the same role, use or purpose, such as replacing a worker with a substitute.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hug</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to embrace</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hold</vocabulary> (in one's arms, that is). It can also mean <vocabulary>to hug</vocabulary>, especially in the form of 抱きしめる.

Keep in mind that depending on the context, 抱く can be a euphemism for something way more sexual than just hugging. Not always, of course, but pretty often, so just be careful how you use it! 抱きしめる is the better option if you're talking about regular old hugs.
data.reading_mnemonic:
What are you going <vocabulary>to embrace</vocabulary>? How about your <reading>da</reading>d (だ)? Or if he's not around, maybe an <reading>e</reading>-<reading>da</reading>d (いだ)? You know, like a digital version of a dad.

The two readings for this word have different nuances. だく is more for physical holding and hugging, as in 赤ちゃんを抱く (to hold a baby). But when it's something you hold in your heart, like an emotion or feeling, use the いだく reading: 疑問を抱く (to hold doubts) or 夢を抱く (to have a dream), for example.

meanings.meaning: To Go Hand In Hand With

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>accompany</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to accompany</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be accompanied by</vocabulary>.

This word is both transitive and intransitive. So it works both when bringing someone with you, like 助手を伴って来る (to come with an assistant), or when going along with someone else, like 上司に伴って行く (to go with one's boss). When it's about physically accompanying someone, it's often used together with a movement verb.

伴う is also used figuratively to talk about consequences that tend <vocabulary>to go hand in hand with</vocabulary> something, like 変化にはリスクが伴う (change comes with risk). In this case, 伴う is usually used by itself.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 埋まる is "to be buried." This verb is also <vocabulary>to be buried</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get buried</vocabulary>. 

However, there's a slight difference between them. 埋まる focuses on the subject itself getting buried or filled, while 埋もれる highlights the sense of something being hidden or obscured by being covered. So you could use it to describe a yard covered in snow or your talent being overshadowed in a competitive environment. 

You can remember this nuance because it's <reading>more rare</reading> (もれる) to see something completely buried and covered up.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 埋める.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>wrap</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to wrap</vocabulary>. 

包む can be used in both literal and figurative ways, so it can be used for wrapping up gifts, enveloping someone in love, or even for fog or light enveloping an area. In cultural contexts, it also sometimes implies the act of giving a financial gift, since in Japan things are often wrapped nicely before being given — even stacks of bills.
data.reading_mnemonic:
You never wrap things once, you always wrap them twice. And then you double that. It's a <reading>two two</reading> (つつ) wrapping technique.

つつむ is the reading we want you to focus on, but it's good to know that 包む can be read as くるむ as well. くるむ is used when you wrap something up carefully and protectively, like a baby in a blanket. つつむ on the other hand, has broader use and is commonly used for wrapping things like presents.

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sink</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to sink something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to submerge something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. So instead of describing something sinking on its own, you use 沈める when you sink an enemy ship or submerge yourself in a bathtub. 

You know this because you can't sink anything until you get that <reading>mail</reading> (める) saying, "Yes, proceed with sinking!" You've got to have that mail if you want to sink something, or else everyone will blame you for the missing ship — or for you disappearing under the water.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
If you want to <kanji>distract</kanji> someone, try saying something <vocabulary>confusing</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>misleading</vocabulary> to them. They'll be so busy trying confusedly to interpret your comment that they'll become totally unable to focus on whatever it is they were originally doing.

紛らわしい is an adjective for things which are confusing because they're <vocabulary>easy to mix up</vocabulary> or easy to be misled by. Think similar-looking kanji (末 and 未, anyone?), places with the same name (London, as in England or Canada?), and celebrities you just can't seem to tell apart. Sometimes, it can refer to intentionally deceptive things too, like a button on a website tricking you into signing up for something. Either way, if it's easy to confuse for something else, then you can probably say it's 紛らわしい.

<vocabulary>Blade</vocabulary> in hand, you charge at your foes hollering "<reading>Yah</reading>! <reading>Eee</reading>! <reading>Baa</reading>!" (やいば). data.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Ten thousand</kanji> <kanji>year</kanji>s! That's a lot of time. This is the word for the turned-English Japanese phrase, <vocabulary>banzai</vocabulary>!

万歳 is a cheerful word used to shout "<vocabulary>hooray</vocabulary>!" when celebrating something good. Because it's usually said with both arms raised, the action of <vocabulary>raising one's arms</vocabulary> can also be referred to as 万歳. This is often used when talking to children, like when telling them to raise their arms to take off a shirt.

And since raising your hands can also mean "<vocabulary>I give up</vocabulary>" in Japan, 万歳 can sometimes mean that as well. So basically, it's either "Yay, we did it!" or "That's it, I'm done." It really covers all your bases!
data.reading_mnemonic:
The reading isn't the same as 万's normal reading. It's ばん instead of まん. And 歳 gets rendaku'd. But, since the word "banzai" is so well known, you probably can remember this reading: ばんざい (<vocabulary>Hooray</vocabulary>)!

And if it's too hard and you can't remember, you can still say ばんざい (<vocabulary>I give up</vocabulary>). Basically, you're gonna end up saying ばんざい either way, so you'll remember it eventually… in theory, at least.

〜達 is stuck onto the end of nouns (usually people or animals) to make them plural. It can also be used with a person's name, like マリア達. In that case, it refers to Maria and the group of people she's with (rather than a bunch of Maria clones or something).

If you want to pluralize something, <reading>touch</reading> (たち) it to something else. One friend touches another friend, well now they're friends. Plural friends! All thanks to the good ol' pluralizing suffix touch!

Oh, and don't type the 〜 out when writing the answer. It's just there to let you know that there's usually something attached in front of this word.

You can remember this because you usually need つ (two) hands to fire something off properly, whether it's a slingshot or a hit in baseball.

It's used to describe things like shooting arrows, firing bullets, letting animals loose into the wild, or even strongly emitting something like light or an offensive smell. data.reading_mnemonic:
The reading can be either the on'yomi or kun'yomi, and you know both.

Between the two, the on'yomi はんせん is the standard reading. As is often the case with on'yomi compounds, it has a more technical feel, so it is commonly used in formal references to sailing ships either in technical books or fiction.

The kun'yomi ほぶね, on the other hand, has a softer, more traditionally Japanese tone, like how people in the past might have referred to it in everyday life. You'll often see it in older songs or literature, but it can also appear in modern works to convey a nostalgic vibe.

data.meaning_mnemonic: This is a <radical>stick</radical>, sticking straight up. It even looks like a stick.
This looks a lot like a <radical>gun</radical> pointing to the right. You have a handle on the left, and the barrel pointing to the right. Imagine it hanging in a case on the wall in a museum.
There's a leaf on top and a stem going down out of it, making this the <radical>leaf</radical> radical. It's a pretty wide and flat leaf, so if it helps you can imagine it as a lily pad leaf.
Do you know those rice paddy hats? The ones shaped just like this radical? That's why this radical is a <radical>hat</radical>.
The three horns represent the <radical>triceratops</radical>, one of the most awesome dinosaurs ever.

Doesn't this look like someone on their knees, holding their clasped hands out and begging for something (forgiveness, their life, a promotion, etc.)? That's why this radical is known as the <radical>beggar</radical>.
Can you see the <radical>horns</radical>? You could put these horns on anything. Donkeys, people, monkeys, and so on. That's exactly what we'll be doing when we learn kanji that have horns too.
On the ground there are a bunch of <radical>spikes</radical> coming out. You wouldn't want to step on those, now would you?

On the top part of the head (冂) radical, there is a horn radical with one extra spike in the middle. This is a horned helmet with one extra spike. Who were famous for having horned helmets like that? The Vikings! That's why this radical is called <radical>Viking</radical>.

This looks like a stick-figure foot on the left kicking at something, which makes it the radical for <radical>kick</radical>. See the shin and foot swinging up for the kick? You can think of that part on the right as the edge of a ball that's about to be kicked.
See the rolling <radical>hills</radical> with the road going off into the background to another hill? That's why this is the hills radical.

There's the bottom of a shoe with spikes coming out of it. Only one kind of shoe is like this, and that's a <radical>cleat</radical>. You know, like those studded shoes athletes wear. Soccer cleats, baseball cleats, running cleats… You knew they were called cleats, right?
This is the <radical>pope</radical> radical. Why? Because it looks like a pope hat! This one's got a big old cross on top, and it can only be worn by the pope.

This is the <radical>Chinese</radical> radical. Why? Because it looks like a traditional Chinese pagoda! One of those towers with a bunch of tiered roofs, you know? Sure, lots of Asian countries have pagodas, but let's be honest — the Chinese probably came up with them first.
You have the radical twenty and the kanji one. Put those together and you get 21. What's another name for 21? That's <radical>blackjack</radical>.

There's a lid on top of something you're trying to keep private. It's your <radical>trash</radical>. You wouldn't want people going through your private trash, which is why we put lids on our trash cans. It's also illegal to look through someone's trash, so make sure you never do that.

This is the radical for <radical>bear</radical>, because it looks like the letter B — B for bear! You know this one is "bear" and not "building" because it's all boxy, like a stocky, chunky bear who's all fat and ready to hibernate.
See the T and F that make up this radical? Those letters stand for <radical>tofu</radical>, our favorite bean curd blocks.

This is the <radical>spring</radical> radical, because it looks like a new plant shoot has pushed its way up through layers of dirt, snow, and ice to announce the coming of spring. Spring is the season (and the radical) full of new, growing life!

This is a <radical>cape</radical>, like the kind a superhero would wear. Use your imagination to picture a hero facing left, with a cape tied around their neck and hanging down their back. With that cape on, they're ready to save the world!
Someone's lying on the ground with his mouth open hoping to swallow up passers-by. This guy's a weirdo — a real <radical>creeper</radical>.

It's the drunkard from before, but this time she's leaning on some kind of horizontal surface. Knowing her, it's probably the counter of a <radical>bar</radical>. Hopefully she's not causing too much trouble for the bar staff with her drunken antics.

Don't confuse this with triceratops. <radical>Grass</radical> is closer together, and a little bushier, like this. It's also more random and squished down in parts. If you see a bush of lines like this, it's probably going to be grass.

This radical has a figure reaching out both hands at you with some dirt on his head. This is a <radical>zombie</radical>, and he must have just recently dug himself out of the grave by the looks of it.
See the <radical>squid</radical> shape here? There's its pointy head, its eyes, and its tentacles (two, anyway). Pretty squid-like if you ask me!
The "soil mouth" is the mouth that eats the soil. The animal that does this best is the <radical>worm</radical>. Nom nom nom.

There's a canopy with a grid-like frame near the top. It's a <radical>yurt</radical> with a window! Yurts are those dome-shaped huts nomads use. Once you've set up a canopy with a window frame, you've basically built one. Imagine gazing out that window, kicking back in your yurt. Yurt sweet yurt!
See the energy bursting outward? That's an <radical>explosion</radical>. Boom!
It has a leaf and it's connected to something that has lots of little sections. This looks just like a short, stubby thing of <radical>corn</radical>.

There is a hat covering the moon and it's holding a knife. Wait, that's no moon. It's a space station! It's the <radical>Death Star</radical>! It's pretending to be a moon under that hat. And it's armed! Don't let the Death Star stab your planet to death.
The letter "E" is for "<radical>egg</radical>" - easy enough, right?
This is the <radical>comb</radical> radical. Look at all those little things sticking out. You could easily use this to comb your hair.
This is the left side of the kanji 朝, so we'll call it <radical>morning</radical> too.
In the water is a barb on the ground. It's <radical>coral</radical>. Coral may look pretty, but if you slip in the water and step on it, you're gonna get scratched up. That stuff is roooough.
The <radical>trident</radical> goes up, sticking through a fish (or whatever). AQUAAMANNNN!
See the <radical>cactus</radical> coming out of the ground? It's happy to see you!
Inside this guy's forehead you have a spoon and a bunch of hair, not to mention whatever that is in the top left. That's the mind of a <radical>psychopath</radical> right there.
Look at this radical. Can you see it floating in space? Can you see the antennae and reflectors? That's because it's a <radical>satellite</radical>.
You see a leaf ear, better known as an <radical>elf</radical>! Elves are just humans who have ears that are pointy like leaves.

Oh no, you let the pope's hat get snatched by a lion! You get it back, but it's all crooked, so you've got to make it <radical>straight</radical> again. The pope needs a straight, dignified hat, so you'd better straighten that thing out.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>good</radical>.

This is the <radical>warehouse</radical> radical. Do you see the roof with all the shelving units underneath? There's even a ladder to help you reach the taller shelves. Imagine all the things you could store in your warehouse.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>chapter</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>guy</radical>.
The products trees make? That's <radical>syrup</radical>. Delicious maple syrup, for example. Mmmm!

Who wears cleats and takes your measurements for so long that icicles start forming on your body? Your <radical>commander</radical>. The commander is very, very particular. And everyone knows the commander has to get everything exactly right. So taking your measurements takes SO long that icicles grow out of your nose. But that's okay. You have to impress your new commander, darn it!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>lack</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to lack something</vocabulary>. 

欠く is often used for intangible qualities someone lacks, like flexibility or consideration. But it can also be used for physical things, especially in the context of basic necessities. It sounds kind of advanced and formal, so it tends to pop up more in writing than in casual speech.

Note that this is a transitive verb, so it takes a direct object — someone is actively lacking something, like あの人の行動は常識を欠いている (their behavior lacks common sense).
data.reading_mnemonic: If your life seems <vocabulary>to lack something</vocabulary>, like excitement or meaning, the best thing you can do is hop in your <reading>ca</reading>r (か). Take your car out on the open road and go search for whatever it is you're lacking. You'll find it — we believe in you!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji 外 means <kanji>outside</kanji>, and the meaning of this verb is somewhat related. It means <vocabulary>to remove</vocabulary> something. Think of it like this — if you remove your watch, you are putting it "outside" of its usual spot (your wrist), right?

Like many verbs ending in す, this verb is transitive. It's used for when you intentionally take something and put it outside of where it's supposed to be — so depending on the context, it can also mean <vocabulary>to exclude</vocabulary> someone, or even <vocabulary>to miss something</vocabulary> (like a target). See how all these meanings relate to the idea of something ending up outside its intended spot?

You don't know how long that thing you're removing has been there — or what kind of weird toxic stuff may have accumulated around it — so it's better to be safe than sorry.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>deposit</kanji>, and this word is for when someone is depositing something (or someone) with you, because they want you <vocabulary>to look after</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to take care of</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to hold on to</vocabulary> it.

Remember that 預ける is used when you leave something with someone else to take care of temporarily. 預かる, on the other hand, is used when you're the one receiving something to look after. You can remember this because you're great at taking care of cargo (かる). You're always looking after everyone's cargo, but you're happy to hold on to it for them.

Also note that even though 預かる ends with かる and kind of looks intransitive, it's actually an exception! It'll pretty much always have a direct object to specify what you're looking after.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>underworld</kanji> <kanji>dirt</kanji> is another word for the <vocabulary>realm of the dead</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>underworld</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>Hades</vocabulary>. Like the word 冥界 (also in this level), it's rather poetic, and mostly used in written contexts involving spirituality, Buddhism, and ancient mythologies.

There are a few set expressions that only use 冥土, though. One example is 冥土の土産, "a souvenir to take to the realm of the dead". It refers to something abstract that is so valuable, it's worth taking to the underworld, such as the solution to a great mystery, or a happy memory.

Another expression is 冥土の旅支度, which means "preparations for the journey to the realm of the dead", and can refer to the preparation of the deceased before a funeral, as wells as certain preparations made by Buddhists while they're still alive.

You'll also see this word written as 冥途 sometimes.

auxiliary_meanings.meaning: To Be In Light Of Something

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You learned this kanji means "model," but it can also mean "<kanji>take into account</kanji>," so the verb version means <vocabulary>to take something into account</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be in light of</vocabulary>.

鑑みる literally comes from the idea of "looking at something closely to judge it." It's a formal word used to describe the act of thoughtfully considering something based on things like prior experiences or surrounding circumstances.

It's a transitive verb, but it can take を or に to mark the thing you're taking into account. Both particles are grammatically correct, but に sounds slightly more formal, which often matches the contexts where this word is used.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This verb uses the kun'yomi of the kanji. You haven't learned that yet, so here's mnemonic to help you:

If you want <vocabulary>to take something into account</vocabulary>, you'll need to <reading>考</reading>える (かんが) about it really hard first. And when you do that thinking, it has <vocabulary>to be in light of</vocabulary> lots of other factors. Taking all those factors into account will help guide your next move, you know?

Historically, the name has been associated with scholars and writers, including prominent Heian period statesman, scholar, and poet Sugawara-no-michizane (菅原道真) and noblewoman, writer, and poet Sugawara-no-takasue-no-musume (菅原孝標女), also known more simply as Lady Sarashina in the English speaking world.
