context_sentences.en: How did you get this far out of town?
context_sentences.ja: こんな町外れまで、どうやって来たの？

meanings.meaning: To Go Out Into The World
To Be Released To The Public

auxiliary_meanings.meaning: To Get Out Into The World
To Be Out In The World

data.meaning_mnemonic: Here we have <kanji>world</kanji> with the particle に, following by the verb 出る (to go out). Put that together and this means <vocabulary>to go out into the world</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be published</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be released to the public</vocabulary> in some way or another. Once it's out there in the world, there's even a chance for it <vocabulary>to become renowned</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic: This uses kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which you should already know by now, so I think you're good to go!

context_sentences.en: It's a dream come true to have my work published.
context_sentences.ja: 自分の作品が世に出るなんて、夢みたいだ。

context_sentences.en: Once a photo or video goes out in the world, it becomes a digital tattoo and stays on the Internet forever.
context_sentences.ja: 一度世に出た写真やビデオは、デジタルタトゥーとなってずっとネットに残るんだよ。

context_sentences.en: In today's concert, I will perform pieces that have never before been released to the public.
context_sentences.ja: 今日のコンサートでは、今まで世に出る機会がなかった曲たちを演奏します。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Here you have <kanji>other</kanji> and <kanji>person</kanji> joined together by the particle の, which shows that "other" is describing "person". So this means <vocabulary>someone else</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>other people</vocabulary>.

This is more general than 他人, which you already learned. 他の人 can be anyone that's not the speaker, or not the person being talked about. 他人, on the other hand, has an added implication that the person is someone unknown or unrelated.
data.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kanji's kun'yomi readings, which you've already learned. As long as you remember those, you should be good to go!

context_sentences.en: Fine, I'll have someone else do it!
context_sentences.ja: いいよ、他の人にしてもらうから！

context_sentences.en: Oh, you don't want it? Then I'll give it to someone else.
context_sentences.ja: え、いらないの？じゃあ、他の人にあげるね。

context_sentences.en: Huh, so you deceived someone else!
context_sentences.ja: へー、それで他の人をだましたんだ！

data.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 北口 from a couple levels ago, and how 入り口 means "entrance" and 出口 means "exit?" Combine that 口 meaning with the kanji for <kanji>west</kanji>, and you get <vocabulary>west exit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>west entrance</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic: This follows the same pattern as 入り口, 出口, and 北口, so it uses kun'yomi readings. And just like with those, make sure to watch out for the rendaku that changes くち to ぐち!

context_sentences.en: The elevator is located at the west exit.
context_sentences.ja: エレベーターは西口にあります。

context_sentences.en: I'll be at the cafe at the west exit!
context_sentences.ja: 西口のカフェにいますね！

context_sentences.en: I always take a cab from the west exit.
context_sentences.ja: いつも西口からタクシーにのります。

data.meaning_mnemonic: Adding "third generation" to someone's name means that they are the third generation of people with that name. In this case, the person's name is ナポレオン (Napoleon), so this means <vocabulary>Napoleon The Third</vocabulary>, also written as <vocabulary>Napoleon III</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic: The kanji here are pronounced exactly the same as in the standalone word 三世. That is, it's a jukugo word which uses the on'yomi for both kanji.

context_sentences.en: Today, we're going to learn about Napoleon The Third.
context_sentences.ja: 今日は、ナポレオン三世について学びましょう。

context_sentences.en: Napoleon III was born in the year 1808.
context_sentences.ja: ナポレオン三世は1808年に生まれた。

context_sentences.en: Napoleon Bonaparte is more famous than Napoleon III, isn't he?
context_sentences.ja: ナポレオン・ボナパルトはナポレオン三世より有名ですよね。

data.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>self</kanji> <kanji>photograph</kanji> is exactly that: a <vocabulary>selfie</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi of 自, which you learned with the kanji, and the kun'yomi of 撮, which you learned with the word 撮る. Though it's a bit of an unusual combo, you can probably guess the first one since it's such a common reading, and the second one because of the り on the end. Just watch out for rendaku, which turns とり into どり.

context_sentences.en: I took a selfie with my smartphone.
context_sentences.ja: スマホで自撮りした。

context_sentences.en: Oh, I don't have my selfie stick.
context_sentences.ja: あれ、自撮り棒がない。

context_sentences.en: Here are some tips on how to take a good selfie easily.
context_sentences.ja: 簡単に上手な自撮りができるコツをお伝えします。

data.meaning_mnemonic: What <kanji>season</kanji>s should you keep an <kanji>eye</kanji> on? The seasons that are <vocabulary>turning point</vocabulary>s in your life. Keep an eye on those seasons, because you don't want to miss the <vocabulary>critical juncture</vocabulary>s and <vocabulary>milestone</vocabulary>s.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi of both kanji. You haven't learned that yet for 節, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

The real <vocabulary>turning point</vocabulary> in your life was when you got yourself a <reading>few she</reading>ep (ふし). Owning a few sheep was a true <vocabulary>milestone</vocabulary> for you. Now you have all the wool sweaters and cheese you could ever want!

context_sentences.en: The coming-of-age ceremony is an important milestone in one's life.
context_sentences.ja: 成人式は、大切な人生の節目です。

context_sentences.en: Then that year, something happened that would become a major turning point in my life.
context_sentences.ja: そしてその年、人生の大きな節目になる出来事が起こったんです。

context_sentences.en: In hindsight, I guess that was a critical juncture.
context_sentences.ja: 今から思うと、あれが一つの節目だったんだろうね。

data.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>joint</kanji> <kanji>joint</kanji>s are your <vocabulary>various joints</vocabulary>, or even <vocabulary>every joint</vocabulary> in your body, or a specific body part. When we're not talking about the joints in your body, this means something like <vocabulary>various parts</vocabulary>, referring to various parts of a whole.
data.reading_mnemonic: This is just the kun'yomi of 節, which you learned with 節目, repeated twice. Keep in mind that the second ふし gets rendaku'd to ぶし!

context_sentences.en: Every joint in my body is throbbing somehow.
context_sentences.ja: なんか体の節々がズキズキする。

context_sentences.en: That person makes some harsh word choices, huh?
context_sentences.ja: あの人、言葉の節々にトゲがあるよね。

context_sentences.en: Saori woke up with pains in various joints.
context_sentences.ja: 早織は節々の痛みを感じて目を覚ました。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You already know that 一千 is "<kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>thousand</kanji>," and that 万 is "<kanji>ten thousand</kanji>." Add all those zeros together (or multiply 1,000 with 10,000) and you end up with <vocabulary>ten million</vocabulary>. 

You learned that 千 is the more common and default way to say 1,000 and 一千 is sometimes used for emphasis or clarity. Well, to say ten million, you almost always say it as 一千万. I mean, who wouldn't want to emphasize ten million! It's ten million, you know?
data.reading_mnemonic: You already learned how to read both 一千 and 万, so just put those two readings together and you're good to go!

context_sentences.en: I wish I had ten million dollars.
context_sentences.ja: 一千万ドルがほしいなぁ。

context_sentences.en: I won ten million yen in the lottery!
context_sentences.ja: ロトで一千万円ゲットしたんだ！

context_sentences.en: Ten million people came to the concert.
context_sentences.ja: コンサートには一千万人の人がきました。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji 田 means <kanji>rice paddy</kanji>, so it should be easy to work out that this word also means <vocabulary>rice paddy</vocabulary>.

田んぼ is a common way to say "rice paddy," especially in casual conversation. You can tell because if you ever came across a ju<reading>mbo</reading> (んぼ) rice paddy, you'd probably say something like, "Whoa, that's one jumbo 田んぼ!" When a 田んぼ is that jumbo, the surprise makes your speech naturally more relaxed and informal.
data.reading_mnemonic: This word has hiragana attached to the kanji, which is a good sign that the reading is kun'yomi. You learned that reading when you learned the kanji, so you should be good to go.

context_sentences.en: There are a lot of rice paddies in Asia.
context_sentences.ja: アジアには田んぼがたくさんある。

context_sentences.en: This is a rice field for jasmine rice.
context_sentences.ja: これはジャスミンライスの田んぼです。

context_sentences.en: Please do not enter the paddy in high heels.
context_sentences.ja: 田んぼにハイヒールで入らないで下さい。

data.meaning_mnemonic: What's a "third day moon"? It's a <vocabulary>crescent moon</vocabulary>. A crescent moon is the newly visible moon that appears on the third day of the month in the lunar calendar that Japanese people used back in the day.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This word combines the vocab words 三日 and 月, so it uses their readings, except they're slightly different here: there's no small っ in 三日, and 月 has rendaku. Sounds complicated, but the changes actually make the word easier to pronounce. (Try it yourself — みかづき is easier to say than みっかつき, right?) Here's a mnemonic to remember the みか and づ parts, just in case:

You're out with your friend Mika one night when a <vocabulary>crescent moon</vocabulary> appears. What do you say to her? "<reading>Mika</reading>, <reading>du</reading>de (みかづ)! It's a crescent moon!" 

Hint: To get the character づ, type "du" on your keyboard.

context_sentences.en: There's a crescent moon today.
context_sentences.ja: 今日は三日月です。

context_sentences.en: You have eyes that are like a crescent moon.
context_sentences.ja: 三日月のような目をしてますね。

context_sentences.en: You can see the crescent moon well from the top of the mountain.
context_sentences.ja: 山の上から三日月がよく見える。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You might already know 市場 means "market," like in 株式市場 (stock market). So is this a <kanji>brocade</kanji> market? Well, "brocade" actually refers to the name of a street here, not brocade fabrics. It's a place name, so we can just call this the <vocabulary>Nishiki Market</vocabulary>!

錦市場 is a famous food market on a street called 錦小路 (Nishiki Kōji) in Kyoto, and it's packed with delicious local specialties. Give it a quick search if you haven't heard of it! Maybe your next travel destination?
data.reading_mnemonic: As you could probably guess from the meaning, 錦 is read にしき here. 市場 is usually read with kun'yomi when it refers to a real, physical street market. You haven't learned this reading for 市場 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: There's one thing you look for when you visit Nishiki Market: an itchy baa (いちば). Sheep go "baa," and the ones you buy must be exceptionally itchy. Itchy baas produce the best mutton and wool, so you keep an eye out for them whenever you go to Nishiki Market!

context_sentences.en: I went to Nishiki Market in Kyoto on Sunday.
context_sentences.ja: 日曜日に京都の錦市場に行きました。

context_sentences.en: These are chopsticks I bought at Nishiki Market.
context_sentences.ja: これは錦市場で買ったお箸です。

context_sentences.en: I bought tamago-yaki at Nishiki Market and ate it while walking around.
context_sentences.ja: 錦市場で卵焼きを買って食べ歩きをしました。

data.meaning_mnemonic: You're looking at <kanji>heaven</kanji>'s <kanji>river</kanji>, or the river of heaven. There's only one river in heaven (i.e., the sky), and that's the <vocabulary>Milky Way</vocabulary>!
data.reading_mnemonic:
This is two individual words connected with a の, so it uses kun'yomi readings. You haven't learned this reading for 天 yet, so we've got a mnemonic to help you. Also watch out for the rendaku on 川, turning it into がわ!

What does the <vocabulary>Milky Way</vocabulary> remind you of? It kind of looks like a shining piece of <reading>armor</reading> (あま). Look at it in the sky, shimmering like a piece of silver armor. Uncanny, no? 

To summarize: The 天 is read あま here, and the 川 gets rendaku'd to がわ. Add a の inbetween and the full reading for this vocab is あまのがわ!

context_sentences.en: Oh, I can see the Milky Way!
context_sentences.ja: あ、天の川が見える！

context_sentences.en: On a clear day, you can also see the Milky Way.
context_sentences.ja: 天気の良い日には、天の川を見ることもできます。

context_sentences.en: The two can meet by crossing the Milky Way just once a year. Isn't that romantic?
context_sentences.ja: 二人は年に一回だけ、天の川を渡って会うことができるんです。ロマンチックでしょ？

data.meaning_mnemonic: You <reading>chort</reading>le (ちょっと) <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary> at a silly joke. You can’t help chortling <vocabulary>for a moment</vocabulary>. Go ahead, chortle just a little, for just a moment, to help you remember this word.

context_sentences.en: Oh, wait a moment!
context_sentences.ja: あ、ちょっとまって！

context_sentences.en: I think it's a little different.
context_sentences.ja: ちょっとちがう気がする。

context_sentences.en: I'll think about it a little.
context_sentences.ja: ちょっと考えてみるよ。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
From <reading>Ohio</reading> (おはよう), you shout <vocabulary>good morning</vocabulary>. Why Ohio? Because that's where you woke up this morning. Imagine yourself waking up in Ohio, and wishing everyone "good morning" at the top of your lungs.

おはよう is a casual way to say "good morning." It can also be written in kanji, but hiragana is much more common.

context_sentences.en: Good morning, Miho-chan!
context_sentences.ja: ミホちゃん、おはよう！

context_sentences.en: I texted "good morning" to Mike.
context_sentences.ja: マイクに「おはよう」とメールをした。

context_sentences.en: Ugh, I'm sleepy... morning.
context_sentences.ja: うーっ、ねむいー、おはよう。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
ホテル comes from the English word <vocabulary>hotel</vocabulary> and the meaning is exactly the same!

The only thing to watch out for is that the "l" on the end becomes ル, because that's the closest sound in Japanese.

context_sentences.en: Did you book a hotel already?
context_sentences.ja: ホテル、もうとった？

context_sentences.en: I'm just about to check out of the hotel.
context_sentences.ja: 今、ホテルをチェックアウトするところ。

context_sentences.en: Which hotel will you stay at?
context_sentences.ja: どこのホテルにステイするの？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Colle</reading>ct (これ) <vocabulary>this one</vocabulary> right here! Go ahead, collect this one.

You can use これ to talk about anything that's close to you. Things that are close to you are easy to collect, after all!

context_sentences.en: This one is Mt Fuji.
context_sentences.ja: これがふじ山です。

context_sentences.en: This is a pen.
context_sentences.ja: これはペンです。

context_sentences.en: Give me two of these, please.
context_sentences.ja: これを二つ下さい。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
It's only <reading>through</reading> (する) doing things that we get better at them, so you need <vocabulary>to do</vocabulary> them as much as you can.

する basically means <vocabulary>to do</vocabulary>, but it’s incredibly versatile and goes beyond its English equivalent. Besides being used alone, it can be put together with a whole range of nouns to turn them into verbs. We call these する verbs and you'll learn a lot of them as we go along!

context_sentences.en: What do you want to do for Christmas?
context_sentences.ja: クリスマス、どうする？

context_sentences.en: If you don't, someone else will.
context_sentences.ja: あなたがしなくても、だれかがするよ。

context_sentences.en: Shoot there with all your might.
context_sentences.ja: そこで、力いっぱいシュートをするんだ。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Ringo</reading> (リンゴ) just ate your <vocabulary>apple</vocabulary>! You were about to take a bite, and he grabbed it. What is Ringo doing snatching apples? Surely he can afford his own.

Did you know that Ringo Starr once appeared in a Japanese TV commercial for <vocabulary>apple</vocabulary> juice? That might help you remember this word, too!

リンゴ is also commonly written in hiragana, and even in kanji, but you’ll probably see it in katakana the most.

context_sentences.en: Two apple juices, please.
context_sentences.ja: リンゴジュース、二つ下さい。

context_sentences.en: Do you want an apple or a banana?
context_sentences.ja: リンゴかバナナ、いる？

context_sentences.en: This apple tastes bad!
context_sentences.ja: このリンゴ、まずい！

data.meaning_mnemonic:
コーヒー is the katakana version of the English word <vocabulary>coffee</vocabulary>. 

Just watch out for the second syllable, which changes to ヒー in Japanese.

context_sentences.en: Do you want a cup of coffee?
context_sentences.ja: コーヒー、のむ？

context_sentences.en: Should we have a coffee break soon?
context_sentences.ja: そろそろコーヒーブレークにする？

context_sentences.en: One hot coffee, please.
context_sentences.ja: ホットコーヒー、一つ下さい。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Connie Chihua</reading>hua (こんにちは) says <vocabulary>hello</vocabulary>. Connie Chihuahua is an amazing talking chihuahua. She can only say "hello", but that alone is pretty impressive.

こんにちは is a formal way to say "hello". It’s generally used during the daytime, from late morning to early evening. Watch out for the は on the end, which is always pronounced わ.

context_sentences.en: Hello Sensei.
context_sentences.ja: 先生、こんにちは。

context_sentences.en: Hello Aya.
context_sentences.ja: アヤちゃん、こんにちは。

context_sentences.en: Hello, I'm Jenny.
context_sentences.ja: こんにちは、ジェニーです。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
He <reading>eats</reading> (いつ) and eats and eats. <vocabulary>When</vocabulary> does this guy not eat?

いつ is a question word that is used to ask <vocabulary>when</vocabulary>.

context_sentences.en: When will you do it?
context_sentences.ja: いつするの？

context_sentences.en: Until when are you in the U.S.?
context_sentences.ja: いつまでアメリカ？

context_sentences.en: From when will you be in Canada?
context_sentences.ja: いつからカナダ？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Do re</reading> (どれ) mi fa sol la ti... <vocabulary>which one</vocabulary> of these notes are you going to start singing from?

The question word どれ is used to ask <vocabulary>which one</vocabulary> out of three or more choices.

context_sentences.en: Which one of these ties shall I give as a gift?
context_sentences.ja: プレゼントのネクタイ、どれにする？

context_sentences.en: Can you tell which ones are tasty onions?
context_sentences.ja: どれがおいしい玉ねぎか、分かる？

context_sentences.en: Hmm, which one should I cut first?
context_sentences.ja: えっと、どれから切ればいい？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
テレビ comes from the English word <vocabulary>television</vocabulary>. It’s been shortened, which is really common with loanwords in Japanese. The "vi" sound becomes ビ, too.

テレビ is sometimes written as "TV", but even then it’s usually pronounced テレビ.

context_sentences.en: I'm going to speak on TV now.
context_sentences.ja: 今から、テレビでしゃべるんだ。

context_sentences.en: What, you're going on TV?
context_sentences.ja: えっ、テレビに出るの？

context_sentences.en: I'll turn on the TV immediately!
context_sentences.ja: すぐにテレビをつけるよ！

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Wanna play <reading>Un</reading>o (うん)? <vocabulary>Yep</vocabulary>! 'Course I do. I always wanna play Uno.

うん is a casual way to say <vocabulary>yes</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>yeah</vocabulary>, so you’d generally use it with friends and family, and in other informal situations.

context_sentences.en: Yep, let's do that!
context_sentences.ja: うん、そうしよう！

context_sentences.en: Yeah, sorry, that's wrong.
context_sentences.ja: うん、ごめん、ちがう。

context_sentences.en: Yep, it's yummy!
context_sentences.ja: うん、おいしい！

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Want me to write a <reading>hai</reading>ku (はい)? <vocabulary>Yes</vocabulary>, of course!

はい is a formal word for "yes". You can use it to let someone know they’re right, or simply that you’re listening, as well as to respond if someone says your name.

context_sentences.en: "Mr. Chandler." "Yes!"
context_sentences.ja: 「チャンドラーさん」「はい！」

context_sentences.en: Yes, thank you very much.
context_sentences.ja: はい、ありがとうございます。

context_sentences.en: Yes, understood.
context_sentences.ja: はい、分かりました。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
ノート is a shortened form of <vocabulary>notebook</vocabulary>, with an extra "o" on the end since you can’t end a word with "t" in Japanese.

You can also use this to mean <vocabulary>notes</vocabulary>, in the context of taking down notes in a class.

context_sentences.en: If it's that notebook you mean, it's on my desk.
context_sentences.ja: そのノートなら、デスクの上だよ。

context_sentences.en: Did you take good notes on the lesson?
context_sentences.ja: レッスン、ちゃんとノートにまとめた？

context_sentences.en: I need an A4 size notebook, you know.
context_sentences.ja: A4サイズのノートがいるんだよね。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
I <reading>saw your Nara</reading> (さようなら), but I then had to say <vocabulary>goodbye</vocabulary>. It was just a short trip, but at least I saw your Nara.

さようなら is a formal way to say goodbye, so a good word to use with colleagues and teachers.

A quick tip before I say goodbye: さようなら often drops its middle う, becoming さよなら.

context_sentences.en: Goodbye, Sensei.
context_sentences.ja: 先生、さようなら。

context_sentences.en: Goodbye, January. Hello, February.
context_sentences.ja: さようなら、一月。こんにちは、二月。

context_sentences.en: So long, and thanks for all the fish.
context_sentences.ja: さようなら、今までサカナをありがとう。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Con ban, wah!</reading> (こんばんは) cries your friend, just as you say <vocabulary>good evening</vocabulary>. There's a report on the evening news about a con ban (yes, that's a ban on conning people). Wah! Exciting stuff.

You can use こんばんは as a greeting from around 5pm or 6pm, in both formal and informal situations.　Watch out for that は on the end, which is pronounced わ here too.

context_sentences.en: Oh, good evening.
context_sentences.ja: あ、こんばんは。

context_sentences.en: Good evening, everyone.
context_sentences.ja: みなさん、こんばんは。

context_sentences.en: Good evening. Nice work today!
context_sentences.ja: こんばんは〜、おつかれさまです！

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Sorry</reading> (それ), can you grab <vocabulary>that one</vocabulary> for me? Yeah, <vocabulary>that</vocabulary>, thanks!

You can use それ for things that are close to the person you're talking to, or fairly close to both of you.

context_sentences.en: That looks fun!
context_sentences.ja: それ、おもしろそうだね！

context_sentences.en: Oh, you're going to go for that?
context_sentences.ja: え、それにするの？

context_sentences.en: That's not candy, that's an eyeball.
context_sentences.ja: それはキャンディじゃなくて目玉です。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
コンビニ comes from the English word <vocabulary>convenience store</vocabulary>, but who has time for all those syllables? That's why they cut it down to "conveni". So much more convenient that way.

Watch out for the “v” sound, which usually becomes “b” in Japanese, and this word is no exception.

context_sentences.en: Oh, you work part-time at a convenience store?
context_sentences.ja: え、コンビニでバイトしてるの？

context_sentences.en: Convenience store rice balls are so good!
context_sentences.ja: コンビニのおにぎりっておいしいよね！

context_sentences.en: Oh, there's a convenience store over there!
context_sentences.ja: あ、あそこにコンビニがある！

data.meaning_mnemonic: デパート comes from  <vocabulary>department store</vocabulary>. Yet another shortened loanword! There's an extra "o" sound on the end of this one, since a word can't end in "t" in Japanese.

context_sentences.en: I'm in the department store restroom right now.
context_sentences.ja: 今、デパートのトイレにいる。

context_sentences.en: They had that at the department store.
context_sentences.ja: それ、デパートにあったよ。

context_sentences.en: I saw Leo at the department store!
context_sentences.ja: レオなら、デパートで見かけたよ！

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Sue me, Ma Sen!</reading> (すみません), you yell at Ma Sen, before quickly adding "<vocabulary>Excuse me</vocabulary>…<vocabulary>I'm sorry</vocabulary>, so <vocabulary> sorry</vocabulary>!" You shouldn't have shouted at Ma Sen like that. You hope she won’t actually sue you.

You can use すみません both to apologize and to get someone’s attention. This expression is really common in Japan, and dropping it in wherever you can will help you blend right in!

context_sentences.en: Oh, excuse me! I'm sorry!
context_sentences.ja: あ、すみません！ごめんなさい！

context_sentences.en: Excuse me, where's the "Ocean Hotel"?
context_sentences.ja: すみません、オーシャンホテルってどこですか。

context_sentences.en: Excuse me, is now a good time?
context_sentences.ja: すみません、今ちょっといいですか？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Eeh! Eh?</reading> (いいえ) <vocabulary>No</vocabulary>! You’re so surprised by whatever the question was, you can only manage "Eeh! Eh? No!" in response.

いいえ is a formal word for "no", so you can use it to answer politely in the negative.

context_sentences.en: No, it's not.
context_sentences.ja: いいえ、ちがいます。

context_sentences.en: No, you have the wrong person.
context_sentences.ja: いいえ、人ちがいです。

context_sentences.en: No, it's not England. It's Canada.
context_sentences.ja: いいえ、イギリスじゃないです。カナダです。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
"<reading>A gnat, ah!</reading> (あなた). I’m going to get <vocabulary>you</vocabulary>! Yes YOU," you shout as you swat at that pesky gnat buzzing around your head.

あなた is a lot less common than “you” in English, but you’ll come across it in adverts, online forums, and textbooks, where it’s used to address a general, anonymous audience. Some people also use it with their significant other, in which case it sounds intimate, like "darling". In casual conversations, though, it can come off as standoffish, so it's better to use someone's name or social title (like "teacher") instead.

context_sentences.en: Is this your blog?
context_sentences.ja: これ、あなたのブログですか？

context_sentences.en: What would you do in that kind of situation?
context_sentences.ja: こんなとき、あなたならどうしますか？

context_sentences.en: I miss you darling.
context_sentences.ja: あなたがいなくてさみしいです。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how これ means "this one"? Well, この simply means <vocabulary>this</vocabulary>. The difference is that これ is used on its own, whereas この goes before a noun. For example, この人 means "this person".

Notice how words like this starting with こ are close to you? We'll be learning a few more of these, and they all follow the same pattern!

context_sentences.en: Who's this?
context_sentences.ja: この人、だれ？

context_sentences.en: Please look at this page.
context_sentences.ja: このページを見てください。

context_sentences.en: Sorry, my schedule is full on this day.
context_sentences.ja: ごめん、この日はスケジュールがいっぱいなんだ。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You need <reading>a le</reading>ns (あれ)? How about <vocabulary>that one over there</vocabulary>? You’re in a camera shop picking out a new lens, and that one over there looks good.

Use あれ to refer to something that's far from both you and the person you're talking to.

context_sentences.en: Isn't that Emily over there?
context_sentences.ja: あれ、エミリーじゃない？

context_sentences.en: That one over there is my house.
context_sentences.ja: あれがオレのうちだよ。

context_sentences.en: That was terrible, to say the least.
context_sentences.ja: いくらなんでもあれはヒドいよ。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
ドル is the Japanese version of the English word <vocabulary>dollar</vocabulary>. 

The dollar symbol $ is also common in Japanese, and the pronunciation is still ドル.

context_sentences.en: It says this bread costs $5.
context_sentences.ja: このパン、５ドルだって。

context_sentences.en: Is that U.S. dollars? Or is it Canadian dollars?
context_sentences.ja: それって米ドル？それともカナダドル？

context_sentences.en: The dollar to yen rate finally reached 150 yen to the dollar.
context_sentences.ja: ついにドル円のレートが１ドル＝１５０円になった。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how どれ means "which one"? どの has a very similar meaning: <vocabulary>which</vocabulary>. Whereas どれ is used on its own, どの is used before a noun to ask "which" out of three or more options. So for example, どの本 is "which book (out of that pile)?".

Notice how question words often start with a ど? We'll be seeing more of these!

context_sentences.en: Which child is Maria?
context_sentences.ja: どの子がマリアちゃん？

context_sentences.en: I wonder which hotel I should stay at.
context_sentences.ja: どのホテルにしようかな。

context_sentences.en: When can you do it?
context_sentences.ja: どのタイミングでできますか？

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <reading>kni</reading>fe (ない) is <vocabulary>not there</vocabulary>. It's not here and it's not there. It’s missing. It's nowhere to be found, so don't bother looking for it!

context_sentences.en: I don't have any money at all.
context_sentences.ja: お金がぜんぜんない。

context_sentences.en: Do you have scissors?
context_sentences.ja: ハサミ、ない？

context_sentences.en: I don't have scissors, but I do have a cutter.
context_sentences.ja: ハサミはないけど、カッターならあるよ。

context_sentences.en: "Moommm, I want apple!" "I can't give you what I don't have, Hana-chan."
context_sentences.ja: 「ママぁー、りんご、ほしい！」「ないものはないのよ、はなちゃん。」

data.meaning_mnemonic:
If there's a <reading>ca</reading>r <reading>ban</reading> (カバン), you'll need a nice <vocabulary>bag</vocabulary> to carry all your stuff in. You can't just throw it all in the car, so get yourself a nice bag instead.

カバン is used for bags that you can close and that have a fairly rigid structure, like satchels or briefcases, but not more flimsy bags that don't close, like plastic or paper shopping bags.

This word can also be written in hiragana and kanji. All versions are pretty common, but you'll probably see it in katakana the most.

context_sentences.en: Oh, I don't have my bag!
context_sentences.ja: あ、カバンがない！

context_sentences.en: That's funny. I thought I put them in my bag.
context_sentences.ja: おかしいなぁ。カバンに入れたはずなのに。

context_sentences.en: I opted for a larger bag that can hold a lot of stuff.
context_sentences.ja: いっぱい入るよう、大きめのカバンにしたよ。

data.meaning_mnemonic: タクシー is the katakana version of the English word <vocabulary>taxi</vocabulary>. The "xi" sound becomes クシー to fit better with Japanese pronunciation.

context_sentences.en: I can't find a cab at all.
context_sentences.ja: タクシーがぜんぜん見つからないんだよね。

context_sentences.en: Shall we take a cab?
context_sentences.ja: タクシーで行く？

context_sentences.en: Don't use me as a taxi!
context_sentences.ja: タクシー代わりにしないでよ！

data.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how それ means "that one"? その has a very similar meaning: <vocabulary>that</vocabulary>. It's used before a noun that's either close to the person you're talking to, or fairly close to both of you. For example, その本 is "that book", and the book in question might be in the hand of the person you're talking to, or it might be on a shelf not far from you both.

context_sentences.en: That person is famous.
context_sentences.ja: その人、有名人だよ。

context_sentences.en: I'm busy that day.
context_sentences.ja: その日は、いそがしいんだ。

context_sentences.en: At that moment, there was a loud boom.
context_sentences.ja: そのとき、ドーンと大きな音がした。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how あれ means "that one over there"? Well, あの means <vocabulary>that</vocabulary>, and goes before a noun to point out something that is far away from both you and the person you're talking to, such as あの本 (that book over there) or あの子犬 (that puppy over there).

Notice how these words starting with あ are far away from you? We'll be learning a few more of these, and they all follow the same pattern! What's more, you’ll notice that words ending in の tend to go before a noun.

context_sentences.en: I think I've seen that person over there somewhere before.
context_sentences.ja: あの人、どこかで見たことある気がする。

context_sentences.en: Do you remember that day?
context_sentences.ja: あの日のこと、おぼえてる？

context_sentences.en: I should have said "thank you" at the time.
context_sentences.ja: あのとき、「ありがとう」って言えばよかった。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
I want to show you my <reading>demo</reading> (でも), <vocabulary>but</vocabulary> you don't want to see it. <vocabulary>However</vocabulary>, I'm going to show it to you anyway. So there.

Something to watch out for with でも is that it always goes at the beginning of a sentence, not in the middle, like "but" usually does in English. It’s also a fairly casual word, so it’s not normally used in formal situations.

context_sentences.en: But I can't.
context_sentences.ja: でも、できないよ。

context_sentences.en: But are you okay with that?
context_sentences.ja: でも、いいの？

context_sentences.en: But it's 50 percent off, you know?
context_sentences.ja: でも、５０パーセントオフだよ？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You've been getting <reading>madder</reading> (まだ) and madder, and you’re <vocabulary>still</vocabulary> mad. You’re <vocabulary>not yet</vocabulary> as mad as you could be, though.

You can use まだ to talk about a situation that started in the past and continues into the present. Wait! Where are you going? I'm still explaining this! I'm not done yet!

context_sentences.en: I don't know that yet.
context_sentences.ja: それはまだ分からないよ。

context_sentences.en: What, are you still in the bathroom?
context_sentences.ja: え、まだトイレにいるの？

context_sentences.en: If you're looking for Ken, he's still taking a shower.
context_sentences.ja: ケンなら、まだシャワーしてるよ。

data.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how words beginning with こ are close to you? It ends with こ too, which is a clue that we’re talking about a place. So ここ means <vocabulary>here</vocabulary>.

context_sentences.en: Let's eat here!
context_sentences.ja: ここで食べよう！

context_sentences.en: If you're looking for your glasses, they're here.
context_sentences.ja: メガネなら、ここにあるよ。

context_sentences.en: Where am I? Who am I?
context_sentences.ja: ここはどこ？私はだれ？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Oh yah! Two</reading> (おやつ) <vocabulary>snack</vocabulary>s, just for you. Imagine your two snacks. What are they? I bet they're delicious. Oh yah!

おやつ can be anything from candy to cookies to onigiri. Basically, it's anything fairly light that’s eaten between meals.

context_sentences.en: Today I ate a muffin as a snack.
context_sentences.ja: 今日はおやつにマフィンを食べた。

context_sentences.en: Shall we take a snack break?
context_sentences.ja: そろそろおやつにする？

context_sentences.en: Kaori's snacks are always homemade!
context_sentences.ja: カオリちゃんのおやつは、いつも手作りだよ！

data.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how words beginning with ど are often question words, and words ending in こ refer to places? This one's no exception, so どこ means <vocabulary>where</vocabulary>.

context_sentences.en: Where are you going?
context_sentences.ja: どこに行くの？

context_sentences.en: Which McDonald's?
context_sentences.ja: どこのマクドナルド？

context_sentences.en: Where do you come from?
context_sentences.ja: どこから来たの？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Woah, this place is <reading>mossy</reading>, <reading>mossy</reading> (もしもし)! This moss needs clearing up, so you call up the person in charge. <vocabulary>Hello</vocabulary>, says the person on the phone.

もしもし is a <vocabulary>telephone hello</vocabulary>, the standard way to answer the phone in Japan!

context_sentences.en: Hello, this is Yamakawa.
context_sentences.ja: もしもし、山川です。

context_sentences.en: Hello, can you hear me?
context_sentences.ja: もしもし、きこえますか？

context_sentences.en: Hello, what are you doing now?
context_sentences.ja: もしもし、今なにしてるの？

data.meaning_mnemonic: What can be eaten <reading>hot on dough</reading> (ほとんど)? <vocabulary>Most</vocabulary> things can. <vocabulary>Almost all</vocabulary> things, in fact. <vocabulary>Hardly</vocabulary> anything tastes bad when it's hot and served on dough.

context_sentences.en: I've played almost all of the games here.
context_sentences.ja: ここにあるゲーム、ほとんどプレイしたことあるよ。

context_sentences.en: I hardly understand any of this lecture.
context_sentences.ja: このレクチャー、ほとんど分からないんだけど。

context_sentences.en: Most people have smartphones nowadays.
context_sentences.ja: 今どき、スマホなんてほとんどの人がもってるでしょ。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
This comes from the word <vocabulary>glass</vocabulary>, and it refers to the stuff used to make Cinderella's slippers, and windows, in which case it can also mean a <vocabulary>pane of glass</vocabulary>.

We'll learn how to say the other meanings of "glass" later!

context_sentences.en: Is this pen made of glass?
context_sentences.ja: このペン、ガラスで出来てるの？

context_sentences.en: Wow, it looks like Cinderella's glass slipper.
context_sentences.ja: うわー、シンデレラのガラスのくつみたい。

context_sentences.en: You have bird poop on your windshield.
context_sentences.ja: フロントガラスに鳥のフンが付いてるよ。

data.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how words beginning with そ are either close to the person you're talking to, or fairly close to both of you? And how words ending in こ refer to places? This one's no exception. そこ means <vocabulary>there</vocabulary>.

context_sentences.en: I met my teacher there.
context_sentences.ja: そこで先生に会ったよ。

context_sentences.en: If you're looking for snacks, they're there.
context_sentences.ja: おやつなら、そこにあるよ。

context_sentences.en: You don't have to say so much!
context_sentences.ja: そこまで言わなくてもいいじゃない！

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how words beginning with あ show that whatever you're talking about is far away from both you and the person you're talking to? And how words ending in こ refer to places? So what do you think this means? That right, it's <vocabulary>over there</vocabulary>.

Note that even though あそこ means "over there," it's still used to refer to a specific, concrete place, as opposed to a word like 向こう which means "over there" in a broader, more general sense.

context_sentences.en: My house is over there.
context_sentences.ja: 私のうちは、あそこだよ。

context_sentences.en: Let's take a short rest over there!
context_sentences.ja: あそこでちょっと休もう！

context_sentences.en: What's that thing over there?
context_sentences.ja: あそこにあるのは何？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
キロ comes from <vocabulary>kilo</vocabulary>, and it can mean <vocabulary>kilogram</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>kilometer</vocabulary>, or any unit that starts with "kilo" in English.

You can also use abbreviations like "kg" and "km" in Japanese, and they're often just pronounced キロ too.

context_sentences.en: I lost five kilos in one month.
context_sentences.ja: 一ヶ月で五キロやせました。

context_sentences.en: It is roughly 3 km from our house to the school.
context_sentences.ja: うちから学校まで、大体３キロです。

context_sentences.en: This stone sells for only one yen per kilo.
context_sentences.ja: この石は、キロ当たり１円にしかなりません。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
タバコ is the Japanese version of the Portuguese word "tabaco." You probably won’t be shocked to learn that タバコ means <vocabulary>tobacco</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>cigarette</vocabulary> in English!

Watch out for the first syllable, which is タ and not ト. タバコ can also be written in hiragana, and even in kanji, but katakana is the most common by far.

context_sentences.en: Oh, I can smell cigarette smoke.
context_sentences.ja: あ、タバコのにおいがする。

context_sentences.en: I've been struggling to quit smoking.
context_sentences.ja: タバコが中々やめられないんだ。

context_sentences.en: It's not good to smoke while walking.
context_sentences.ja: 歩きタバコはよくないよ。

data.meaning_mnemonic: This is the equivalent of the English word <vocabulary>service</vocabulary>. By extension, it's often used to mean a <vocabulary>freebie</vocabulary>. Though it's generally used as a standard noun, it can also be a verbal noun used with する. In this case, it means <vocabulary>giving a freebie</vocabulary>.

context_sentences.en: The service at that restaurant isn't great, is it?
context_sentences.ja: あのレストランのサービス、ビミョーじゃない？

context_sentences.en: It's on the house.
context_sentences.ja: サービスです。

context_sentences.en: Eh, it's just lip service, isn't it?
context_sentences.ja: えー、ただのリップサービスじゃない？

context_sentences.en: When I bought cream buns, they gave me bread crusts for free.
context_sentences.ja: クリームパン買ったら、パンの耳、サービスしてくれた。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>She cashe</reading>s (しかし) in on everything. <vocabulary>However</vocabulary>, this time you're going to stop her. No more cashing in.

しかし is used at the beginning of a sentence, just like "however." It's pretty formal, and you'll see it much more in written Japanese than spoken Japanese.

context_sentences.en: However, that was a lie.
context_sentences.ja: しかし、それはウソだった。

context_sentences.en: However, it was raining that day.
context_sentences.ja: しかし、その日は雨だった。

context_sentences.en: However, she was found by the queen.
context_sentences.ja: しかし、女王に見つかってしまった。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
パン is the katakana version of the Portuguese word "pão" and means <vocabulary>bread</vocabulary> in English.

If you know the Portuguese, Spanish, or French word for bread, you shouldn't have trouble remembering this word. If not, here's a mnemonic to help you:

You use a <reading>pan</reading> (パン) to make all your <vocabulary>bread</vocabulary>. It's your special bread pan, and all the bread you make with it is delicious.

context_sentences.en: I always eat bread in the mornings.
context_sentences.ja: 朝はいつもパンを食べます。

context_sentences.en: Oh, we're out of bread.
context_sentences.ja: あ、食パン切れてる。

context_sentences.en: It says bread crusts are 100 yen.
context_sentences.ja: パンの耳、百円だって。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Look at this <reading>totem, oh</reading> (とても)! It's <vocabulary>very</vocabulary>, very, very, very lucky, as all totems should be. 

This word has a slightly formal feel to it, and you’ll come across it most in writing.

context_sentences.en: Thank you, I am very happy to hear that.
context_sentences.ja: ありがとう、とてもうれしいです。

context_sentences.en: This is a very precious teddy bear.
context_sentences.ja: これは、とても大切なテディベアなの。

context_sentences.en: That teacher's lecture is very easy to understand.
context_sentences.ja: あの先生のレクチャーはとても分かりやすい。

data.meaning_mnemonic: ビル is the Japanese version of the English word <vocabulary>building</vocabulary>. It usually refers to buildings that are taller than they are wide, most commonly apartment blocks and office buildings.

context_sentences.en: My company is in that office building over there.
context_sentences.ja: うちの会社は、あそこのオフィスビルに入ってるんだよ。

context_sentences.en: I'll call you when I get out of the building.
context_sentences.ja: ビルから出たら、電話するよ。

context_sentences.en: The moon was visible in a gap between the tall buildings.
context_sentences.ja: ビルの谷間に月が見えた。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You've <reading>mow</reading>ed your lawn (もう) <vocabulary>already</vocabulary>? Wow, you're ahead on your mowing. Good work. You'll have to do it again <vocabulary>soon</vocabulary>, though.

This can also mean <vocabulary>yet</vocabulary> in a question, and <vocabulary>anymore</vocabulary> with a negative.

context_sentences.en: I've already seen that anime.
context_sentences.ja: そのアニメ、もう見たよ。

context_sentences.en: I'm almost done!
context_sentences.ja: もうそろそろ終わる！

context_sentences.en: I understand. I won't come here anymore.
context_sentences.ja: 分かった。ここにはもう来ないね。

data.meaning_mnemonic: ワンピース comes from the English word one-piece, but it generally refers to a casual <vocabulary>dress</vocabulary> in Japanese.

context_sentences.en: That dress is so cute!
context_sentences.ja: そのワンピース、めっちゃかわいいね！

context_sentences.en: I bought five dresses at a bargain sale.
context_sentences.ja: バーゲンで、ワンピースを五着も買っちゃった。

context_sentences.en: I spilled coffee on my favorite white dress.
context_sentences.ja: お気に入りの白いワンピースにコーヒーをこぼしてしまった。

data.meaning_mnemonic: マンション comes from the English word "mansion," but it just means an ordinary <vocabulary>apartment building</vocabulary> in Japanese. Depending on context, it can also mean an individual <vocabulary>apartment</vocabulary>. Either way, it’s definitely not a big, luxurious house in Japanese!

context_sentences.en: We can see the fireworks really well from the balcony of my apartment!
context_sentences.ja: うちのマンションのベランダから、花火めっちゃよく見えるよ！

context_sentences.en: Huh, you'd rather live in an apartment than in your own house? Why?
context_sentences.ja: えーっ、マイホームよりマンションに住む方がいいの？なんで？

context_sentences.en: I'm planning to leave this apartment next month.
context_sentences.ja: 私、来月、このマンションを出る予定なんだ。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
オノマトペ comes from the French word “onomatopée” which, as you can probably guess, means <vocabulary>onomatopoeia</vocabulary>.

オノマトペ has a wider meaning than its English equivalent, and it also covers <vocabulary>mimetic word</vocabulary>s, which are words that evoke ideas and actions rather than sounds.

context_sentences.en: This is an onomatopoeia that expresses a sense of softness.
context_sentences.ja: これは、やわらかいイメージを表すオノマトペですね。

context_sentences.en: What is your favorite onomatopoeia and why do you like it?
context_sentences.ja: 好きなオノマトペと、それが好きな理由を教えてください。

context_sentences.en: How do you all learn Japanese onomatopoeias?
context_sentences.ja: 日本語のオノマトペって、みんなどうやって勉強してるの？

data.meaning_mnemonic:
トランプ comes from the English word "trump", as in "a trump card", but it means <vocabulary>deck of cards</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>playing cards</vocabulary> in Japanese.

The Japanese meaning probably comes from card games played by English-speaking Westerners back in the day. Japanese people heard the word "trump" a lot, and assumed it meant a deck of cards.

context_sentences.en: We're going to play poker, so can you go buy some playing cards?

data.meaning_mnemonic:

懐 originally referred to the space between the inner and outer layers of a kimono. As Western-style clothing became standard, it came to mean the inner pocket area around the chest.

Since people often kept money in their 懐, it can figuratively refer to someone's financial capacity, as seen in expressions like 懐が寒い (being short on money). It can also describe a person's capacity to be accepting and tolerant, as in 懐が深い (someone with a "deep heart pocket," meaning they are broad-minded and generous of spirit).

data.meaning_mnemonic:
This word is a combination of 付く (to be attached) and 合う (to suit). You and another person almost seem to be attached at the hip because you suit each other so well, and maybe that's why you chose <vocabulary>to keep company with</vocabulary> each other in the first place.

付き合う is a versatile word for spending time or going along with someone. It's often romantic, like 彼と付き合っている (I'm dating him), but it can be totally neutral too, like 仕事仲間と付き合う (hang out with work friends).

From this, it can also extend to negative situations, like わがままに付き合う (put up with someone's selfishness) or 病気と付き合う (live with an illness). You're "keeping company" with this thing over time — even when it's inconvenient or difficult.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 付く and 合う, so if you remember those, you should be fine here.

真面目 describes someone who takes things seriously and does what's expected of them. It's often used for people who are responsible, hardworking, and sincere, like 真面目な学生 (a serious student).

It's not like the movies where you can cast magic spells just because you're the "chosen one" or something. You've gotta <vocabulary>earnest</vocabulary>ly study your spellbooks and memorize all those enchantments and hexes one by one.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
This word is a combination of お腹 (belly) and 空く (to become empty). When your belly becomes empty, you're going <vocabulary>to get hungry</vocabulary>.

お腹が空く is the most standard expression for saying you're hungry in Japanese. You'll typically use it in the past tense, like お腹が空いた. In conversation, it's common to drop the が, so you'll also hear people say things like お腹空いた！ when they're out with friends or family and want to grab a bite to eat. Note that it's often written in kana, either fully or partly, like お腹がすく.
data.reading_mnemonic:
お腹 uses the reading you learned with the vocabulary, but 空く is actually going to use a new reading here: すく. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

When you start <vocabulary>to get hungry</vocabulary>, you threaten to <reading>sue</reading> (す) the people around you for not feeding you. Some people just get hangry, but you get full-on litigious. You've threatened to sue your friends so many times now that they all habitually carry granola bars and trail mix to keep you from getting even the slightest bit peckish.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how the kanji could also mean <kanji>city</kanji>? Well, that's what the vocab means too: the <vocabulary>city</vocabulary>.

街 refers to the general idea of an <vocabulary>urban area</vocabulary>, rather than a city as an official administrative unit. Compared to 町, it suggests a bigger scale and a busier, more urban feel — places with shops, streets, and activity, like a にぎやかな街 (lively city) or 東京の街を歩く (walk the <vocabulary>city streets</vocabulary> of Tokyo).
data.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it's going to use the kun'yomi reading, which you haven't learned yet. Lucky for you, 街 uses the same reading as another word you know for a place where people live: <reading>町</reading> (まち). Whether you're in a rural town or in the heart of the <vocabulary>city</vocabulary>, there's only one reading you need to remember. Pretty convenient, right?

data.meaning_mnemonic:
When the <kanji>streets</kanji> <kanji>line up</kanji>, they create a <vocabulary>cityscape</vocabulary>.

街並み usually refers to a developed, urban cityscape — imagine rows of buildings and shops with a lively, bustling feel. It can also be used for specific <vocabulary>streetscape</vocabulary>s, often with a distinct atmosphere or some kind of historical or cultural significance, like ヨーロッパの街並み (a European streetscape).

You'll also see it written as 町並み, but this version tends to be used for quieter, more residential townscapes — often with a slightly sleepy, nostalgic vibe.
data.reading_mnemonic: This is a combination of the words 街 and 並, which you've already learned, so you should be able to read this word too. Just be careful with 並, since the み in なみ is sticking out at the end.

The kanji means <kanji>grant</kanji>, but here you're on the receiving end. That's why this verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to be granted</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to receive</vocabulary>.

賜る is a very formal and humble way to talk about being given something. It's used when the speaker wants to place themselves below the giver and show them the utmost respect. You'll see it in things like official speeches, customer service language, or written notices.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Rejoice, for you have been granted a word with an easy reading!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
In the <kanji>streets</kanji>, there's only one kind of <kanji>corner</kanji>: a <vocabulary>street corner</vocabulary>.

街角 literally means a corner where streets meet, as in 街角を曲がる (turn the corner). By extension, it can also refer to <vocabulary>the street</vocabulary> as a public place where everyday city life happens, like 街角でタクシーをひろう (hail a taxi on the street) or 街角の話題 (talk of the town).
data.reading_mnemonic: This word is a combination of the words 街 and 角, so it's actually going to use the kun'yomi readings of both. Just be careful to use the vocab readings rather than the kanji readings and you should be okay here!

data.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>house counter</kanji> <kanji>house</kanji> is a <vocabulary>standalone house</vocabulary>. It's not inside of or attached to anything else — it's a <vocabulary>single-family home</vocabulary>, probably with its own yard and driveway and stuff.

一軒家 is an everyday word that refers to a standalone house, as opposed to an apartment or condo. You'll hear it in real estate, casual conversations about housing, or when describing someone's living situation.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This word is a jukugo word, but it uses a mix of on'yomi and kun'yomi readings. 一 and 軒 use the on'yomi you learned with the kanji, so you should be fine there — just watch out for the いち changing to いっ. 家 uses its kun'yomi や reading, which you've seen with words like 空き家 and 家賃. Here's a mnemonic in case you need help with that one:

Ask most people if they want to live in a <vocabulary>standalone house</vocabulary>, and they'll say "<reading>yah</reading> (や)." No screaming babies next door, no late-night drum solos from the neighbors — yah, it's kind of a no-brainer.

Someone <kanji>grant</kanji>ed you a <kanji>thing</kanji> — woo, you got a <vocabulary>gift</vocabulary>!

賜物 is a formal word for something — often intangible — that you've received as a gift or a blessing. It can carry a nuance of gratitude, like saying something is the <vocabulary>result</vocabulary> of kindness or divine favor, or it can imply something earned through your own sacrifices and hard work — the <vocabulary>fruit</vocabulary> of your labor, in other words.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. 賜 uses a slightly irregular kun'yomi reading in this word, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

People say your sports talent is a divine <vocabulary>gift</vocabulary>, but you know it's <reading>Tama</reading>ra (たま), the local ball girl, who you really have to thank. With her ball girl know-how, Tamara trained you in every sport you know, so your skills are the <vocabulary>result</vocabulary> of her training. Of course, Tamara tells it's all the fruit of your own hard work — what a nice coach she is. Thanks Tamara!

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>peek</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to peek</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to peep at</vocabulary>.

覗く refers to peering or looking into something, often with a sense of curiosity or secrecy. You'll hear it in daily situations like すき間から覗く (to peek through a small gap) or even figuratively, like 様子を覗く (to take a look to see how things are going).
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji. Go back and take a peek at the kanji page again if you forgot!

覗き込む is a more active version of 覗く, meaning "to lean in and look closely into something," often with a sense of earnest intent. Depending on the context, it can also convey a feeling of depth, like you're trying to see beyond just the surface of something.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 覗く and the kanji 込 put together.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 付き合う means "to keep company with," and this is its noun version. When you keep company with someone, you have an <vocabulary>association</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>relationship</vocabulary> with them.

付き合い refers to ongoing interactions or connections with people, like 人付き合い (social relationships) or 長い付き合い (a longstanding association). It can also refer to the obligations that result from such relationships, like 付き合いで飲みに行く (go drinking out of social obligation). You may not want to go, but… society demands it.

You'll also sometimes see it with the honorific お, as in お付き合い — especially when referring to business associations or respectfully talking about romantic relationships.
data.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 付き合う, so if you know that, you should be fine here.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
効く means "to be effective," right? Well, if something is so effective that it can cure your <kanji>eye</kanji> and make you see again, it must have incredible <vocabulary>efficacy</vocabulary>.

効き目 and 効果 both describe something's <vocabulary>effect</vocabulary>, but while 効果 simply refers to the result, 効き目 emphasizes whether it can be felt or seen, particularly with things like medicine or treatments.

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned 原 means "original," but another meaning for it is "field." Combine <kanji>grass</kanji> and <kanji>field</kanji> and you get… a <vocabulary>grass field</vocabulary>!

草原 is for all kinds of grass fields: little local ones, medium-sized <vocabulary>meadow</vocabulary>s, and even vast <vocabulary>grassland</vocabulary>s like the prairie or savanna.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This jukugo word uses on'yomi readings for the kanji. The そう reading for 草 is new for you, so here's a mnemonic:

When you die, you go to a <vocabulary>grass field</vocabulary> full of <reading>sou</reading>ls (そう). Idyllic image of heaven, right? Kind of like the ending scene in Gladiator, except it's not just the main character's soul, it's you and a billion other souls rubbing elbows in a grass field.

Note: The main そうげん reading is used for wide grassy plains and grasslands. The くさはら reading feels smaller and more local, like a patch of tall grass or weeds where kids run around, catch bugs, and occasionally lose a baseball forever.

context_sentences.ja: 草原は広くて静かだから、大体寝落ちして三時間ぐらいワープするか、急に人生について考え始めるかのどっちかになる。

It was common in the Showa era, but today sounds old-fashioned. Occasionally you might still see it used as a title for distinguished women, especially scholars, politicians, writers, and artists.

data.meaning_mnemonic:

Just a side note: The コショウ part can also be written in different ways, such as in kanji, all hiragana, or as コショー, especially on product packaging.

data.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji, which you've already learned. Beware of the little っ stuck in there, and the rendaku magic on 縁 that makes ふち become ぷち. Just imagine chasing after your little <reading>poochie</reading> (ぷち) who just ran off towards the <vocabulary>edge of the cliff</vocabulary>. You catch it, right when it was on the <vocabulary>brink</vocabulary> of sure death. Whew, can't trust poochies to not fall off cliffs when left to their own devices.

context_sentences.en: Standing at the edge of a cliff makes me feel weak in the knees.
context_sentences.ja: 崖っ縁に立つと足がすくむ。

context_sentences.en: I've been pushed to the brink many times, but I've never given up.
context_sentences.ja: 崖っ縁に追い詰められたことは今まで何度もあるけど、一度も諦めたことはないよ。

context_sentences.en: Koichi was an idol when he was younger, but he upset a famous singer and found himself on the brink of losing his position in the entertainment industry.
context_sentences.ja: コウイチは若い頃アイドルだったんだけど、有名歌手を怒らせてしまって、芸能界で崖っ縁に立たされたんだ。

data.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>cut off</kanji> the edge of a <kanji>cliff</kanji>, it creates another that is even steeper and more sheer than the one before — it becomes a <vocabulary>sheer cliff</vocabulary>. This is the kind of <vocabulary>precipice</vocabulary> that looks like it could almost be perpendicular to the ground.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word and uses the on'yomi of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading yet for 崖 though, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

The <vocabulary>sheer cliff</vocabulary> has a <reading>guy</reading> (がい) trying to climb it. The cliff is way too dangerous to climb. As you look more closely, you realize it's your friend, Guy. You yell, "Don't, Guy! That's a 断崖!"

context_sentences.en: These sheer cliffs continue for about another three kilometers.
context_sentences.ja: この断崖はこの先３キロほど続きます。

context_sentences.en: You know Machu Picchu in Peru, the ruins surrounded by sheer cliffs? I'd love to visit it someday.
context_sentences.ja: ペルーにはマチュピチュっていう断崖絶壁に囲まれた遺跡があるでしょう？一度行ってみたいのよね。

context_sentences.en: The resort hotel we stayed at on our honeymoon was built on top of a sheer cliff, so while the views were amazing, it was also quite thrilling.
context_sentences.ja: ハネムーンで泊まったリゾートホテルは断崖の上に建てられていて、眺めが良かった分スリルも味わえました。

auxiliary_meanings.meaning: To Decorate The Edges Of Something
To Form a Border Around Something
To Add A Border To Something

data.meaning_mnemonic:
This word is a combination of 縁 (edge) and 取る (to take). Picture yourself taking the edge of an object and giving it special attention: you're taking that edge in order <vocabulary>to add a border to</vocabulary> it or <vocabulary>to decorate the edges of</vocabulary> it.

This can apply to the edges of all sorts of things, like adding a white border to a photograph (写真を白い枠で縁取る), decorating the edges of a handkerchief with lace (ハンカチをレースで縁取る), or even lining one's eyes with eyeliner (目をアイライナーで縁取る). It can also be used to describe how something happens <vocabulary>to form a border around</vocabulary> something, like trees around a lake (木々が湖を縁取る).
data.reading_mnemonic: This is a combination of the kun'yomi words 縁 (ふち) and 取る (とる), which you've already learned, so you should be able to read this one. Just make sure you remember that とる becomes どる because of rendaku.

context_sentences.en: To outline text, enter your text, then click the "Outline" button.
context_sentences.ja: 文字を縁取るには、テキストを入力した後、「縁取り」ボタンをクリックしてください。

context_sentences.en: I'm thinking of wearing a white dress trimmed with black lace to tomorrow's concert.
context_sentences.ja: 明日のコンサートには、黒いレースで縁取られた白いドレスを着ていこうと思っています。

context_sentences.en: The fallen leaves look as though they're outlining the shape of a person. I wonder if something happened here.
context_sentences.ja: 葉っぱが人の形を縁取るように落ちているけど、ここで何かあったのかな。

data.meaning_mnemonic: When <kanji>snow</kanji> <kanji>crumble</kanji>s down a slope, you have an <vocabulary>avalanche</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This reading is an exception. Let's use this mnemonic to remember it:

If you get stuck under an <vocabulary>avalanche</vocabulary>, <reading>not a ray</reading> (なだれ) of light will reach you. Snow is white, so you might think it's light under there, but nope. Unfortunately, not a single ray of light can penetrate an avalanche, so not only will you be cold, but you'll be stuck in the dark too.

context_sentences.en: Did you see the news about the avalanche this morning?
context_sentences.ja: 今朝の雪崩のニュース、見た？

context_sentences.en: Be careful not to get caught in an avalanche when you go skiing.
context_sentences.ja: スキーに行く時は、雪崩に巻き込まれないように気をつけて。

context_sentences.en: It looks like there was a large avalanche in the mountains of Nagano Prefecture.
context_sentences.ja: 長野県の山で大きな雪崩が起きたみたいです。

data.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 雪崩 is "avalanche" and that the 込 kanji means <kanji>into</kanji>. This word is used figuratively to describe people or things rushing into a place like an avalanche would, so it means <vocabulary>to rush into</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to flood into</vocabulary>. In fact, it's rushing in with such force that the れ slipped out of 雪崩. Whoops.

Note that 雪崩れ込む is often written as なだれ込む, with the first part in kana.
data.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji, so you should be all set. Just be careful with 雪崩, since the れ in なだれ is sticking out of the kanji.

context_sentences.en: As soon as the store opened, a ton of customers rushed in.
context_sentences.ja: 開店と同時に、多くの客が店内に雪崩れ込んだ。

context_sentences.en: Please don't rush toward the exit!
context_sentences.ja: 出口に雪崩れ込まないでください！

context_sentences.en: A few minutes after the earthquake, mud and debris came rushing into the house.
context_sentences.ja: 地震の数分後、土砂が一気に家の中へ雪崩れ込みました。

context_sentences.en: More than 50,000 soldiers from Koichi's army came flooding into Kyoto.
context_sentences.ja: ５万人を超えるコウイチ軍の兵士が京都に雪崩れ込んできた。

data.meaning_mnemonic: You learned that 額 means "amount," but remember that it can also mean "framed picture." A <kanji>framed picture</kanji> is surrounded by <kanji>edge</kanji>s, and this word refers to those edges themselves: the <vocabulary>picture frame</vocabulary> that borders a picture, painting, certificate, and so on.
data.reading_mnemonic: This word consists of the on'yomi reading for 額 and the kun'yomi reading for 縁. You've learned them both so you should be able to read this word too. Just watch out for that rendaku.

context_sentences.en: Of course I put the autograph I got from Ohtani-san in a picture frame right away.
context_sentences.ja: 大谷さんからもらったサイン、もちろんすぐに額縁に入れましたよ。

context_sentences.en: Every day, I wipe the glass of the picture frame while looking at the photo inside.
context_sentences.ja: 毎日、飾ってある写真を見ながら、額縁のガラスを拭いてます。

context_sentences.en: I'd like to use this milk carton as a picture frame, but I can't seem to find a video that shows how to make one.
context_sentences.ja: この牛乳パックを額縁にしたいんだけど、作り方の動画がなかなか見つからないよ。

data.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Eat</kanji>ing <kanji>salt</kanji> is the kind meant for cooking and eating. It's <vocabulary>table salt</vocabulary>.
data.reading_mnemonic:
This word is a jukugo that uses the on'yomi reading for the kanji, but you haven't learned the on'yomi reading for 塩 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Back in the day, you were only allowed to use <vocabulary>table salt</vocabulary> at the <reading>en</reading>d (えん) of the meal. It was precious commodity, so to discourage people from using too much of it you could only use it at the very end of the meal.

context_sentences.en: Apparently, gargling with salt water is good for you.
context_sentences.ja: 食塩水でうがいすると良いらしいよ。

context_sentences.en: You can make your own sports drink with lemon and table salt.
context_sentences.ja: スポーツドリンクはレモンと食塩で手作りできますよ。

context_sentences.en: Ever since Koichi was two years old, he could tell table salt from coffee sugar, and everyone in the village called him a genius.
context_sentences.ja: コウイチは２才のころから食塩とコーヒーシュガーの見分けがつき、村中の人から「天才だ」と言われてました。

data.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>opposite</kanji> <kanji>shore</kanji> is exactly what it sounds like: <vocabulary>the opposite shore</vocabulary>. It's often used to talk about <vocabulary>the other bank</vocabulary> of a river, but it can also mean the other side of a lake, bay, or even the ocean.
data.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. If you know the kanji readings, you should know how to read this too.

context_sentences.en: I could see a large dome on the opposite shore.
context_sentences.ja: 対岸に大きなドームが見えた。

context_sentences.en: That highway runs along the other bank of the river.
context_sentences.ja: その高速道路は川の対岸を走っています。

context_sentences.en: Apparently, the only way to get to the opposite shore is by boat or by swimming.
context_sentences.ja: 対岸にわたるには船に乗るか泳ぐしかないらしい。
